chapters.html:
Executive Summary

This Knowledge Hub is a v0.5 working proposal for how CLM in PWM&FO can develop AI in a controlled and value-creating way. Its purpose is to give stakeholders a shared understanding of the landscape, the practical opportunities, and the capabilities that must be in place before larger decisions are taken.

Working proposition

The opportunity in CLM is real. The harder question is not whether AI can help, but whether each use case is routed through the right platform, connected to the right sources, and governed as an operated service rather than an isolated experiment.

Quick jumps into the deeper sections below:

Use case portfolio Governance & control Idea to production Platform lanes Data architecture Intelligence model

Why CLM / KYC / AML

SEB's AI strategy explicitly points to financial crime prevention and process automation as high-opportunity domains. CLM sits directly in that intersection: KYC and AML are process-heavy, document-heavy, and judgement-heavy workflows where AI can reduce manual burden while strengthening consistency and control when implemented with the right governance model.[4]

Citation markers like [4] jump to Section 13 (References).

The practical opportunity is not autonomous KYC. It is controlled augmentation of FenX-based work: reducing repeated outreach, improving evidence gathering, pre-filling structured data, and giving analysts better prepared starting points for review.

What this v0.5 is meant to clarify

  • Where value is most realistic now — especially in KYC / AML preparation, evidence gathering, and review support.
  • What must be true to scale — product ownership, delivery capacity, governed environments, and reusable patterns.
  • How governance and control should work in practice — clear owners, explicit access boundaries, logging, and human override.
  • Which platform lane fits which use case — M365 and Copilot Studio for shared assistance, Vertex AI / GCP for source-first or deeper governed workloads.
Governance & control in practice

Every production-relevant agent should answer six operational questions clearly: what it does, what data it uses, which permissions it relies on, what outputs it creates, where its logs live, and who can pause or stop it. Broadly shared Copilot-style assistants belong in a governed Copilot Studio lane. Source-first or multi-step work may require a controlled execution lane. Strategy direction does not establish workload or data-class permission.

What this implies for CLM/PWMFO

To capture this opportunity, CLM needs more than tools. It needs sustained product ownership, cross-functional delivery capacity, and a governed execution environment where business, risk, compliance, and engineering can work as one operating system.

The CLM AI Operating Model

This section presents the v0.5 operating model proposal for how CLM can progress AI in a pragmatic and controlled way. It brings together urgency, principles, and governance tiers so stakeholders can evaluate options with shared assumptions and a common vocabulary.

The tiers below govern how much oversight an AI service needs. CLM Intelligence Model (Section 11) describes the underlying layers — Regulatory Engine, Context Graph, Operating Plane, Agentic Execution — that make any tier trustworthy at scale.

The Industry Is Moving — Fast

Generative and agentic AI have matured beyond experimentation. Foundation models now match or exceed task-level human performance across an expanding share of knowledge work. Enterprise deployment platforms from major cloud providers have reached production readiness.[1]

Leading banks are not piloting — they are scaling:

  • BBVA has enabled a team of employees with AI tools, saving an average of three hours per week with 80% daily active usage. They are extending ChatGPT access to 120,000+ employees.[1]
  • JPMorganChase has unified experimentation into a single AI platform serving a team of employees, combining governance, talent investment and Responsible AI practices.[1]
  • Bank of America's AI assistant Erica serves nearly 50 million users and manages 3 billion interactions. Internally, AI tools support nearly 90% of employees.[1]
  • BNY Mellon has integrated AI-powered "digital employees" into existing oversight models, granting them system logins and distinct identities like human teammates under supervision.[1]

KYC & CDD: Among the Highest-Impact Domains

Financial crime compliance alone costs global institutions approximately $200 billion annually.[1] In Accenture's 2025 Banking IT Executives Survey, risk, compliance, and audit ranked as the top priority for AI agent adoption — with 57% expecting broad or fully embedded adoption within three years. KYC, at 56%, was ranked fourth.[1]

Accenture's analysis shows that scaled gen AI adoption over the next three years across the top 200 global banks could: increase revenues by 5%, reduce operating costs by 8%, and cut loan-loss provisions by 16% — a potential $289 billion benefit.[1]

$200BAnnual global KYC/AML cost
57%Expect AI agents in risk/compliance
3hrsSaved weekly per BBVA employee
250KJPMorgan employees on AI platform

The "10× Bank" Concept

Accenture introduces the concept of the "10× bank" — where one person manages a team of AI co-workers to deliver exponentially greater impact. As JPMorganChase's Teresa Heitsenrether framed it: "What would you do if I gave you 10,000 more people at zero cost tomorrow? It's that type of thinking — on scale and parallel capacity — that is going to be possible."[1]

CEO-Sponsored AI Delivers Outsized Returns

Early results show that CEO-sponsored, purpose-driven AI programmes deliver more than 2.5× higher ROI than AI efforts lacking clear vision and leadership support.[1] Already, about a quarter of leading institutions scaling AI report enterprise-level economic gains, achieving profit or EBIT uplifts above 5%.[1]

The Regulatory Window

Regulatory timing creates a specific context for action. The EU AI Act's general provisions are already in force, and the high-risk obligations are now in force as of 2 August 2026. For CLM, the practical implication is immediate: any use case that may influence KYC or CDD judgement should be designed with those obligations in mind from the start.

DateMilestoneCLM Relevance
Dec 2025General provisions in forceProhibited AI practices enforceable. Organisational awareness required.
Aug 2026High-risk obligations in forceAI in creditworthiness and risk assessment classified as high-risk. CLM risk-scoring and CDD tools likely in scope.
OngoingPost-market surveillanceHigh-risk systems require continuous monitoring, incident reporting, periodic conformity assessment.

SEB's internal governance — the AI Classification and Assessment Approach (ACAA) framework — already anticipates much of this through its tiered classification system. Aligning CLM AI adoption with these emerging requirements from the start is substantially less costly than retrofitting compliance later.

Key Insight

Several features of the CLM domain make regulatory navigation possible only with explicit controls and documented review. Much KYC work involves structured data processing against defined criteria — precisely the kind of task where AI systems can be made transparent and auditable. The human-in-the-loop requirement that regulators demand is already a feature of CLM workflows, but the burden of proof still sits with the deployer.

The Compliance-as-Enabler Argument

Consider the alternative: building AI tools without embedded compliance, then submitting them for retroactive approval. This path is slower (rework is always slower than right-work), riskier (regulatory exposure during the gap), and more expensive (rebuild costs exceed build-right costs). The institutions moving fastest in AI are those with the most mature governance frameworks — not despite the frameworks, but because of them.[2]

Reading scope

SensAIa has a reported conditional approval dated 27 August 2024. Closure of the conditions and current operation are not established by the supplied material.

SEB's Existing AI Landscape

SEB is not starting from zero. The organisation has established material foundations that a CLM AI initiative would build upon rather than replace.

🎙️ SensAIa

PWM&FO's own call transcription and summarisation platform. Built on Python / FastAPI / React, deployed on GCP Cloud Run. Already NPAC-approved and operational. Demonstrates the division can conceive, build, approve, and operate AI in production.[5]

📧 Axiom

Email extraction pipeline using RegEx, embedding models, and LLMs. Provides a reference architecture for document processing that maps directly to CLM use cases.[5]

🏪 AI Showroom

Platform enabling internal exploration of AI capabilities, lowering barriers to experimentation across the organisation.[5]

🤖 SEBx Agentic AI

Collaboration with NVIDIA exploring multi-agent architectures using Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK). The Global Market Outlook agent provides a concrete template for the orchestrator pattern.[5]

🧪 AI-Powered Testing

TestPilotX, PerfPilotX, JmeterCopilot — AI-driven quality assurance tools demonstrating SEB's commitment to AI across the development lifecycle.[5]

🔒 Privacy-Preserving AI

SEBx collaboration with KTH on Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning (PML), generating synthetic data for AI training without exposing client information.[5]

Observation

The gap in CLM is not technological — SEB has the cloud platform, the approved models, and working reference implementations. The gap is organisational: a structured framework for deciding what to build, how to govern it, and who owns the outcome.

GCP Model Estate (governance-controlled)

Approved model availability is governed centrally and can change over time. Use the current AI Governance Forum / approved-model register as the source of truth before solution design. The table below is an indicative CLM-oriented view, not a binding allowlist.[6]

ModelPrimary UseCLM Application
Gemini family (approved variants per current register)Reasoning and generationCDD evaluation support, SoW corroboration, narrative drafting support
Approved fast Gemini variant(s)Lower-latency inferenceDocument classification, extraction, routing support
Approved embedding model(s)Semantic retrievalPolicy search, client document retrieval, evidence linking
Approved multilingual capability (where enabled)Cross-language understandingMultilingual document interpretation and comparison

The Nordic Position

Deloitte's March 2026 analysis of agentic AI in CLM identified that while global KYC vendors are consolidating around composable, AI-enabled platforms, Nordic banks generally trail behind the adoption curve.[2]

This creates a dual dynamic:

  • Risk: Being left behind as vendor capabilities advance and competitors gain efficiency advantages.
  • Opportunity: Learning from early movers' mistakes while building on established governance foundations that Nordic banks — with their strong regulatory cultures — already possess.

Deloitte CLM Benchmarks (March 2026)

From institutions piloting agentic AI in KYC:[2]

67%Review time reduction (90→30 min)
65%Onboarding compression (14→5 days)
90%Revisit rate reduction (49%→<5%)

These numbers should be treated as directional indicators, not guaranteed targets. Actual outcomes depend on data quality, process complexity, model performance, and organisational readiness. The honest framing: results in this range are achievable; specific results depend on specific conditions.

KYC Vendor Landscape Trends

  • Vendor consolidation — the market is moving toward composable platforms rather than point solutions
  • AI-native vs. AI-augmented — new entrants are building AI-first, while incumbents are retrofitting; the architectural difference matters
  • Build vs. buy calculus is shifting — the declining cost of building custom AI (especially on platforms like Vertex AI) is making internal development viable for differentiated capabilities
Ownership Before Deployment
01
Ownership Before Deployment
Every AI application has a named human owner before it goes live. No ownerless AI. The owner is accountable for performance, errors, and maintenance.

Ownership is not a formality — it is the single most important control. When something breaks on a Monday morning, there must be a name, not a committee. The owner makes decisions about the application's future: when to retrain, when to kill, when to scale.

This applies at every tier. A Tier 1 meeting summariser has an owner. A Tier 3 risk-scoring agent has an owner. The governance burden differs; the ownership requirement does not.

Practical test: If you cannot name the owner, the application does not go live.

SEB alignment: SEB AI Governance requires named model owners for all registered AI/ML models.[4]

Risk Scales with Actual Exposure
02
Risk Scales with Actual Exposure
Review time and approval depth match the risk level — not the seniority of the requestor. Low-risk tools could potentially move in days, not months.

A tool that summarises meeting notes requires different governance than one that pre-scores client risk. Over-governing low-risk applications kills experimentation; under-governing high-risk applications creates regulatory exposure.

The four-tier governance model in Section 2 operationalises this principle, aligning with SEB's ACAA categories and Model Risk Management tiers — creating a single classification exercise rather than parallel processes.[4]

Goal: Teams can ship productivity tools in days; decision-support agents receive thorough review. Neither fast-tracking dangerous things nor slow-tracking harmless ones.

Anti-pattern: Requiring NPAC approval for an internal meeting summariser. Equally: deploying a client-facing risk tool with only team-level sign-off.

Observable Before Autonomous
03
Observable Before Autonomous
New AI outputs run alongside human decisions before any autonomous logic is enabled. No autonomy until the observation period produces evidence.

Every new AI capability starts in observation mode — its outputs are visible to analysts but do not trigger actions. The AI's suggestions run in parallel with human decisions, building a track record that can be measured, audited, and evaluated.

Only after a defined observation period produces statistically meaningful evidence — accuracy, consistency, edge case handling — can the application move toward greater autonomy, and only with appropriate governance approval for its tier.

Practical implication: Show AI observations alongside human decisions for 30–90 days before asking Risk to approve AI-assisted decisions. Evidence-based promotion, not faith-based deployment.

Regulatory alignment: EU AI Act Article 14 (Human Oversight), SEB AI Ethics Principle 1 (Autonomy — human agency preserved).[4]

Reuse Over Reinvention
04
Reuse Over Reinvention
Every component built — a summariser, a logging wrapper, an approved data pattern — is made available to the next use case. CLM AI Portfolio used to scale throughout the organisation. Build once, reuse broadly.

Compliance reinvention is the hidden tax on AI adoption. Every team that builds its own logging wrapper, its own prompt templates, its own GCP configuration from scratch is paying that tax unnecessarily.

Pre-approved building blocks — approved data access patterns for FenX, legal-reviewed prompt templates, monitoring wrappers, testing harnesses — should be built once and shared via the Builder Council's patterns repository on SEB GitHub Enterprise.

Economics: The marginal cost of the second use case should be dramatically lower than the first. If it isn't, the architecture is wrong.

Practical test: Before building any new component, ask: "Does this already exist somewhere in the CLM AI portfolio or Data & Analytics's toolkit?"

Auditable by Design
05
Auditable by Design
Every application produces outputs that Risk can audit without reading the underlying code. If we cannot explain the decision trail, we do not ship it.

Not "the model weights were trained on these data" but "here is why this output was produced for this specific case." Explainability is not a reporting exercise — it is a design constraint that shapes how applications are built from the start.

SEB's existing commitment to Vertex Explainable AI and SHAP provides tooling; this principle demands consistent application. Every Tier 2+ AI output must be traceable to specific inputs and reasoning steps.[4]

Regulatory alignment: EU AI Act transparency obligations, SEB AI Ethics Requirement 4 (Transparency), GDPR Article 22 (right to explanation).

Design implication: Logging, lineage tracking, and output explanations are not optional add-ons — they are core infrastructure, built before the model, not after.

Adoption Is a Product Problem
06
Adoption Is a Product Problem
An AI tool without colleague adoption creates zero value. Workflow fit, output clarity, and colleague education are as important as the model.

The best model in the world, deployed into a workflow nobody uses, produces nothing. Adoption is not a training problem to solve after launch — it is a product design problem to solve before build.

Every initiative should answer: Who is the user? What is their current workflow? Where does AI fit into that workflow naturally? What does the user need to understand about the output to trust it? How will we measure whether people actually use it?

Practical implication: The portfolio is front-loaded with Tier 1-2 solutions specifically because widespread usage of simple tools builds the cultural and operational foundation for adopting more complex ones. Business Champions participate in design, not just acceptance testing.

Key insight: Adoption is a product problem before a technology problem. Specific knowledge inside SEB creates AI advantages no external consultant can replicate — identify and exploit those.

Reading scope

Governance explanations record source guidance and working interpretations. Confirm current applicability and decision authority for the actual task. This Hub does not assign a formal legal/risk classification or grant approval.

The Four Tiers at a Glance

Scan this table to understand each tier in 30 seconds. The right tier for your use case depends on what the AI does, what data it touches, and who is affected by its output.

Tier Name What It Does Who Approves Speed SEB Alignment
Tier 1 Productivity Assistants Helps individuals work — drafting, summarising, translating. User always reviews output. Team-level + line manager Days ACAA Cat 1
Tier 2 Workflow Automation Automates structured tasks in processes — extraction, classification, pre-population. Human reviews every output. Product Manager / Product Owner + Risk & Compliance review Weeks ACAA Cat 2, MRM Tier 2–3
Tier 3 Decision-Support Agents Provides structured recommendations that directly inform human decisions about clients. Regulatory significance. NPAC + Group Non-Financial Risk + Compliance Months ACAA Cat 3, MRM Tier 1, EU AI Act high-risk
Tier 4 Autonomous Process Agents Executes multi-step processes with limited human intervention. Human oversight at defined checkpoints. NPAC + Group Risk Committee + Divisional Head Quarters ACAA Cat 4, full regulatory engagement
The 80/20 Rule

Target 80% of use cases in Tier 1 and 2. This is deliberate: Tier 1–2 applications move fast, build trust, demonstrate value, and create the organisational muscle for Tier 3. Reserve Risk bandwidth for the applications that truly need it. Many of the highest-value CLM applications sit at Tier 2.

Common Mapping Mistakes

❌ Over-classifying

Treating an internal meeting summariser as Tier 3 because it "uses AI." If the output is reviewed by the user, doesn't touch client-sensitive data, and doesn't inform client decisions — it's Tier 1. Over-classification kills experimentation.

❌ Under-classifying

Calling a client risk pre-scorer "just a tool" to avoid governance. If the output directly shapes how an analyst evaluates a client — it's Tier 3. Under-classification creates regulatory exposure.

❌ Confusing data access with risk

Assuming any system that touches client data is automatically Tier 3. The question is not what data it reads but what decisions it influences. A system that extracts names from documents (Tier 2) is different from one that scores client risk (Tier 3).

The Classification Decision Tree

Start at the top — the highest-risk question — and work down. Stop at the first "Yes." That is your tier. Each card expands for the supporting logic, examples, and governance cue. This ensures you never accidentally under-classify.

Question 4
Question 4
Does the AI execute multi-step processes with limited human intervention? (e.g., end-to-end onboarding orchestration, continuous monitoring with automated escalation) → Tier 4

What this means: The AI operates as an autonomous agent — it chains multiple actions, makes intermediate decisions, and produces outcomes with limited human gates between steps.

Key indicators:

  • System takes actions (not just generates output) across multiple steps
  • Humans only intervene on exceptions or final review, not between steps
  • AI decides what to do next based on prior AI outputs
  • Kill-switch / circuit-breaker mechanism required

CLM examples: Fully automated periodic review processing, autonomous CDD agent that screens, classifies, and routes without human intervention, real-time sanctions monitoring with automated blocking.

Governance: Executive sponsorship, Board Risk Committee awareness, NPAC + Group NFR, red-team testing, continuous monitoring, kill-switch mechanism. Quarters to deploy.

Question 3
Question 3
Does the AI output directly inform human decisions about clients? (e.g., risk scores, SoW corroboration verdicts, EDD trigger recommendations) → Tier 3

What this means: A human makes the final decision, but the AI output materially shapes that decision. The human depends on the AI's assessment to evaluate, score, or treat a client.

Key indicators:

  • AI generates risk scores, classifications, or recommendations about specific clients
  • Output feeds into regulatory-mandated processes (KYC, AML, CDD)
  • Decisions based on AI output have material consequences for clients
  • EU AI Act Art. 13 explainability applies — outputs must be interpretable

CLM examples: KAICY extracting KYC data for CDD risk classification, AI-generated EDD trigger recommendations, client risk scoring models, SoW corroboration assessment.

Governance: NPAC approval, Group NFR sign-off, bias assessment (80% rule), DPIA, NPA via NAMIS, explainability approach (SHAP/LIME), monthly drift monitoring. Months to deploy.

Critical boundary: If a human reviews every output but the AI shapes how they evaluate the client, it's still Tier 3. The question is influence, not autonomy.

Question 2
Question 2
Does the AI automate tasks within a defined business process using client/business data? (e.g., document extraction, case routing, data pre-population) → Tier 2

What this means: The AI performs a defined task using client or business data, but doesn't directly influence how clients are evaluated or treated. A human checks output before any action.

Key indicators:

  • Processes client PII, transaction data, or KYC documents
  • Spot-check or exception-based review (not full review of every output)
  • Output feeds a workflow but doesn't directly drive client decisions
  • EU AI Act Art. 52 transparency applies — users know they interact with AI

CLM examples: AI extracting entity data from corporate PDFs (analyst verifies), automated case note drafting from transcripts, batch data classification, intelligent case routing.

Governance: Model card, ACAA portal, data processing agreement, Risk & Compliance review, quarterly review cadence. Weeks to deploy.

Upgrade risk: If the data includes risk scores or KYC classification data AND the output indirectly shapes client treatment, this escalates to Tier 3. The classifier detects this automatically.

Question 1
Question 1
Does the AI assist individuals with general productivity tasks? (e.g., drafting, summarising, translating, searching — output always reviewed before use) → Tier 1

What this means: The AI helps an individual work faster, but every output is reviewed before use. No client data is processed, and the output doesn't feed business processes or decisions.

Key indicators:

  • Individual user invokes AI manually, reviews all output
  • Processes only public data, policies, or internal operational data
  • No client PII in inputs or outputs
  • Output is used by the same person who generated it

CLM examples: Copilot drafting internal emails, summarising meeting notes, translating policy documents, searching internal knowledge bases, generating presentation drafts.

Governance: Usage guidelines, line manager awareness. No formal risk assessment required. Days to deploy.

Watch out: If the AI starts processing client data (even for drafting), it upgrades to Tier 2. If the drafted content goes to clients without additional human review, reassess.

Worked Examples

The ACAA Classification

Every new AI use case must complete an ACAA Classification (AI Act Classification Assessment) before development begins. The ACAA template follows a four-section structure:[4]

ACAA SectionPurposeKey Questions
Section I — Pre-assessmentDetermine if the system qualifies as AI under the EU AI Act7-element test: inference capability, autonomy level, input types, output types, purpose, adaptiveness, design intent
Section II — Role of OrganisationDetermine SEB's legal roleProvider, Deployer, Importer, or Distributor? (SEB is typically Deployer when using GCP models)
Section III — Risk ClassificationMap to EU AI Act risk levelsPart 1: Screen 7 prohibited practices. Part 2: Assess against high-risk categories (incl. "creditworthiness and establishing a credit score")
Section IV — Result & Sign-offDocument outcome, assign follow-upClassification result, follow-up actions required, sign-off authority

ACAA ↔ Governance Tier Alignment

The ACAA outcome maps directionally to the governance tier model:

ACAA OutcomeEU AI ActGovernance TierAction
Not AI / Minimal riskUnregulatedTier 1Usage guidelines only
AI system, limited riskArt. 52 transparencyTier 2Transparency obligations — users informed they interact with AI
AI system, potentially high-riskAnnex III, Art. 8–15Tier 3Full conformity assessment, DPIA, human oversight design
Prohibited practice identifiedArt. 5 — bannedN/ARedesign or kill the use case

Note: Governance Tier 4 (autonomous agents) is not a separate ACAA category — it represents operational complexity within high-risk classification requiring additional oversight controls.

ACAA Naming Standard

Template title format: "AACA for [System Name]". ID format: YYYYMMDD_division_systemname. Example: 20260501_PWMFO_KAICY. The completed assessment must be stored on the ACAA Classification Portal ↗.

Action

Start your ACAA classification at the ACAA Classification Portal ↗. For questions, contact the AI Governance Forum ↗.

EU AI Act High-Risk Requirements (Art. 9–15)

From 2 August 2026 onward, Tier 3 systems must comply with:[3]

  • Art. 9: Risk management system — identify and mitigate risks throughout the AI lifecycle
  • Art. 10: Data governance — training data must be relevant, representative, free from errors
  • Art. 11: Technical documentation — detailed description of system, purpose, performance
  • Art. 12: Record-keeping — automatic logging of events during operation
  • Art. 13: Transparency — clear information about AI nature and limitations
  • Art. 14: Human oversight — measures enabling effective human intervention
  • Art. 15: Accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity maintained throughout lifecycle

CLM Examples

  • CDD Evaluation Agent — assessing client risk profiles, producing draft risk scores with rationale
  • Source of Wealth corroboration — cross-referencing declared SoW against external data
  • Enhanced Due Diligence trigger analysis
  • Periodic review prioritisation using multiple risk signals

SEB Alignment: ACAA Category 3 (high risk). NPAC mandatory. MRM Tier 1. Subject to EU AI Act high-risk obligations now in force (from 2 August 2026).[3]

Key Internal Documents

📋 Model Risk Instructions

The definitive framework for model risk management at SEB. Covers tiering decision tree, model owner responsibilities, and review requirements.

Risk Instructions & Policies (Intranet) ↗

🤖 AI Risk Instruction

"Instruction for Artificial Intelligence Risks" — SEB Group's primary AI risk document. Mandatory reading before any Tier 2+ deployment.

Developer Garden — Model Risk Mgmt ↗

Central repository documenting intended uses, model mechanics, performance, risks, and training data for all registered models.

Model Cards Repository (GitHub Enterprise) ↗

⚖️ AI Ethics Guide

SEB's 4 principles (autonomy, harm prevention, fairness, explainability) + 7 requirements. Cheat sheet covers general AI, customer-facing, and generative AI.

Developer Garden — AI Ethics ↗

The Model Risk Process

Before any model can be operationalised (Tier 2+):

1. Owner proposes tier
The model owner assesses the use case using the 5-question tiering decision tree (Q1: critical decisions? Q2: legal/regulatory? Q3a: high reliance? Q4: high exposure? Q5: high complexity?) and suggests an appropriate MRM tier.
2. CRO Function approves tier
A Model Risk Manager within the CRO Function reviews and approves the proposed tier. Escalation to GRMC/Model Risk Forum required if: (a) disagreement on tier, or (b) model is assessed as Tier 1.
3. NPAC (if required)
For significant new AI systems, NPAC must formally approve before production. The committee votes across 6 areas: Compliance, Risk, Legal, Security & Cyber, Data Management, and Technology. Approval typically includes conditions to close before launch.
4. Model validation
Tier 1: independent validation by CRO (annual or biennial). Tier 2: validation by model owner every 2 years. Tier 3: validation by model owner every 3 years. All documented in validation report.
5. Ongoing monitoring & inventory
Model registered in EnRiCo (Enterprise Risk Connect). Model owner responsible for continuous monitoring, performance tracking, and annual inventory attestation (deadline: April 30). Contact: modelriskmanagement@seb.se

NPAC Precedent — SensAIa (Approved 27 Aug 2024)

SensAIa — PWM&FO's AI call transcription service — provides the direct precedent for KAICY's NPA process. Key facts from the approval:

DimensionSensAIa ValueKAICY Implication
MRM TierTier 2 (moderate risk)KAICY likely Tier 1b or Tier 2 — depends on reliance level (Q3a) and whether output directly drives client decisions
NAMIS ID018543KAICY will need its own NAMIS entry
Conditions8 conditions across 5 areasExpect similar: DPIA, LIA, client info strategy, model tiering, AI Act Art. 5, risk acceptance, STEP/DSD, maintenance establishment
ValidationEvery 2 years, by model ownerSame cadence likely for KAICY Tier 2; annual CRO validation if Tier 1
Model ownersThree named owners within PWM&FO Data OfficeKAICY needs named owners before submission
Practical Insight

SensAIa was approved with conditions — meaning you can get approval before all conditions are closed, as long as they are closed before launch. This is the normal pattern: submit, get conditional approval, close conditions in parallel with final build. Do not wait until everything is perfect to submit.

The SEB AI Operating Model — Division–Hub Contract

SEB's AI operating model (per Way-to-Engage ↗) defines a three-body structure. Understanding CLM's position within it is essential:

BodyOwnsProvides
AI Hub (Central)Strategy, governance, reference architectureStrategic direction, central guardrails, shared tools & platforms
Divisions (CLM sits here)Use-case identification, business value, adoption & changeBusiness problems, outcome ownership, governance/risk for non-trivial solutions
Technology AreasEnd-to-end delivery, lifecycle ownershipEngineering execution, platform operations
⚠️ Critical Boundary

Divisions own business value and change. The AI Hub does NOT own divisional adoption, prioritization, or business value realization. If CLM waits for the AI Hub to prioritize CLM use cases, we are violating the operating model — that responsibility sits with us.

Tool Selection Rule

SEB's official guidance: "Start in M365 Copilot → Scale in Copilot Studio → Engineer in Vertex AI." Divisions are expected to choose the simplest sufficient tool. Moving right increases lifecycle management, governance burden, and AI expertise requirements.

PersonaToolGovernance OwnerCLM Lane
Business UserM365 CopilotHandled centrally (lowest division burden)Fast Lane
Citizen DeveloperPower Platform (Copilot Studio, AI Builder, Power Automate)Division drives governance & risk assessment, AACA for AI featuresPower Lane
AI ExpertVertex AI on GCPDivision must own full risk (highest burden)Governed Lane
Strategic Advice

Make Risk your co-author, not your gatekeeper. Bring Risk and Compliance into the design phase for Tier 2 and 3. Ask them: "What does the output need to look like for you to approve it?" Then build to that spec. This converts months of back-and-forth into a single design conversation.

Enterprise AI Strategy Alignment

CLM’s AI approach is not standalone — it implements SEB’s enterprise AI & Automation sub-strategy.[23] The strategy positions AI as “a native capability across the bank, embedded in how we work, design products, build systems, operate processes, and meet customer expectations.” CLM maps directly to the three strategic pillars:

SEB ICT Strategy PillarCLM Alignment
Human + AI Interactions
Secure, explainable, human-aligned machine-to-machine interactions		Client conversation → structured KYC data with evidence traceability. Human always in the loop for consequential decisions.
Domain-Specific Accuracy & Sovereign AI
Small domain-specific models, RAG, proprietary data/terminology		FenX data policy ontology + call transcripts as proprietary RAG corpus. Domain accuracy > generic fluency.
Observability & Control
Orchestration layers with auditability and policy enforcement		BigQuery tracing, override rate monitoring, compliance metrics, human escalation gates.

SEB’s five-phase transformation path places CLM initiatives in Phase 3 (CRM / Process & Data) — dependent on core and infrastructure foundations already delivered.

The Three-Track Speed Framework

Speed and compliance are not opposites — they are achieved by routing initiatives through the appropriate governance track based on risk, not treating all AI the same:

🟢 Fast Lane — Tier 1 Tools

Platform: M365 Copilot, Copilot Studio (Custom Agents environment)

Governance: Self-governed under Change Risk Management (1st line). No NPAC needed.

Timeline: Days to weeks, not months.

Examples: Meeting summaries, policy Q&A agents, report drafting, internal knowledge search, document templates.

Principle: Build many, build fast, learn rapidly. Governance is lightweight because risk is low. These tools build AI literacy and trust across the organisation.

⚡ Power Lane — Tier 1–2 Solutions

Platform: Power Platform (Dedicated environments for C4 data)

Governance: AACA for AI Builder/Copilot Studio. Model risk assessment for custom models. Dedicated env request.

Timeline: Weeks. Faster than GCP because low-code, but requires environment provisioning.

Examples: Document field extraction (AI Builder), FenX data integration (Power Automate + HTTP), KYC Copilot agent with client data (Copilot Studio in Dedicated), review alerting, CLM dashboards, approval workflows.

Principle: The business builder’s production path. Power Platform bridges the gap between Copilot productivity tools and full GCP engineering. CLM analysts and process owners can build and own these — no engineering dependency.

⚠️ Governed Lane — Tier 2–3 Systems

Platform: Vertex AI on GCP

Governance: Full 6-pillar AI Risk Assessment, model tiering, NPAC for significant changes.

Timeline: Months — but accelerated by SensAIa precedent and parallel execution.

Examples: KYC data extraction from transcripts (KAICY), SoW corroboration, CDD evaluation, multi-agent orchestration, agentic workflows.

Principle: Move deliberately. Proportionate rigour. Each governance step has a known owner, contact, and timeline. Pre-clear governance while building — submit early with conditions.

The three lanes are not a hierarchy to climb — they are parallel tracks for different types of work. A CLM analyst shipping a policy Q&A agent in the Fast Lane does not compete with engineering building KAICY in the Governed Lane. They run simultaneously. The Fast Lane builds AI literacy and trust. The Power Lane delivers operational tooling. The Governed Lane solves the hard problems. All three create value.

NPA Reform — Institutional Tailwind

The Change Risk Management reform (autumn 2026) is an explicit institutional mandate to reduce time-to-market:

  • 1st-line ownership of change risk — business areas (not committees) own day-to-day risk assessment for non-significant changes
  • NPA reserved for significant changes only — 2nd-line independent oversight applies only when genuinely material
  • Unnecessary committee layers eliminated — the reform explicitly targets bureaucratic overhead
  • Non-financial risk milestones embedded into development — risk is designed in, not reviewed at the end

For CLM AI: Tier 1 tools bypass NPA entirely. Tier 2–3 systems still require NPAC but with clearer criteria, faster process, and fewer layers. The SensAIa precedent (same committee, same stakeholders) further compresses cycle time.

“This strengthens risk ownership in the business and creates better conditions for effective control.” — CRO

⚠️ Anti-Pattern Warning

From SEB’s own enterprise operating model: “Creating a small AI team inside the division, centralising all ideas into it, and claiming alignment — this violates the hub-and-spoke model.”

The correct pattern: Division owns business value and change. The AI Hub owns central strategy, architecture, and platforms. A “mini-hub” inside CLM that duplicates what the enterprise AI Hub already provides is organisational waste. CLM should consume what the Hub offers and focus energy on what only CLM can provide: domain knowledge, use case identification, adoption, and business value realisation.

Key Insight

The tier model is not a hierarchy to climb — it is a classification system to navigate. The instinct to reach for Tier 3–4 "impressive" applications before mastering Tier 1–2 is the most common AI adoption failure pattern. Start where governance is light, impact is real, and trust is built.

The SEB AI Operating Model — Division–Hub Contract

panels.model-context:
The Industry Is Moving — Fast

Generative and agentic AI have matured beyond experimentation. Foundation models now match or exceed task-level human performance across an expanding share of knowledge work. Enterprise deployment platforms from major cloud providers have reached production readiness.[1]

Leading banks are not piloting — they are scaling:

  • BBVA has enabled a team of employees with AI tools, saving an average of three hours per week with 80% daily active usage. They are extending ChatGPT access to 120,000+ employees.[1]
  • JPMorganChase has unified experimentation into a single AI platform serving a team of employees, combining governance, talent investment and Responsible AI practices.[1]
  • Bank of America's AI assistant Erica serves nearly 50 million users and manages 3 billion interactions. Internally, AI tools support nearly 90% of employees.[1]
  • BNY Mellon has integrated AI-powered "digital employees" into existing oversight models, granting them system logins and distinct identities like human teammates under supervision.[1]

KYC & CDD: Among the Highest-Impact Domains

Financial crime compliance alone costs global institutions approximately $200 billion annually.[1] In Accenture's 2025 Banking IT Executives Survey, risk, compliance, and audit ranked as the top priority for AI agent adoption — with 57% expecting broad or fully embedded adoption within three years. KYC, at 56%, was ranked fourth.[1]

Accenture's analysis shows that scaled gen AI adoption over the next three years across the top 200 global banks could: increase revenues by 5%, reduce operating costs by 8%, and cut loan-loss provisions by 16% — a potential $289 billion benefit.[1]

$200BAnnual global KYC/AML cost
57%Expect AI agents in risk/compliance
3hrsSaved weekly per BBVA employee
250KJPMorgan employees on AI platform

The "10× Bank" Concept

Accenture introduces the concept of the "10× bank" — where one person manages a team of AI co-workers to deliver exponentially greater impact. As JPMorganChase's Teresa Heitsenrether framed it: "What would you do if I gave you 10,000 more people at zero cost tomorrow? It's that type of thinking — on scale and parallel capacity — that is going to be possible."[1]

CEO-Sponsored AI Delivers Outsized Returns

Early results show that CEO-sponsored, purpose-driven AI programmes deliver more than 2.5× higher ROI than AI efforts lacking clear vision and leadership support.[1] Already, about a quarter of leading institutions scaling AI report enterprise-level economic gains, achieving profit or EBIT uplifts above 5%.[1]

The Regulatory Window

Regulatory timing creates a specific context for action. The EU AI Act's general provisions are already in force, and the high-risk obligations are now in force as of 2 August 2026. For CLM, the practical implication is immediate: any use case that may influence KYC or CDD judgement should be designed with those obligations in mind from the start.

DateMilestoneCLM Relevance
Dec 2025General provisions in forceProhibited AI practices enforceable. Organisational awareness required.
Aug 2026High-risk obligations in forceAI in creditworthiness and risk assessment classified as high-risk. CLM risk-scoring and CDD tools likely in scope.
OngoingPost-market surveillanceHigh-risk systems require continuous monitoring, incident reporting, periodic conformity assessment.

SEB's internal governance — the AI Classification and Assessment Approach (ACAA) framework — already anticipates much of this through its tiered classification system. Aligning CLM AI adoption with these emerging requirements from the start is substantially less costly than retrofitting compliance later.

Key Insight

Several features of the CLM domain make regulatory navigation possible only with explicit controls and documented review. Much KYC work involves structured data processing against defined criteria — precisely the kind of task where AI systems can be made transparent and auditable. The human-in-the-loop requirement that regulators demand is already a feature of CLM workflows, but the burden of proof still sits with the deployer.

The Compliance-as-Enabler Argument

Consider the alternative: building AI tools without embedded compliance, then submitting them for retroactive approval. This path is slower (rework is always slower than right-work), riskier (regulatory exposure during the gap), and more expensive (rebuild costs exceed build-right costs). The institutions moving fastest in AI are those with the most mature governance frameworks — not despite the frameworks, but because of them.[2]

Reading scope

SensAIa has a reported conditional approval dated 27 August 2024. Closure of the conditions and current operation are not established by the supplied material.

SEB's Existing AI Landscape

SEB is not starting from zero. The organisation has established material foundations that a CLM AI initiative would build upon rather than replace.

🎙️ SensAIa

PWM&FO's own call transcription and summarisation platform. Built on Python / FastAPI / React, deployed on GCP Cloud Run. Already NPAC-approved and operational. Demonstrates the division can conceive, build, approve, and operate AI in production.[5]

📧 Axiom

Email extraction pipeline using RegEx, embedding models, and LLMs. Provides a reference architecture for document processing that maps directly to CLM use cases.[5]

🏪 AI Showroom

Platform enabling internal exploration of AI capabilities, lowering barriers to experimentation across the organisation.[5]

🤖 SEBx Agentic AI

Collaboration with NVIDIA exploring multi-agent architectures using Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK). The Global Market Outlook agent provides a concrete template for the orchestrator pattern.[5]

🧪 AI-Powered Testing

TestPilotX, PerfPilotX, JmeterCopilot — AI-driven quality assurance tools demonstrating SEB's commitment to AI across the development lifecycle.[5]

🔒 Privacy-Preserving AI

SEBx collaboration with KTH on Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning (PML), generating synthetic data for AI training without exposing client information.[5]

Observation

The gap in CLM is not technological — SEB has the cloud platform, the approved models, and working reference implementations. The gap is organisational: a structured framework for deciding what to build, how to govern it, and who owns the outcome.

GCP Model Estate (governance-controlled)

Approved model availability is governed centrally and can change over time. Use the current AI Governance Forum / approved-model register as the source of truth before solution design. The table below is an indicative CLM-oriented view, not a binding allowlist.[6]

ModelPrimary UseCLM Application
Gemini family (approved variants per current register)Reasoning and generationCDD evaluation support, SoW corroboration, narrative drafting support
Approved fast Gemini variant(s)Lower-latency inferenceDocument classification, extraction, routing support
Approved embedding model(s)Semantic retrievalPolicy search, client document retrieval, evidence linking
Approved multilingual capability (where enabled)Cross-language understandingMultilingual document interpretation and comparison

The Nordic Position

Deloitte's March 2026 analysis of agentic AI in CLM identified that while global KYC vendors are consolidating around composable, AI-enabled platforms, Nordic banks generally trail behind the adoption curve.[2]

This creates a dual dynamic:

  • Risk: Being left behind as vendor capabilities advance and competitors gain efficiency advantages.
  • Opportunity: Learning from early movers' mistakes while building on established governance foundations that Nordic banks — with their strong regulatory cultures — already possess.

Deloitte CLM Benchmarks (March 2026)

From institutions piloting agentic AI in KYC:[2]

67%Review time reduction (90→30 min)
65%Onboarding compression (14→5 days)
90%Revisit rate reduction (49%→<5%)

These numbers should be treated as directional indicators, not guaranteed targets. Actual outcomes depend on data quality, process complexity, model performance, and organisational readiness. The honest framing: results in this range are achievable; specific results depend on specific conditions.

KYC Vendor Landscape Trends

  • Vendor consolidation — the market is moving toward composable platforms rather than point solutions
  • AI-native vs. AI-augmented — new entrants are building AI-first, while incumbents are retrofitting; the architectural difference matters
  • Build vs. buy calculus is shifting — the declining cost of building custom AI (especially on platforms like Vertex AI) is making internal development viable for differentiated capabilities
panels.model-principles:
Ownership Before Deployment
01
Ownership Before Deployment
Every AI application has a named human owner before it goes live. No ownerless AI. The owner is accountable for performance, errors, and maintenance.

Ownership is not a formality — it is the single most important control. When something breaks on a Monday morning, there must be a name, not a committee. The owner makes decisions about the application's future: when to retrain, when to kill, when to scale.

This applies at every tier. A Tier 1 meeting summariser has an owner. A Tier 3 risk-scoring agent has an owner. The governance burden differs; the ownership requirement does not.

Practical test: If you cannot name the owner, the application does not go live.

SEB alignment: SEB AI Governance requires named model owners for all registered AI/ML models.[4]

Risk Scales with Actual Exposure
02
Risk Scales with Actual Exposure
Review time and approval depth match the risk level — not the seniority of the requestor. Low-risk tools could potentially move in days, not months.

A tool that summarises meeting notes requires different governance than one that pre-scores client risk. Over-governing low-risk applications kills experimentation; under-governing high-risk applications creates regulatory exposure.

The four-tier governance model in Section 2 operationalises this principle, aligning with SEB's ACAA categories and Model Risk Management tiers — creating a single classification exercise rather than parallel processes.[4]

Goal: Teams can ship productivity tools in days; decision-support agents receive thorough review. Neither fast-tracking dangerous things nor slow-tracking harmless ones.

Anti-pattern: Requiring NPAC approval for an internal meeting summariser. Equally: deploying a client-facing risk tool with only team-level sign-off.

Observable Before Autonomous
03
Observable Before Autonomous
New AI outputs run alongside human decisions before any autonomous logic is enabled. No autonomy until the observation period produces evidence.

Every new AI capability starts in observation mode — its outputs are visible to analysts but do not trigger actions. The AI's suggestions run in parallel with human decisions, building a track record that can be measured, audited, and evaluated.

Only after a defined observation period produces statistically meaningful evidence — accuracy, consistency, edge case handling — can the application move toward greater autonomy, and only with appropriate governance approval for its tier.

Practical implication: Show AI observations alongside human decisions for 30–90 days before asking Risk to approve AI-assisted decisions. Evidence-based promotion, not faith-based deployment.

Regulatory alignment: EU AI Act Article 14 (Human Oversight), SEB AI Ethics Principle 1 (Autonomy — human agency preserved).[4]

Reuse Over Reinvention
04
Reuse Over Reinvention
Every component built — a summariser, a logging wrapper, an approved data pattern — is made available to the next use case. CLM AI Portfolio used to scale throughout the organisation. Build once, reuse broadly.

Compliance reinvention is the hidden tax on AI adoption. Every team that builds its own logging wrapper, its own prompt templates, its own GCP configuration from scratch is paying that tax unnecessarily.

Pre-approved building blocks — approved data access patterns for FenX, legal-reviewed prompt templates, monitoring wrappers, testing harnesses — should be built once and shared via the Builder Council's patterns repository on SEB GitHub Enterprise.

Economics: The marginal cost of the second use case should be dramatically lower than the first. If it isn't, the architecture is wrong.

Practical test: Before building any new component, ask: "Does this already exist somewhere in the CLM AI portfolio or Data & Analytics's toolkit?"

Auditable by Design
05
Auditable by Design
Every application produces outputs that Risk can audit without reading the underlying code. If we cannot explain the decision trail, we do not ship it.

Not "the model weights were trained on these data" but "here is why this output was produced for this specific case." Explainability is not a reporting exercise — it is a design constraint that shapes how applications are built from the start.

SEB's existing commitment to Vertex Explainable AI and SHAP provides tooling; this principle demands consistent application. Every Tier 2+ AI output must be traceable to specific inputs and reasoning steps.[4]

Regulatory alignment: EU AI Act transparency obligations, SEB AI Ethics Requirement 4 (Transparency), GDPR Article 22 (right to explanation).

Design implication: Logging, lineage tracking, and output explanations are not optional add-ons — they are core infrastructure, built before the model, not after.

Adoption Is a Product Problem
06
Adoption Is a Product Problem
An AI tool without colleague adoption creates zero value. Workflow fit, output clarity, and colleague education are as important as the model.

The best model in the world, deployed into a workflow nobody uses, produces nothing. Adoption is not a training problem to solve after launch — it is a product design problem to solve before build.

Every initiative should answer: Who is the user? What is their current workflow? Where does AI fit into that workflow naturally? What does the user need to understand about the output to trust it? How will we measure whether people actually use it?

Practical implication: The portfolio is front-loaded with Tier 1-2 solutions specifically because widespread usage of simple tools builds the cultural and operational foundation for adopting more complex ones. Business Champions participate in design, not just acceptance testing.

Key insight: Adoption is a product problem before a technology problem. Specific knowledge inside SEB creates AI advantages no external consultant can replicate — identify and exploit those.
panels.model-tiers:
Reading scope

Governance explanations record source guidance and working interpretations. Confirm current applicability and decision authority for the actual task. This Hub does not assign a formal legal/risk classification or grant approval.

The Four Tiers at a Glance

Scan this table to understand each tier in 30 seconds. The right tier for your use case depends on what the AI does, what data it touches, and who is affected by its output.

Tier Name What It Does Who Approves Speed SEB Alignment
Tier 1 Productivity Assistants Helps individuals work — drafting, summarising, translating. User always reviews output. Team-level + line manager Days ACAA Cat 1
Tier 2 Workflow Automation Automates structured tasks in processes — extraction, classification, pre-population. Human reviews every output. Product Manager / Product Owner + Risk & Compliance review Weeks ACAA Cat 2, MRM Tier 2–3
Tier 3 Decision-Support Agents Provides structured recommendations that directly inform human decisions about clients. Regulatory significance. NPAC + Group Non-Financial Risk + Compliance Months ACAA Cat 3, MRM Tier 1, EU AI Act high-risk
Tier 4 Autonomous Process Agents Executes multi-step processes with limited human intervention. Human oversight at defined checkpoints. NPAC + Group Risk Committee + Divisional Head Quarters ACAA Cat 4, full regulatory engagement
The 80/20 Rule

Target 80% of use cases in Tier 1 and 2. This is deliberate: Tier 1–2 applications move fast, build trust, demonstrate value, and create the organisational muscle for Tier 3. Reserve Risk bandwidth for the applications that truly need it. Many of the highest-value CLM applications sit at Tier 2.

Common Mapping Mistakes

❌ Over-classifying

Treating an internal meeting summariser as Tier 3 because it "uses AI." If the output is reviewed by the user, doesn't touch client-sensitive data, and doesn't inform client decisions — it's Tier 1. Over-classification kills experimentation.

❌ Under-classifying

Calling a client risk pre-scorer "just a tool" to avoid governance. If the output directly shapes how an analyst evaluates a client — it's Tier 3. Under-classification creates regulatory exposure.

❌ Confusing data access with risk

Assuming any system that touches client data is automatically Tier 3. The question is not what data it reads but what decisions it influences. A system that extracts names from documents (Tier 2) is different from one that scores client risk (Tier 3).
panels.model-classify:
The Classification Decision Tree

Start at the top — the highest-risk question — and work down. Stop at the first "Yes." That is your tier. Each card expands for the supporting logic, examples, and governance cue. This ensures you never accidentally under-classify.

Question 4
Question 4
Does the AI execute multi-step processes with limited human intervention? (e.g., end-to-end onboarding orchestration, continuous monitoring with automated escalation) → Tier 4

What this means: The AI operates as an autonomous agent — it chains multiple actions, makes intermediate decisions, and produces outcomes with limited human gates between steps.

Key indicators:

  • System takes actions (not just generates output) across multiple steps
  • Humans only intervene on exceptions or final review, not between steps
  • AI decides what to do next based on prior AI outputs
  • Kill-switch / circuit-breaker mechanism required

CLM examples: Fully automated periodic review processing, autonomous CDD agent that screens, classifies, and routes without human intervention, real-time sanctions monitoring with automated blocking.

Governance: Executive sponsorship, Board Risk Committee awareness, NPAC + Group NFR, red-team testing, continuous monitoring, kill-switch mechanism. Quarters to deploy.

Question 3
Question 3
Does the AI output directly inform human decisions about clients? (e.g., risk scores, SoW corroboration verdicts, EDD trigger recommendations) → Tier 3

What this means: A human makes the final decision, but the AI output materially shapes that decision. The human depends on the AI's assessment to evaluate, score, or treat a client.

Key indicators:

  • AI generates risk scores, classifications, or recommendations about specific clients
  • Output feeds into regulatory-mandated processes (KYC, AML, CDD)
  • Decisions based on AI output have material consequences for clients
  • EU AI Act Art. 13 explainability applies — outputs must be interpretable

CLM examples: KAICY extracting KYC data for CDD risk classification, AI-generated EDD trigger recommendations, client risk scoring models, SoW corroboration assessment.

Governance: NPAC approval, Group NFR sign-off, bias assessment (80% rule), DPIA, NPA via NAMIS, explainability approach (SHAP/LIME), monthly drift monitoring. Months to deploy.

Critical boundary: If a human reviews every output but the AI shapes how they evaluate the client, it's still Tier 3. The question is influence, not autonomy.

Question 2
Question 2
Does the AI automate tasks within a defined business process using client/business data? (e.g., document extraction, case routing, data pre-population) → Tier 2

What this means: The AI performs a defined task using client or business data, but doesn't directly influence how clients are evaluated or treated. A human checks output before any action.

Key indicators:

  • Processes client PII, transaction data, or KYC documents
  • Spot-check or exception-based review (not full review of every output)
  • Output feeds a workflow but doesn't directly drive client decisions
  • EU AI Act Art. 52 transparency applies — users know they interact with AI

CLM examples: AI extracting entity data from corporate PDFs (analyst verifies), automated case note drafting from transcripts, batch data classification, intelligent case routing.

Governance: Model card, ACAA portal, data processing agreement, Risk & Compliance review, quarterly review cadence. Weeks to deploy.

Upgrade risk: If the data includes risk scores or KYC classification data AND the output indirectly shapes client treatment, this escalates to Tier 3. The classifier detects this automatically.

Question 1
Question 1
Does the AI assist individuals with general productivity tasks? (e.g., drafting, summarising, translating, searching — output always reviewed before use) → Tier 1

What this means: The AI helps an individual work faster, but every output is reviewed before use. No client data is processed, and the output doesn't feed business processes or decisions.

Key indicators:

  • Individual user invokes AI manually, reviews all output
  • Processes only public data, policies, or internal operational data
  • No client PII in inputs or outputs
  • Output is used by the same person who generated it

CLM examples: Copilot drafting internal emails, summarising meeting notes, translating policy documents, searching internal knowledge bases, generating presentation drafts.

Governance: Usage guidelines, line manager awareness. No formal risk assessment required. Days to deploy.

Watch out: If the AI starts processing client data (even for drafting), it upgrades to Tier 2. If the drafted content goes to clients without additional human review, reassess.

Worked Examples

Apply the decision tree to real CLM scenarios:

Items marked Click to expand contain detailed guidance.

"We want Copilot to help analysts draft internal case notes"
"We want Copilot to help analysts draft internal case notes"

Q4: Multi-step autonomous process? No.
Q3: Output informs client decisions? No — internal notes, analyst reviews before saving.
Q2: Automates business process with client data? No — assists individual drafting.
Q1: General productivity? Yes.

→ Tier 1 — Usage guidelines, line manager awareness. Days to deploy.

"We want AI to extract entity data from corporate registration PDFs"
"We want AI to extract entity data from corporate registration PDFs"

Q4: Multi-step autonomous? No.
Q3: Informs client decisions? No — extracts data, analyst verifies every extraction.
Q2: Automates structured task with business data? Yes.

→ Tier 2 — Model card, data classification, quarterly review. Product owner + Risk review. Weeks to deploy.

"We want AI to pre-score client risk and recommend CDD classifications"
"We want AI to pre-score client risk and recommend CDD classifications"

Q4: Multi-step autonomous? No — analyst makes final decision.
Q3: Output directly informs client decisions? Yes — the risk score materially shapes how the analyst evaluates the client.

→ Tier 3 — Full model registration, NPAC approval, Group Non-Financial Risk sign-off, bias assessment, explainability (SHAP), drift detection. Months to deploy.

"We want an agent to run end-to-end periodic reviews with human gates"
"We want an agent to run end-to-end periodic reviews with human gates"

Q4: Multi-step process with limited human intervention? Yes — orchestrator coordinates document collection, data verification, risk scoring, narrative generation, with human approval at defined checkpoints.

→ Tier 4 — Everything in Tier 3 plus executive sponsorship, Board Risk Committee awareness, real-time monitoring, kill switches, red-team testing. Quarters to deploy.

The ACAA Classification

Every new AI use case must complete an ACAA Classification (AI Act Classification Assessment) before development begins. The ACAA template follows a four-section structure:[4]

ACAA SectionPurposeKey Questions
Section I — Pre-assessmentDetermine if the system qualifies as AI under the EU AI Act7-element test: inference capability, autonomy level, input types, output types, purpose, adaptiveness, design intent
Section II — Role of OrganisationDetermine SEB's legal roleProvider, Deployer, Importer, or Distributor? (SEB is typically Deployer when using GCP models)
Section III — Risk ClassificationMap to EU AI Act risk levelsPart 1: Screen 7 prohibited practices. Part 2: Assess against high-risk categories (incl. "creditworthiness and establishing a credit score")
Section IV — Result & Sign-offDocument outcome, assign follow-upClassification result, follow-up actions required, sign-off authority

ACAA ↔ Governance Tier Alignment

The ACAA outcome maps directionally to the governance tier model:

ACAA OutcomeEU AI ActGovernance TierAction
Not AI / Minimal riskUnregulatedTier 1Usage guidelines only
AI system, limited riskArt. 52 transparencyTier 2Transparency obligations — users informed they interact with AI
AI system, potentially high-riskAnnex III, Art. 8–15Tier 3Full conformity assessment, DPIA, human oversight design
Prohibited practice identifiedArt. 5 — bannedN/ARedesign or kill the use case

Note: Governance Tier 4 (autonomous agents) is not a separate ACAA category — it represents operational complexity within high-risk classification requiring additional oversight controls.

ACAA Naming Standard

Template title format: "AACA for [System Name]". ID format: YYYYMMDD_division_systemname. Example: 20260501_PWMFO_KAICY. The completed assessment must be stored on the ACAA Classification Portal ↗.

Action

Start your ACAA classification at the ACAA Classification Portal ↗. For questions, contact the AI Governance Forum ↗.

SEB Governance Bodies & Key Documents

Understanding who approves what is essential for moving applications through governance efficiently. Here is the complete map:[4]

Governance Bodies

Key Internal Documents

Risk Instructions & Policies (Intranet) ↗

The Model Risk Process

Before any model can be operationalised (Tier 2+):

1. Owner proposes tier
The model owner assesses the use case using the 5-question tiering decision tree (Q1: critical decisions? Q2: legal/regulatory? Q3a: high reliance? Q4: high exposure? Q5: high complexity?) and suggests an appropriate MRM tier.
2. CRO Function approves tier
A Model Risk Manager within the CRO Function reviews and approves the proposed tier. Escalation to GRMC/Model Risk Forum required if: (a) disagreement on tier, or (b) model is assessed as Tier 1.
3. NPAC (if required)
For significant new AI systems, NPAC must formally approve before production. The committee votes across 6 areas: Compliance, Risk, Legal, Security & Cyber, Data Management, and Technology. Approval typically includes conditions to close before launch.
4. Model validation
Tier 1: independent validation by CRO (annual or biennial). Tier 2: validation by model owner every 2 years. Tier 3: validation by model owner every 3 years. All documented in validation report.
5. Ongoing monitoring & inventory
Model registered in EnRiCo (Enterprise Risk Connect). Model owner responsible for continuous monitoring, performance tracking, and annual inventory attestation (deadline: April 30). Contact: modelriskmanagement@seb.se

NPAC Precedent — SensAIa (Approved 27 Aug 2024)

SensAIa — PWM&FO's AI call transcription service — provides the direct precedent for KAICY's NPA process. Key facts from the approval:

DimensionSensAIa ValueKAICY Implication
MRM TierTier 2 (moderate risk)KAICY likely Tier 1b or Tier 2 — depends on reliance level (Q3a) and whether output directly drives client decisions
NAMIS ID018543KAICY will need its own NAMIS entry
Conditions8 conditions across 5 areasExpect similar: DPIA, LIA, client info strategy, model tiering, AI Act Art. 5, risk acceptance, STEP/DSD, maintenance establishment
ValidationEvery 2 years, by model ownerSame cadence likely for KAICY Tier 2; annual CRO validation if Tier 1
Model ownersThree named owners within PWM&FO Data OfficeKAICY needs named owners before submission
Practical Insight

SensAIa was approved with conditions — meaning you can get approval before all conditions are closed, as long as they are closed before launch. This is the normal pattern: submit, get conditional approval, close conditions in parallel with final build. Do not wait until everything is perfect to submit.

The SEB AI Operating Model — Division–Hub Contract

SEB's AI operating model (per Way-to-Engage ↗) defines a three-body structure. Understanding CLM's position within it is essential:

BodyOwnsProvides
AI Hub (Central)Strategy, governance, reference architectureStrategic direction, central guardrails, shared tools & platforms
Divisions (CLM sits here)Use-case identification, business value, adoption & changeBusiness problems, outcome ownership, governance/risk for non-trivial solutions
Technology AreasEnd-to-end delivery, lifecycle ownershipEngineering execution, platform operations
⚠️ Critical Boundary

Divisions own business value and change. The AI Hub does NOT own divisional adoption, prioritization, or business value realization. If CLM waits for the AI Hub to prioritize CLM use cases, we are violating the operating model — that responsibility sits with us.

Tool Selection Rule

SEB's official guidance: "Start in M365 Copilot → Scale in Copilot Studio → Engineer in Vertex AI." Divisions are expected to choose the simplest sufficient tool. Moving right increases lifecycle management, governance burden, and AI expertise requirements.

PersonaToolGovernance OwnerCLM Lane
Business UserM365 CopilotHandled centrally (lowest division burden)Fast Lane
Citizen DeveloperPower Platform (Copilot Studio, AI Builder, Power Automate)Division drives governance & risk assessment, AACA for AI featuresPower Lane
AI ExpertVertex AI on GCPDivision must own full risk (highest burden)Governed Lane
Strategic Advice

Make Risk your co-author, not your gatekeeper. Bring Risk and Compliance into the design phase for Tier 2 and 3. Ask them: "What does the output need to look like for you to approve it?" Then build to that spec. This converts months of back-and-forth into a single design conversation.

Enterprise AI Strategy Alignment

CLM’s AI approach is not standalone — it implements SEB’s enterprise AI & Automation sub-strategy.[23] The strategy positions AI as “a native capability across the bank, embedded in how we work, design products, build systems, operate processes, and meet customer expectations.” CLM maps directly to the three strategic pillars:

SEB ICT Strategy PillarCLM Alignment
Human + AI Interactions
Secure, explainable, human-aligned machine-to-machine interactions		Client conversation → structured KYC data with evidence traceability. Human always in the loop for consequential decisions.
Domain-Specific Accuracy & Sovereign AI
Small domain-specific models, RAG, proprietary data/terminology		FenX data policy ontology + call transcripts as proprietary RAG corpus. Domain accuracy > generic fluency.
Observability & Control
Orchestration layers with auditability and policy enforcement		BigQuery tracing, override rate monitoring, compliance metrics, human escalation gates.

SEB’s five-phase transformation path places CLM initiatives in Phase 3 (CRM / Process & Data) — dependent on core and infrastructure foundations already delivered.

The Three-Track Speed Framework

Speed and compliance are not opposites — they are achieved by routing initiatives through the appropriate governance track based on risk, not treating all AI the same:

🟢 Fast Lane — Tier 1 Tools

Platform: M365 Copilot, Copilot Studio (Custom Agents environment)

Governance: Self-governed under Change Risk Management (1st line). No NPAC needed.

Timeline: Days to weeks, not months.

Examples: Meeting summaries, policy Q&A agents, report drafting, internal knowledge search, document templates.

Principle: Build many, build fast, learn rapidly. Governance is lightweight because risk is low. These tools build AI literacy and trust across the organisation.

⚡ Power Lane — Tier 1–2 Solutions

Platform: Power Platform (Dedicated environments for C4 data)

Governance: AACA for AI Builder/Copilot Studio. Model risk assessment for custom models. Dedicated env request.

Timeline: Weeks. Faster than GCP because low-code, but requires environment provisioning.

Examples: Document field extraction (AI Builder), FenX data integration (Power Automate + HTTP), KYC Copilot agent with client data (Copilot Studio in Dedicated), review alerting, CLM dashboards, approval workflows.

Principle: The business builder’s production path. Power Platform bridges the gap between Copilot productivity tools and full GCP engineering. CLM analysts and process owners can build and own these — no engineering dependency.

⚠️ Governed Lane — Tier 2–3 Systems

Platform: Vertex AI on GCP

Governance: Full 6-pillar AI Risk Assessment, model tiering, NPAC for significant changes.

Timeline: Months — but accelerated by SensAIa precedent and parallel execution.

Examples: KYC data extraction from transcripts (KAICY), SoW corroboration, CDD evaluation, multi-agent orchestration, agentic workflows.

Principle: Move deliberately. Proportionate rigour. Each governance step has a known owner, contact, and timeline. Pre-clear governance while building — submit early with conditions.

The three lanes are not a hierarchy to climb — they are parallel tracks for different types of work. A CLM analyst shipping a policy Q&A agent in the Fast Lane does not compete with engineering building KAICY in the Governed Lane. They run simultaneously. The Fast Lane builds AI literacy and trust. The Power Lane delivers operational tooling. The Governed Lane solves the hard problems. All three create value.

NPA Reform — Institutional Tailwind

The Change Risk Management reform (autumn 2026) is an explicit institutional mandate to reduce time-to-market:

  • 1st-line ownership of change risk — business areas (not committees) own day-to-day risk assessment for non-significant changes
  • NPA reserved for significant changes only — 2nd-line independent oversight applies only when genuinely material
  • Unnecessary committee layers eliminated — the reform explicitly targets bureaucratic overhead
  • Non-financial risk milestones embedded into development — risk is designed in, not reviewed at the end

For CLM AI: Tier 1 tools bypass NPA entirely. Tier 2–3 systems still require NPAC but with clearer criteria, faster process, and fewer layers. The SensAIa precedent (same committee, same stakeholders) further compresses cycle time.

“This strengthens risk ownership in the business and creates better conditions for effective control.” — CRO

⚠️ Anti-Pattern Warning

From SEB’s own enterprise operating model: “Creating a small AI team inside the division, centralising all ideas into it, and claiming alignment — this violates the hub-and-spoke model.”

The correct pattern: Division owns business value and change. The AI Hub owns central strategy, architecture, and platforms. A “mini-hub” inside CLM that duplicates what the enterprise AI Hub already provides is organisational waste. CLM should consume what the Hub offers and focus energy on what only CLM can provide: domain knowledge, use case identification, adoption, and business value realisation.
panels.ctx-industry:
The Industry Is Moving — Fast

Generative and agentic AI have matured beyond experimentation. Foundation models now match or exceed task-level human performance across an expanding share of knowledge work. Enterprise deployment platforms from major cloud providers have reached production readiness.[1]

Leading banks are not piloting — they are scaling:

  • BBVA has enabled a team of employees with AI tools, saving an average of three hours per week with 80% daily active usage. They are extending ChatGPT access to 120,000+ employees.[1]
  • JPMorganChase has unified experimentation into a single AI platform serving a team of employees, combining governance, talent investment and Responsible AI practices.[1]
  • Bank of America's AI assistant Erica serves nearly 50 million users and manages 3 billion interactions. Internally, AI tools support nearly 90% of employees.[1]
  • BNY Mellon has integrated AI-powered "digital employees" into existing oversight models, granting them system logins and distinct identities like human teammates under supervision.[1]

KYC & CDD: Among the Highest-Impact Domains

Financial crime compliance alone costs global institutions approximately $200 billion annually.[1] In Accenture's 2025 Banking IT Executives Survey, risk, compliance, and audit ranked as the top priority for AI agent adoption — with 57% expecting broad or fully embedded adoption within three years. KYC, at 56%, was ranked fourth.[1]

Accenture's analysis shows that scaled gen AI adoption over the next three years across the top 200 global banks could: increase revenues by 5%, reduce operating costs by 8%, and cut loan-loss provisions by 16% — a potential $289 billion benefit.[1]

$200BAnnual global KYC/AML cost
57%Expect AI agents in risk/compliance
3hrsSaved weekly per BBVA employee
250KJPMorgan employees on AI platform

The "10× Bank" Concept

Accenture introduces the concept of the "10× bank" — where one person manages a team of AI co-workers to deliver exponentially greater impact. As JPMorganChase's Teresa Heitsenrether framed it: "What would you do if I gave you 10,000 more people at zero cost tomorrow? It's that type of thinking — on scale and parallel capacity — that is going to be possible."[1]

CEO-Sponsored AI Delivers Outsized Returns

Early results show that CEO-sponsored, purpose-driven AI programmes deliver more than 2.5× higher ROI than AI efforts lacking clear vision and leadership support.[1] Already, about a quarter of leading institutions scaling AI report enterprise-level economic gains, achieving profit or EBIT uplifts above 5%.[1]
panels.ctx-regulatory:
The Regulatory Window

Regulatory timing creates a specific context for action. The EU AI Act's general provisions are already in force, and the high-risk obligations are now in force as of 2 August 2026. For CLM, the practical implication is immediate: any use case that may influence KYC or CDD judgement should be designed with those obligations in mind from the start.

DateMilestoneCLM Relevance
Dec 2025General provisions in forceProhibited AI practices enforceable. Organisational awareness required.
Aug 2026High-risk obligations in forceAI in creditworthiness and risk assessment classified as high-risk. CLM risk-scoring and CDD tools likely in scope.
OngoingPost-market surveillanceHigh-risk systems require continuous monitoring, incident reporting, periodic conformity assessment.

SEB's internal governance — the AI Classification and Assessment Approach (ACAA) framework — already anticipates much of this through its tiered classification system. Aligning CLM AI adoption with these emerging requirements from the start is substantially less costly than retrofitting compliance later.

Key Insight

Several features of the CLM domain make regulatory navigation possible only with explicit controls and documented review. Much KYC work involves structured data processing against defined criteria — precisely the kind of task where AI systems can be made transparent and auditable. The human-in-the-loop requirement that regulators demand is already a feature of CLM workflows, but the burden of proof still sits with the deployer.

The Compliance-as-Enabler Argument

Consider the alternative: building AI tools without embedded compliance, then submitting them for retroactive approval. This path is slower (rework is always slower than right-work), riskier (regulatory exposure during the gap), and more expensive (rebuild costs exceed build-right costs). The institutions moving fastest in AI are those with the most mature governance frameworks — not despite the frameworks, but because of them.[2]
