panels.ctx-nordic:
The Nordic Position

Deloitte's March 2026 analysis of agentic AI in CLM identified that while global KYC vendors are consolidating around composable, AI-enabled platforms, Nordic banks generally trail behind the adoption curve.[2]

This creates a dual dynamic:

  • Risk: Being left behind as vendor capabilities advance and competitors gain efficiency advantages.
  • Opportunity: Learning from early movers' mistakes while building on established governance foundations that Nordic banks — with their strong regulatory cultures — already possess.

Deloitte CLM Benchmarks (March 2026)

From institutions piloting agentic AI in KYC:[2]

67%Review time reduction (90→30 min)
65%Onboarding compression (14→5 days)
90%Revisit rate reduction (49%→<5%)

These numbers should be treated as directional indicators, not guaranteed targets. Actual outcomes depend on data quality, process complexity, model performance, and organisational readiness. The honest framing: results in this range are achievable; specific results depend on specific conditions.

KYC Vendor Landscape Trends

  • Vendor consolidation — the market is moving toward composable platforms rather than point solutions
  • AI-native vs. AI-augmented — new entrants are building AI-first, while incumbents are retrofitting; the architectural difference matters
  • Build vs. buy calculus is shifting — the declining cost of building custom AI (especially on platforms like Vertex AI) is making internal development viable for differentiated capabilities

chapters.title: Culture & People
chapters.html:
Culture & People

AI adoption is not primarily a technology problem — it is a people problem. The culture that surrounds AI determines whether tools get used or gather dust, and the roles people play determine whether capability is built or outsourced. This section covers both.

The Bureaucracy Trap

Regulated industries face a specific risk: responding to every new technology with more process, more approvals, more documentation. When this instinct dominates, the result is bureaucratic paralysis — the theoretical ability to adopt AI exists but practical barriers make it nearly impossible.

Symptoms: multi-month approvals for low-risk tools, documentation exceeding solution complexity, governance bodies with growing backlogs, a pervasive sense that "it's easier to just do it manually."

The tier model is explicitly designed to counter this. Tier 1-2 creates a "fast lane" for low-risk initiatives while maintaining rigour for Tier 3-4.

What "Culture of Usage" Looks Like

  • Analysts routinely use AI as naturally as email or spreadsheets
  • Ideas flow upward — practitioners are the primary source of use case ideas
  • Feedback is continuous — deployed tools are actively improved, not left static
  • Learning is celebrated — discovering a prototype didn't work (and why) is as valued as shipping a success
  • Metrics focus on outcomes — review cycle time, completeness rates, satisfaction — not number of tools deployed

Practical Enablers

🧪 Sandbox Environment

Dedicated space where CLM practitioners experiment with approved models against anonymised/synthetic data. No governance overhead. Builds intuition for what AI can and cannot do.

📢 Weekly "Show and Tell"

30-minute recurring session. Anyone demonstrates something built, tried, or learned. No slides required. Format: "I tried this → here's what happened → here's what I learned."

📚 AI Literacy Programme

All CLM team members — not just builders. Goal: sufficient mental model of what AI does, what it's good and bad at, and how to evaluate outputs critically. Reduces both fear and over-trust.

🏆 Early Wins, Visible Impact

Portfolio front-loaded with high-adoption, low-risk Tier 1 tools. Widespread usage of simple tools builds the cultural foundation for more complex adoption.

Industry Evidence on AI Adoption

Consulting firms consistently find that AI adoption is a people and operating model problem, not a technology problem. Key findings from April 2026:

🔄 Peer-to-Peer Beats Top-Down

“Peer influence and existing delegation habits — rather than mandates from the top — drive real AI use.”

Implication: Focus on champion users and visible results. Let adoption spread organically. Management mandates create compliance, not usage.

Source: BCG, April 2026

🧬 Organisational Metabolism

“Companies must go beyond adoption to continuously absorb new technologies and translate them into value. Organisational metabolism will define AI leaders.”

Implication: The goal is not one successful deployment — it is building the muscle to continuously absorb new AI capabilities as they emerge.

Source: BCG, April 2026

⚠️ AI-Labelled Reorgs Underperform

“AI-focused organisational changes underperform other reorganisations. AI transformation success depends on redesigning how people work, not deploying new technology.”

Implication: Don’t create “AI departments.” Don’t label it “AI transformation.” Embed AI capability into existing workflows and structures.

Source: Bain, April 2026

📐 You Can’t Scale What You Can’t Govern

“You can’t scale what you can’t govern — and you can’t govern what you can’t structure. Trust and data quality are the foundation for agentic AI at scale.”

Implication: Governance infrastructure (tier classification, monitoring, audit trails) must be built before ambitious deployments, not after.

Source: Bain, April 2026

🎯 Impactful Adoption Starts at the Top

“Leaders must champion AI adoption for all employees so that everyone — not just engineers — can build with AI.”

Implication: AI literacy is a leadership responsibility. When leaders visibly use AI tools and champion experiments, permission propagates downward.

Source: BCG, April 2026

🏥 AI Won’t Fix Broken Processes

“AI capabilities improve quickly but realising value depends on how fundamentally organisations rethink delivery.”

Implication: Applying AI to a bad process amplifies the badness, faster. Fix the process first, then AI accelerates the improved version.

Source: BCG, April 2026

The Builder Council

A recurring, lightweight forum for all designated builders within CLM — engineers, technically skilled analysts, and selected non-technical staff who create AI tools. Not a governance body. Not a steering committee. A practitioner community for the people chosen to build.

Purpose

  • Cross-pollination — builders working on different tools share patterns, libraries, and hard-won lessons ("this GCP configuration works; this one doesn't")
  • Quality through peer review — code reviews, architecture discussions, and shared standards emerge organically from practitioners, not from top-down mandates
  • Ownership culture — reinforces the principle that the builder owns the application. The Council is where owners help each other maintain that ownership effectively
  • Onboarding accelerator — new builders inherit institutional knowledge faster through direct contact with experienced practitioners
  • Feedback loop to product — builders surface technical constraints, feasibility assessments, and improvement ideas directly to the product function

Format

🔄 Bi-Weekly Sync (30 min)

What's shipping, what's stuck, what's learned. No slides. Screen-sharing encouraged. Format: round-table status + one deeper technical topic per session.

📋 Shared Patterns Repository

A living collection on SEB GitHub Enterprise: approved prompt templates, GCP deployment configs, monitoring setups, testing patterns. Build once, reuse many times — avoiding repeated compliance reinvention.

🔍 Peer Architecture Reviews

Before any Tier 2+ tool enters build phase, a lightweight peer review within the Council. Not governance — practical: "have you considered X? We hit this issue on Y."

🤝 Data & Analytics Liaison

One Council member serves as primary liaison with Data & Analytics — consolidating platform requests, sharing learnings bi-directionally, ensuring CLM builders are aware of new platform capabilities.

Key Distinction

The Builder Council is not another approval gate. It has no veto power. It exists to make builders better at their craft and to create the connective tissue between independently owned applications. The moment it becomes bureaucratic, it has failed its purpose.

"About half of bank employees say they lack adequate training or clear accountability when AI makes errors, revealing capability and governance gaps. Employees are enthusiastic — the barriers are about preparedness, not willingness." — Accenture Banking Top Trends 2026[1]
Reading scope

SensAIa has a reported conditional approval dated 27 August 2024. Closure of the conditions and current operation are not established by the supplied material.

Five Role Groups

🎯
Product & Strategy

Owns the "what" and "why." Maintains the use case backlog, drives prioritisation, defines success metrics, ensures alignment between AI initiatives and CLM objectives. Translates between business needs and technical possibilities. Manages the portfolio view — ensuring individual initiatives contribute to a coherent whole.

💡
Business Champions

Subject matter experts from within CLM — KYC analysts, CDD reviewers, onboarding specialists, relationship managers. The people who know workflows intimately, who can tell you in five minutes whether a prototype is useful. They participate in ideation, provide feedback during prototyping, validate production outputs, and serve as peer advocates during rollout. Their role is active co-design, not passive receipt.

🔧
Builders

Selected CLM members who make things work — software engineers, data engineers, ML engineers, and designated non-technical staff with the curiosity and domain knowledge to create AI tools using low-code platforms. Not everyone builds; builders are specifically chosen and supported. A hybrid model is proposed:

  • Core internal capability — a small permanent team that prototypes quickly, builds Tier 1-2 independently, and serves as technical interlocutor for Tier 3-4 work
  • Collaborative capacity — partnership with Data & Analytics for infrastructure, platform, and complex model development
  • Domain advantage — internal builders carry CLM domain knowledge that external teams cannot replicate, enabling faster iteration and more relevant solutions

SensAI and KAICY demonstrate this model in practice: both built by Bain, deployed on GCP, with SEB taking over ownership and operation. SensAI is NPAC-reported in the source; current operation is not established. KAICY is developed and undergoing NPAC. Together they show that the division can build and operate production AI when the operating model is right.[5]

🛡️
Risk & Compliance Partners

Not gatekeepers — partners. Present from ideation, not summoned at deployment. When a use case is scoped, compliance informs tier classification. When a prototype is built, compliance review ensures regulatory alignment is designed in. The relevant SEB bodies: AI Governance Forum, Data Protection Officer (DPOR), Group Non-Financial Risk.[4]

☁️
Technology Platform Partners

Teams owning infrastructure: GCP platform services, Vertex AI, IAM, security. Not part of CLM but essential collaborators. The relationship should be structured around service agreements — what CLM needs from the platform, what the platform needs from CLM — rather than ad hoc requests.[7]

The "Builder" Ethos

The most successful AI-adopting organisations share a trait: they cultivate builders — people who default to making something work rather than writing about why it might work. This is distinct from "move fast and break things." Builders in a regulated environment are disciplined: they prototype within guardrails, test before they ship, document what they build. But they bias toward measured action with evidence.

Cultivating this within CLM means:

  • Creating space — designated time, sandbox environments, psychological permission to try and fail
  • Celebrating learning — a prototype that revealed the problem was different than expected is as valuable as a successful deployment
  • Reducing distance — when elapsed time from "what if…" to "let me show you" is days, not months, the organisation learns faster
  • Recognising all contributions — the analyst who identified the bottleneck is as important as the engineer who built the solution

headings.title: 📐 You Can’t Scale What You Can’t Govern
🎯 Impactful Adoption Starts at the Top

panels.people-culture:
The Bureaucracy Trap

Regulated industries face a specific risk: responding to every new technology with more process, more approvals, more documentation. When this instinct dominates, the result is bureaucratic paralysis — the theoretical ability to adopt AI exists but practical barriers make it nearly impossible.

Symptoms: multi-month approvals for low-risk tools, documentation exceeding solution complexity, governance bodies with growing backlogs, a pervasive sense that "it's easier to just do it manually."

The tier model is explicitly designed to counter this. Tier 1-2 creates a "fast lane" for low-risk initiatives while maintaining rigour for Tier 3-4.

What "Culture of Usage" Looks Like

  • Analysts routinely use AI as naturally as email or spreadsheets
  • Ideas flow upward — practitioners are the primary source of use case ideas
  • Feedback is continuous — deployed tools are actively improved, not left static
  • Learning is celebrated — discovering a prototype didn't work (and why) is as valued as shipping a success
  • Metrics focus on outcomes — review cycle time, completeness rates, satisfaction — not number of tools deployed

Practical Enablers

🧪 Sandbox Environment

Dedicated space where CLM practitioners experiment with approved models against anonymised/synthetic data. No governance overhead. Builds intuition for what AI can and cannot do.

📢 Weekly "Show and Tell"

30-minute recurring session. Anyone demonstrates something built, tried, or learned. No slides required. Format: "I tried this → here's what happened → here's what I learned."

📚 AI Literacy Programme

All CLM team members — not just builders. Goal: sufficient mental model of what AI does, what it's good and bad at, and how to evaluate outputs critically. Reduces both fear and over-trust.

🏆 Early Wins, Visible Impact

Portfolio front-loaded with high-adoption, low-risk Tier 1 tools. Widespread usage of simple tools builds the cultural foundation for more complex adoption.

Industry Evidence on AI Adoption

Consulting firms consistently find that AI adoption is a people and operating model problem, not a technology problem. Key findings from April 2026:

🔄 Peer-to-Peer Beats Top-Down

“Peer influence and existing delegation habits — rather than mandates from the top — drive real AI use.”

Implication: Focus on champion users and visible results. Let adoption spread organically. Management mandates create compliance, not usage.

Source: BCG, April 2026

🧬 Organisational Metabolism

“Companies must go beyond adoption to continuously absorb new technologies and translate them into value. Organisational metabolism will define AI leaders.”

Implication: The goal is not one successful deployment — it is building the muscle to continuously absorb new AI capabilities as they emerge.

Source: BCG, April 2026

⚠️ AI-Labelled Reorgs Underperform

“AI-focused organisational changes underperform other reorganisations. AI transformation success depends on redesigning how people work, not deploying new technology.”

Implication: Don’t create “AI departments.” Don’t label it “AI transformation.” Embed AI capability into existing workflows and structures.

Source: Bain, April 2026

📐 You Can’t Scale What You Can’t Govern

“You can’t scale what you can’t govern — and you can’t govern what you can’t structure. Trust and data quality are the foundation for agentic AI at scale.”

Implication: Governance infrastructure (tier classification, monitoring, audit trails) must be built before ambitious deployments, not after.

Source: Bain, April 2026

🎯 Impactful Adoption Starts at the Top

“Leaders must champion AI adoption for all employees so that everyone — not just engineers — can build with AI.”

Implication: AI literacy is a leadership responsibility. When leaders visibly use AI tools and champion experiments, permission propagates downward.

Source: BCG, April 2026

🏥 AI Won’t Fix Broken Processes

“AI capabilities improve quickly but realising value depends on how fundamentally organisations rethink delivery.”

Implication: Applying AI to a bad process amplifies the badness, faster. Fix the process first, then AI accelerates the improved version.

Source: BCG, April 2026

The Builder Council

A recurring, lightweight forum for all designated builders within CLM — engineers, technically skilled analysts, and selected non-technical staff who create AI tools. Not a governance body. Not a steering committee. A practitioner community for the people chosen to build.

Purpose

  • Cross-pollination — builders working on different tools share patterns, libraries, and hard-won lessons ("this GCP configuration works; this one doesn't")
  • Quality through peer review — code reviews, architecture discussions, and shared standards emerge organically from practitioners, not from top-down mandates
  • Ownership culture — reinforces the principle that the builder owns the application. The Council is where owners help each other maintain that ownership effectively
  • Onboarding accelerator — new builders inherit institutional knowledge faster through direct contact with experienced practitioners
  • Feedback loop to product — builders surface technical constraints, feasibility assessments, and improvement ideas directly to the product function

Format

🔄 Bi-Weekly Sync (30 min)

What's shipping, what's stuck, what's learned. No slides. Screen-sharing encouraged. Format: round-table status + one deeper technical topic per session.

📋 Shared Patterns Repository

A living collection on SEB GitHub Enterprise: approved prompt templates, GCP deployment configs, monitoring setups, testing patterns. Build once, reuse many times — avoiding repeated compliance reinvention.

🔍 Peer Architecture Reviews

Before any Tier 2+ tool enters build phase, a lightweight peer review within the Council. Not governance — practical: "have you considered X? We hit this issue on Y."

🤝 Data & Analytics Liaison

One Council member serves as primary liaison with Data & Analytics — consolidating platform requests, sharing learnings bi-directionally, ensuring CLM builders are aware of new platform capabilities.

Key Distinction

The Builder Council is not another approval gate. It has no veto power. It exists to make builders better at their craft and to create the connective tissue between independently owned applications. The moment it becomes bureaucratic, it has failed its purpose.

chapters.title: From Idea to Production — The Use Case Lifecycle
chapters.html:
From Idea to Production — The Use Case Lifecycle

Every AI initiative in CLM follows the same journey — from a rough idea to a monitored production system. The stages are the same whether you are building an AI application or an AI agent. What changes is the depth of governance and the environment lane selected for delivery. Click each stage below.

Inspect a stage and its proposed responsibilities. This route does not grant approval.

Ideation — Capturing Use Cases

Anyone in CLM can surface an idea — analysts, compliance officers, team leads, operations staff. You do not need technical skills. The only requirement is a real pain point.

How We Capture Use Cases

Ideas are submitted through a simple, low-friction template — not a business case, not a slide deck. The point is to lower the bar so good ideas don't get lost in process. Submit via the shared backlog (Teams channel, form, or direct to the Product Manager).

The Idea Template

FieldWhat to WriteExample
What is painful today?Describe the task, how often, and how long it takes"I spend 2 hours per periodic review copying data between FenX and the review template."
What would help?What would the AI ideally do?"An AI that pre-fills the template from FenX data."
Who would use it?How many people, which teams?"All 15 analysts in my team, potentially 60+ across CLM."
How often?Daily, weekly, per review?"Every periodic review — roughly 8–12 times per analyst per week."

How Ideas Are Prioritised

The Product Manager triages all incoming ideas against four criteria:

Impact
How many people benefit? How much time or risk is reduced? A tool used daily by 60 analysts ranks higher than one used monthly by 5.
Feasibility
Can this be built with approved tools and available data? Does the data exist, and is it accessible? Low feasibility = park or re-scope.
Governance fit
What tier does this fall into? Tier 1–2 ideas that deliver quick wins are prioritised early to build momentum and trust.
Strategic alignment
Does it advance CLM's core priorities — onboarding quality, review efficiency, compliance automation, or data completeness?

Connection to the Portfolio

Prioritised ideas feed directly into the AI Portfolio (Section 8). The portfolio is not a separate wish list — it is the accumulated output of this ideation and prioritisation process. Ideas that pass Gate 1 become portfolio items with a tier classification, an owner, and a target horizon:

  • Horizon 1 — Can start now with existing tools and data
  • Horizon 2 — Requires a dependency (e.g., FenX go-live, new data source)
  • Horizon 3 — Exploratory — needs research or external capability

The Product Manager's Role

The Product Manager is the connective tissue across the entire lifecycle. At the ideation stage, they:

  • Curate the backlog — group related ideas, spot duplicates, identify patterns across teams
  • Triage and prioritise — apply the four criteria above, recommend what to scope next
  • Maintain visibility — ensure the backlog is transparent so anyone can see what's been submitted, what's in progress, and what's been parked (and why)
  • Bridge teams — someone in Stockholm may have already solved what Luxembourg is struggling with. The PM connects these dots.
  • Protect focus — say no to ideas that don't fit, or defer them with a clear rationale

CLM Examples of Past Ideas

  • "Can AI summarise my client meeting notes into a structured CRM entry?" → Became a Tier 1 Copilot agent
  • "Can we auto-check SoW documents against declared income?" → Scoped as Tier 3 (KAICY)
  • "Can we extract KYC data from client call transcripts?" → Scoped as Tier 2–3 (KAICY)

Output: One-paragraph idea in the shared backlog. No slides, no business case yet.

Scoping

The product function and a builder assess the idea together. The goal is to answer four questions quickly — not to produce a 30-page document:

  1. Governance tier — Does this touch client data? Influence decisions? The answer determines the governance path (see Section 5).
  2. Technical feasibility — Can this be built with SEB-approved models (Gemini, Copilot) and existing infrastructure? What data sources are needed?
  3. Effort & impact — Days or months? How many people benefit?
  4. Environment lane — Where should it run to ensure control and visibility? M365 for personal assistance, Copilot Studio/Power Platform for shared business workflows, or Vertex AI/GCP for source-first regulated orchestration.

Tier Quick Reference

TierTypical CLM Use CaseScoping TimeWho Scopes
Tier 1Meeting summariser, policy Q&A bot, data formatter1–2 daysDesignated builder + product
Tier 2CDD pre-population, document extraction, report drafting3–5 daysProduct + builder + DPOR
Tier 3Risk scoring, SoW corroboration, EDD automation1–2 weeksProduct + builder + Risk & Compliance

Output: One-page scoping note with tier classification, data sources identified, rough effort estimate, and a named environment lane decision (with rationale).

Prototype

A working prototype — not a slide deck, not a mockup — real software that demonstrates the core capability. The prototype proves two things: the AI can do what we think it can, and the people who would use it actually find it helpful.

How to Prototype — By Tier

The goal of prototyping is to answer one question fast: does this AI actually help the people who would use it? The approach scales with the tier — lighter tools for lower risk, more rigour for higher.

TierWhat You BuildWho Tests ItTimeline
Tier 1A working bot or prompt using approved low-code tools (e.g., Copilot). No coding required.3–5 target users from the teamHours to days
Tier 2A working agent connected to real (anonymised) data. Structured inputs and outputs.3–5 target users + product owner1–2 weeks
Tier 3Full prototype against representative data. Accuracy measured and documented.Analysts + Risk & Compliance review2–4 weeks

The critical test: show it to the people who would use it daily. A prototype that impresses leadership but confuses analysts is not ready to move forward.

Output: Working demo, user feedback summary, and a clear decision: proceed, pivot, or park.

Build

This is where the prototype becomes a reliable, everyday tool. What "building" means depends entirely on the tier — and critically, not all builders are engineers. CLM selects designated builders from across the organisation — people with the curiosity, judgement, and domain knowledge to create tools that work. Some are technical; some are not. All are supported through the Builder Council (Section 3).

Key Insight

Building is not an open-ended free-for-all — it is a designated role. Selected CLM members are empowered as builders, including non-technical staff who use approved low-code tools. Everyone else uses the applications these builders create. This keeps quality high, governance traceable, and knowledge concentrated in people who are trained and supported.

Building by Tier

TierWho BuildsHow They BuildWhat It Looks Like
Tier 1 Designated business builders — selected CLM members trained on approved tools Approved no-code / low-code tools (e.g., Copilot) Configure prompts, select data sources, test with colleagues, get line manager sign-off, share with team
Tier 2 Business builders with technical builder support, or technical builders independently Low-code + some scripting: approved agent builders, custom Copilot agents, lightweight Python scripts Connect to data sources, set up structured outputs, add basic monitoring, DPOR consultation, document in model card
Tier 3–4 Dedicated engineering team with product owner Full engineering: CI/CD pipelines, testing frameworks, integration with FenX/CRM, MRM compliance Production-grade code, comprehensive testing, NPAC submission, monitoring infrastructure, model cards, audit trails

The Builder Council Connection

All builders — whether business or technical — are part of the Builder Council (Section 3). This is where designated builders get support, share patterns, and learn from each other. The wider CLM organisation contributes ideas (Ideation) and feedback (Prototype, Deploy), but the build work is done by people who are selected, trained, and connected through this community.

Common Build Activities by Tier

ActivityTier 1Tier 2Tier 3+
Prompt engineering✓✓✓
User testing✓✓✓
Data source connection—✓✓
Model card—✓✓
Code review / CI/CD—Optional✓
Integration testing—BasicComprehensive
NPAC submission—✓ (precedent: SensAIa)✓
MRM engagement—✓ (Tier 2 validation)✓
Monitoring setupUsage onlyUsage + qualityFull observability

Output: A working, tested tool ready for its users — with governance documentation appropriate to its tier.

Deploy & Operate

The tool goes live. What happens next depends on the tier — but every deployed tool gets some level of monitoring.

Operate as a service (applications and agents)

Production AI should be run as a visible service portfolio, not as isolated solutions. The same control logic applies to both applications and agents: named owner, approved environment, audit trail, and a tested stop/fallback path.

Deployment by Tier

TierHow It’s DeployedMonitoringReview Cadence
Tier 1 Shared with team via approved platform (e.g., Copilot). Line manager aware. Usage tracking — is it being used? Is it helpful? Annual or on significant change
Tier 2 Deployed to target user group. Training / onboarding for users. Usage + output quality sampling + user feedback Quarterly
Tier 3–4 Phased rollout with observation period. Full monitoring from day one. Performance (accuracy, latency, error rates), compliance metrics (explainability samples, bias checks via 80% rule), override rates Semi-annual + continuous automated monitoring[4]

The Operate Mindset

Deployment is not the finish line — it is the start of a feedback loop. Every tool should get better over time based on how people actually use it. The questions to track:

  • Adoption: Are people actually using it? If not, why?
  • Quality: Are the outputs accurate and useful?
  • Efficiency: Is it saving the time we expected?
  • Drift: Has performance changed over time? (Tier 2+ with automated checks)

Minimum Operations Dashboard (Portfolio View)

Control lensApplication viewAgent view
InventoryApplication name, owner, user group, lifecycle statusAgent/workflow name, owner, trigger mode (chat/manual/event), lifecycle status
Data boundaryConnected sources, data class (C1-C4), personal-data scopeTools/connectors, knowledge sources, personal-data scope, external call boundaries
Runtime qualityAdoption, task completion quality, incident trendTool-call success rate, handoff quality, override rate, incident trend
Governance statusACAA/MRM/NPA status, review date, conditionsACAA/MRM/NPA status, review date, conditions
Control actionabilityWho can pause/disable and what manual fallback is activeWho can pause/disable, revoke connectors/service account, and what manual fallback is active
Portfolio evidence (calm readout)

The CLM portfolio work indicates that value is already reasonably mapped, and that execution depends more on sequencing and environment readiness than on finding new ideas. In practical terms: run a few low-friction cases early, while preparing the governed path for the heavier regulated cases.

Environment Readiness Baseline (Before Production)

Baseline checkMicrosoft lane (Power Platform / Copilot Studio)Google lane (Vertex AI / GCP)
Environment separationDedicated Dev/Test/Prod environments with controlled admin accessDedicated Dev/Test/Prod projects/folders with policy inheritance
Data movement controlDLP policies with connector classification (Business/Non-business/Blocked)IAM least-privilege + VPC Service Controls perimeter for exfiltration reduction
Release governanceManaged solutions + pipelines for controlled promotionVersioned model/pipeline promotion via Model Registry and deployment workflow controls
AuditabilityDataverse/tenant audit logging and environment activity traceabilityCloud Audit Logs + operational monitoring/alerting
Kill switchDisable copilot/flow, block connector, revoke environment accessDisable endpoint/service, revoke service-account permissions, isolate project/perimeter access

Suggested sequencing from portfolio practice

TrackNear-term intentWhy this is pragmatic
Track A — Visible momentumStart with deterministic/data-quality or KPI-style casesFaster learning cycle, lower governance friction, immediate operational feedback
Track B — Foundation buildIn parallel, establish environment, access model, and delivery ownershipPrevents late-stage delivery stalls when regulated cases enter build/deploy
Track C — Regulated flagshipProgress one high-value governed case through full lifecycleCreates reusable governance and architecture patterns for subsequent cases

Output: Live tool + appropriate monitoring + scheduled review.

Reading scope

Governance explanations record source guidance and working interpretations. Confirm current applicability and decision authority for the actual task. This Hub does not assign a formal legal/risk classification or grant approval.

Gate Descriptions

Three governance gates sit between the delivery stages. Each gate asks one fundamental question — and the answer determines whether the use case proceeds, loops back, or is parked.

GateQuestionTier 1–2 Decision ByTier 3–4 Decision By
Gate 1 — PrioritisationIs this the right thing to build next?Product ownerDomain leadership + Risk awareness
Gate 2 — Build DecisionCan this be built, governed, and operated at production quality? (Tier 3–4: assessed against the 6-pillar AI Risk Instruction)Product owner + builder+ Risk & Compliance sign-off
Gate 3 — Deployment ApprovalIs this technically sound, governance-compliant, and operationally ready?Technical review (Tier 2: NPAC approval — see SensAIa precedent)+ NPAC approval (or Change Risk Management 1st-line decision body post-reform)

Minimum Control Checklist Before a Gate Can Pass

The email discussion on AI agents points to a practical governance test: before a use case progresses, someone should be able to answer what the agent does, what it touches, who owns it, and how it is stopped. If those answers are missing, the use case is not gate-ready.

Control questionWhat must be explicitTypical home
What exists?Agent name, purpose, use case boundary, whether it is chat-only or workflow-drivenUse case brief / register
Which environment runs it?Named lane (M365, Copilot Studio/Power Platform, Vertex AI/GCP) with rationale and ownerScoping note + architecture decision record
What data is used?Source systems, data class, whether personal or client-identifiable data is processedData assessment + DPIA input
What actions are allowed?Read, draft, recommend, write back, trigger workflow, call external APIsArchitecture + control design
What is logged?Prompts, outputs, overrides, approvals, incidents, retention periodRunbook + technical documentation
Who can stop it?Named owner, escalation path, pause/disable mechanism, fallback manual processOperational readiness / runbook
The Builder Council

At every stage of this lifecycle, the Builder Council (see Section 3 — Culture & People) serves as the practitioner community where builders share patterns, conduct peer architecture reviews, and iterate on solutions. It is not a gate — it is the forum where knowledge compounds. Bi-weekly sync, shared patterns repo, D&A liaison.

Mapping to SEB’s Official Model Lifecycle (MRM Instruction)

The MRM Instruction defines 10 phases. Our 5-stage delivery model maps to them as follows:

SEB MRM PhaseHub StageWhat Happens Here
Model (change) originationIdeation + ScopingUse case identified, tier classified, initial risk awareness
DevelopmentPrototype + BuildModel/agent built, tested, iterated
Initial validationBuild (Gate 2)Model validation per Tier 2/3 Guideline (7 sections)
ApprovalGate 3NPAC submission and conditional approval
Implementation / deploymentDeploy & OperateProduction release, phased rollout
UseDeploy & OperateLive operation, user adoption
Model monitoringDeploy & OperateContinuous: accuracy, drift, bias checks, override rates
Periodic validationDeploy & Operate (recurring)Tier 2: biennial. Tier 1 (MRM): triennial
Periodic approvalDeploy & Operate (recurring)Re-approval by CRO Function (Tier 2) or model owner (Tier 3 MRM)
Decommission(Exit)Model retired, documentation archived, users migrated

Source: Instruction for Model Risk Management, Section 5.3 — “Model (change) origination; development; initial validation; approval; implementation/deployment; use; model monitoring; periodic validation; periodic approval; and decommission.”

Ownership Clarity

A recurring failure pattern: ambiguous ownership — "the business owns the outcome but IT owns the system but compliance owns the risk but nobody owns the data." This table eliminates the ambiguity.

WhatOwnerAccountable For
Use case prioritisation & roadmapProduct function (CLM)Deciding what gets built and when
Technical implementationBuilder teamHow it gets built and that it works
Governance & complianceRisk & Compliance partnerRegulatory and policy requirements
Data quality & accessData owner (per SEB governance)Data accuracy, authorisation, classification
Operational performanceProduct + Builder (shared)Solutions perform within thresholds
User adoption & feedbackBusiness championsSolutions are used and improved

RASIC 2.0 — AI Use Case Execution Model

Source: GBS Data & Analytics, released 15 May 2026. LEAF-aligned 8-stage execution framework with 63 activities across 9 roles. Scope: GBS/GCP AI use cases.

What This Is

The RASIC 2.0 is SEB’s official responsibility matrix for AI use case execution. It defines who does what at each stage — from ideation to production monitoring. Every CLM AI use case must follow this model. The Initiative Lead is the pivot role that drives execution across all stages.

The 8 Execution Stages

Stage 1: Ideation
Use case identification, initial value assessment, alignment with strategic priorities. Key output: Use case brief with problem statement and expected impact.
Stage 2: Assessment
Feasibility analysis, data availability check, initial complexity and risk estimation. Key output: Go/no-go recommendation with risk and effort estimates.
Stage 3: Scoping
Define MVP scope, success criteria, technical approach, resource requirements. Key output: Scoping document with delivery plan and team requirements.
Stage 4: Risk Assessment
Dedicated governance stage. Complete ACAA classification + BIA (Business Impact Assessment) + NPAP (New Product Approval Process). Key output: Risk classification, regulatory mapping, approval path confirmed.
Stage 5: Development
Heaviest stage (13 activities). Enterprise governance tax: 99 numbers, STEP registration, TORAF, Collibra DIC registration, GCP environment setup (dev/acc/prod), model development, testing, documentation. Key output: Working solution in acceptance environment.
Stage 6: Infrastructure
IT infrastructure provisioning + UAT (User Acceptance Testing). 7 activities covering production environment, security hardening, performance testing. Key output: Production-ready infrastructure with UAT sign-off.
Stage 7: Deployment
Production deployment, user onboarding, change management, monitoring activation. Key output: Live system with operational runbook.
Stage 8: Operations
Ongoing monitoring, model performance tracking, drift detection, periodic revalidation. Key output: Continuous operation within defined thresholds.

The 9 Roles

RolePrimary ResponsibilityActive Stages

Stage 5 Reality Check

Stage 5 (Development) carries 13 activities including enterprise registration requirements (STEP ID, 99 numbers, TORAF, Collibra DIC). These are not optional for GCP workloads. Factor 2–4 weeks of governance activities into every delivery timeline — this is the enterprise governance tax that all GBS/GCP use cases must pay. Plan for it; don’t discover it mid-sprint.

Key Principles from RASIC 2.0

Initiative Lead is the Pivot

The Initiative Lead is the only role active across ALL 8 stages. They are the continuity thread. Without a named Initiative Lead, execution stalls at handoff points. This role maps to Product Manager or Technical Lead in practice.

Risk Assessment is a Dedicated Stage

Stage 4 is not a checkbox within another stage — it is a full stage requiring ACAA + BIA + NPAP. This reflects SEB’s learned experience: governance embedded in development creates delays; governance as a dedicated stage creates clarity.

Solution Architect is New

RASIC 2.0 adds Solution Architect as a formal role. This reflects the complexity of GCP + FenX + multi-agent systems. The SA ensures integration patterns are consistent and non-functional requirements (security, performance, resilience) are designed in, not retrofitted.

panels.lc-ideation:
Ideation — Capturing Use Cases

Anyone in CLM can surface an idea — analysts, compliance officers, team leads, operations staff. You do not need technical skills. The only requirement is a real pain point.

How We Capture Use Cases

Ideas are submitted through a simple, low-friction template — not a business case, not a slide deck. The point is to lower the bar so good ideas don't get lost in process. Submit via the shared backlog (Teams channel, form, or direct to the Product Manager).

The Idea Template

FieldWhat to WriteExample
What is painful today?Describe the task, how often, and how long it takes"I spend 2 hours per periodic review copying data between FenX and the review template."
What would help?What would the AI ideally do?"An AI that pre-fills the template from FenX data."
Who would use it?How many people, which teams?"All 15 analysts in my team, potentially 60+ across CLM."
How often?Daily, weekly, per review?"Every periodic review — roughly 8–12 times per analyst per week."

How Ideas Are Prioritised

The Product Manager triages all incoming ideas against four criteria:

Impact
How many people benefit? How much time or risk is reduced? A tool used daily by 60 analysts ranks higher than one used monthly by 5.
Feasibility
Can this be built with approved tools and available data? Does the data exist, and is it accessible? Low feasibility = park or re-scope.
Governance fit
What tier does this fall into? Tier 1–2 ideas that deliver quick wins are prioritised early to build momentum and trust.
Strategic alignment
Does it advance CLM's core priorities — onboarding quality, review efficiency, compliance automation, or data completeness?

Connection to the Portfolio

Prioritised ideas feed directly into the AI Portfolio (Section 8). The portfolio is not a separate wish list — it is the accumulated output of this ideation and prioritisation process. Ideas that pass Gate 1 become portfolio items with a tier classification, an owner, and a target horizon:

  • Horizon 1 — Can start now with existing tools and data
  • Horizon 2 — Requires a dependency (e.g., FenX go-live, new data source)
  • Horizon 3 — Exploratory — needs research or external capability

The Product Manager's Role

The Product Manager is the connective tissue across the entire lifecycle. At the ideation stage, they:

  • Curate the backlog — group related ideas, spot duplicates, identify patterns across teams
  • Triage and prioritise — apply the four criteria above, recommend what to scope next
  • Maintain visibility — ensure the backlog is transparent so anyone can see what's been submitted, what's in progress, and what's been parked (and why)
  • Bridge teams — someone in Stockholm may have already solved what Luxembourg is struggling with. The PM connects these dots.
  • Protect focus — say no to ideas that don't fit, or defer them with a clear rationale

CLM Examples of Past Ideas

  • "Can AI summarise my client meeting notes into a structured CRM entry?" → Became a Tier 1 Copilot agent
  • "Can we auto-check SoW documents against declared income?" → Scoped as Tier 3 (KAICY)
  • "Can we extract KYC data from client call transcripts?" → Scoped as Tier 2–3 (KAICY)

Output: One-paragraph idea in the shared backlog. No slides, no business case yet.
panels.lc-scoping:
Scoping

The product function and a builder assess the idea together. The goal is to answer four questions quickly — not to produce a 30-page document:

  1. Governance tier — Does this touch client data? Influence decisions? The answer determines the governance path (see Section 5).
  2. Technical feasibility — Can this be built with SEB-approved models (Gemini, Copilot) and existing infrastructure? What data sources are needed?
  3. Effort & impact — Days or months? How many people benefit?
  4. Environment lane — Where should it run to ensure control and visibility? M365 for personal assistance, Copilot Studio/Power Platform for shared business workflows, or Vertex AI/GCP for source-first regulated orchestration.

Tier Quick Reference

TierTypical CLM Use CaseScoping TimeWho Scopes
Tier 1Meeting summariser, policy Q&A bot, data formatter1–2 daysDesignated builder + product
Tier 2CDD pre-population, document extraction, report drafting3–5 daysProduct + builder + DPOR
Tier 3Risk scoring, SoW corroboration, EDD automation1–2 weeksProduct + builder + Risk & Compliance

Output: One-page scoping note with tier classification, data sources identified, rough effort estimate, and a named environment lane decision (with rationale).
panels.lc-prototype:
Prototype

A working prototype — not a slide deck, not a mockup — real software that demonstrates the core capability. The prototype proves two things: the AI can do what we think it can, and the people who would use it actually find it helpful.

How to Prototype — By Tier

The goal of prototyping is to answer one question fast: does this AI actually help the people who would use it? The approach scales with the tier — lighter tools for lower risk, more rigour for higher.

TierWhat You BuildWho Tests ItTimeline
Tier 1A working bot or prompt using approved low-code tools (e.g., Copilot). No coding required.3–5 target users from the teamHours to days
Tier 2A working agent connected to real (anonymised) data. Structured inputs and outputs.3–5 target users + product owner1–2 weeks
Tier 3Full prototype against representative data. Accuracy measured and documented.Analysts + Risk & Compliance review2–4 weeks

The critical test: show it to the people who would use it daily. A prototype that impresses leadership but confuses analysts is not ready to move forward.

Output: Working demo, user feedback summary, and a clear decision: proceed, pivot, or park.
panels.lc-build:
Build

This is where the prototype becomes a reliable, everyday tool. What "building" means depends entirely on the tier — and critically, not all builders are engineers. CLM selects designated builders from across the organisation — people with the curiosity, judgement, and domain knowledge to create tools that work. Some are technical; some are not. All are supported through the Builder Council (Section 3).

Key Insight

Building is not an open-ended free-for-all — it is a designated role. Selected CLM members are empowered as builders, including non-technical staff who use approved low-code tools. Everyone else uses the applications these builders create. This keeps quality high, governance traceable, and knowledge concentrated in people who are trained and supported.

Building by Tier

TierWho BuildsHow They BuildWhat It Looks Like
Tier 1 Designated business builders — selected CLM members trained on approved tools Approved no-code / low-code tools (e.g., Copilot) Configure prompts, select data sources, test with colleagues, get line manager sign-off, share with team
Tier 2 Business builders with technical builder support, or technical builders independently Low-code + some scripting: approved agent builders, custom Copilot agents, lightweight Python scripts Connect to data sources, set up structured outputs, add basic monitoring, DPOR consultation, document in model card
Tier 3–4 Dedicated engineering team with product owner Full engineering: CI/CD pipelines, testing frameworks, integration with FenX/CRM, MRM compliance Production-grade code, comprehensive testing, NPAC submission, monitoring infrastructure, model cards, audit trails

The Builder Council Connection

All builders — whether business or technical — are part of the Builder Council (Section 3). This is where designated builders get support, share patterns, and learn from each other. The wider CLM organisation contributes ideas (Ideation) and feedback (Prototype, Deploy), but the build work is done by people who are selected, trained, and connected through this community.

Common Build Activities by Tier

ActivityTier 1Tier 2Tier 3+
Prompt engineering✓✓✓
User testing✓✓✓
Data source connection—✓✓
Model card—✓✓
Code review / CI/CD—Optional✓
Integration testing—BasicComprehensive
NPAC submission—✓ (precedent: SensAIa)✓
MRM engagement—✓ (Tier 2 validation)✓
Monitoring setupUsage onlyUsage + qualityFull observability

Output: A working, tested tool ready for its users — with governance documentation appropriate to its tier.
panels.lc-deploy:
Deploy & Operate

The tool goes live. What happens next depends on the tier — but every deployed tool gets some level of monitoring.

Operate as a service (applications and agents)

Production AI should be run as a visible service portfolio, not as isolated solutions. The same control logic applies to both applications and agents: named owner, approved environment, audit trail, and a tested stop/fallback path.

Deployment by Tier

TierHow It’s DeployedMonitoringReview Cadence
Tier 1 Shared with team via approved platform (e.g., Copilot). Line manager aware. Usage tracking — is it being used? Is it helpful? Annual or on significant change
Tier 2 Deployed to target user group. Training / onboarding for users. Usage + output quality sampling + user feedback Quarterly
Tier 3–4 Phased rollout with observation period. Full monitoring from day one. Performance (accuracy, latency, error rates), compliance metrics (explainability samples, bias checks via 80% rule), override rates Semi-annual + continuous automated monitoring[4]

The Operate Mindset

Deployment is not the finish line — it is the start of a feedback loop. Every tool should get better over time based on how people actually use it. The questions to track:

  • Adoption: Are people actually using it? If not, why?
  • Quality: Are the outputs accurate and useful?
  • Efficiency: Is it saving the time we expected?
  • Drift: Has performance changed over time? (Tier 2+ with automated checks)

Minimum Operations Dashboard (Portfolio View)

Control lensApplication viewAgent view
InventoryApplication name, owner, user group, lifecycle statusAgent/workflow name, owner, trigger mode (chat/manual/event), lifecycle status
Data boundaryConnected sources, data class (C1-C4), personal-data scopeTools/connectors, knowledge sources, personal-data scope, external call boundaries
Runtime qualityAdoption, task completion quality, incident trendTool-call success rate, handoff quality, override rate, incident trend
Governance statusACAA/MRM/NPA status, review date, conditionsACAA/MRM/NPA status, review date, conditions
Control actionabilityWho can pause/disable and what manual fallback is activeWho can pause/disable, revoke connectors/service account, and what manual fallback is active
Portfolio evidence (calm readout)

The CLM portfolio work indicates that value is already reasonably mapped, and that execution depends more on sequencing and environment readiness than on finding new ideas. In practical terms: run a few low-friction cases early, while preparing the governed path for the heavier regulated cases.

Environment Readiness Baseline (Before Production)

Baseline checkMicrosoft lane (Power Platform / Copilot Studio)Google lane (Vertex AI / GCP)
Environment separationDedicated Dev/Test/Prod environments with controlled admin accessDedicated Dev/Test/Prod projects/folders with policy inheritance
Data movement controlDLP policies with connector classification (Business/Non-business/Blocked)IAM least-privilege + VPC Service Controls perimeter for exfiltration reduction
Release governanceManaged solutions + pipelines for controlled promotionVersioned model/pipeline promotion via Model Registry and deployment workflow controls
AuditabilityDataverse/tenant audit logging and environment activity traceabilityCloud Audit Logs + operational monitoring/alerting
Kill switchDisable copilot/flow, block connector, revoke environment accessDisable endpoint/service, revoke service-account permissions, isolate project/perimeter access

Suggested sequencing from portfolio practice

TrackNear-term intentWhy this is pragmatic
Track A — Visible momentumStart with deterministic/data-quality or KPI-style casesFaster learning cycle, lower governance friction, immediate operational feedback
Track B — Foundation buildIn parallel, establish environment, access model, and delivery ownershipPrevents late-stage delivery stalls when regulated cases enter build/deploy
Track C — Regulated flagshipProgress one high-value governed case through full lifecycleCreates reusable governance and architecture patterns for subsequent cases

Output: Live tool + appropriate monitoring + scheduled review.
panels.lc-gates:
Reading scope

Governance explanations record source guidance and working interpretations. Confirm current applicability and decision authority for the actual task. This Hub does not assign a formal legal/risk classification or grant approval.

Gate Descriptions

Three governance gates sit between the delivery stages. Each gate asks one fundamental question — and the answer determines whether the use case proceeds, loops back, or is parked.

GateQuestionTier 1–2 Decision ByTier 3–4 Decision By
Gate 1 — PrioritisationIs this the right thing to build next?Product ownerDomain leadership + Risk awareness
Gate 2 — Build DecisionCan this be built, governed, and operated at production quality? (Tier 3–4: assessed against the 6-pillar AI Risk Instruction)Product owner + builder+ Risk & Compliance sign-off
Gate 3 — Deployment ApprovalIs this technically sound, governance-compliant, and operationally ready?Technical review (Tier 2: NPAC approval — see SensAIa precedent)+ NPAC approval (or Change Risk Management 1st-line decision body post-reform)

Minimum Control Checklist Before a Gate Can Pass

The email discussion on AI agents points to a practical governance test: before a use case progresses, someone should be able to answer what the agent does, what it touches, who owns it, and how it is stopped. If those answers are missing, the use case is not gate-ready.

Control questionWhat must be explicitTypical home
What exists?Agent name, purpose, use case boundary, whether it is chat-only or workflow-drivenUse case brief / register
Which environment runs it?Named lane (M365, Copilot Studio/Power Platform, Vertex AI/GCP) with rationale and ownerScoping note + architecture decision record
What data is used?Source systems, data class, whether personal or client-identifiable data is processedData assessment + DPIA input
What actions are allowed?Read, draft, recommend, write back, trigger workflow, call external APIsArchitecture + control design
What is logged?Prompts, outputs, overrides, approvals, incidents, retention periodRunbook + technical documentation
Who can stop it?Named owner, escalation path, pause/disable mechanism, fallback manual processOperational readiness / runbook
The Builder Council

At every stage of this lifecycle, the Builder Council (see Section 3 — Culture & People) serves as the practitioner community where builders share patterns, conduct peer architecture reviews, and iterate on solutions. It is not a gate — it is the forum where knowledge compounds. Bi-weekly sync, shared patterns repo, D&A liaison.

Mapping to SEB’s Official Model Lifecycle (MRM Instruction)

The MRM Instruction defines 10 phases. Our 5-stage delivery model maps to them as follows:

SEB MRM PhaseHub StageWhat Happens Here

DevelopmentPrototype + BuildModel/agent built, tested, iterated
Initial validationBuild (Gate 2)Model validation per Tier 2/3 Guideline (7 sections)
ApprovalGate 3NPAC submission and conditional approval
Implementation / deploymentDeploy & OperateProduction release, phased rollout
UseDeploy & OperateLive operation, user adoption
Model monitoringDeploy & OperateContinuous: accuracy, drift, bias checks, override rates
Periodic validationDeploy & Operate (recurring)Tier 2: biennial. Tier 1 (MRM): triennial
Periodic approvalDeploy & Operate (recurring)Re-approval by CRO Function (Tier 2) or model owner (Tier 3 MRM)
Decommission(Exit)Model retired, documentation archived, users migrated

Source: Instruction for Model Risk Management, Section 5.3 — “Model (change) origination; development; initial validation; approval; implementation/deployment; use; model monitoring; periodic validation; periodic approval; and decommission.”

A recurring failure pattern: ambiguous ownership — "the business owns the outcome but IT owns the system but compliance owns the risk but nobody owns the data." This table eliminates the ambiguity.

panels.lc-rasic:
RASIC 2.0 — AI Use Case Execution Model

Source: GBS Data & Analytics, released 15 May 2026. LEAF-aligned 8-stage execution framework with 63 activities across 9 roles. Scope: GBS/GCP AI use cases.

What This Is

The RASIC 2.0 is SEB’s official responsibility matrix for AI use case execution. It defines who does what at each stage — from ideation to production monitoring. Every CLM AI use case must follow this model. The Initiative Lead is the pivot role that drives execution across all stages.

The 8 Execution Stages

Stage 1: Ideation
Use case identification, initial value assessment, alignment with strategic priorities. Key output: Use case brief with problem statement and expected impact.
Stage 2: Assessment
Feasibility analysis, data availability check, initial complexity and risk estimation. Key output: Go/no-go recommendation with risk and effort estimates.
Stage 3: Scoping
Define MVP scope, success criteria, technical approach, resource requirements. Key output: Scoping document with delivery plan and team requirements.
Stage 4: Risk Assessment
Dedicated governance stage. Complete ACAA classification + BIA (Business Impact Assessment) + NPAP (New Product Approval Process). Key output: Risk classification, regulatory mapping, approval path confirmed.
Stage 5: Development
Heaviest stage (13 activities). Enterprise governance tax: 99 numbers, STEP registration, TORAF, Collibra DIC registration, GCP environment setup (dev/acc/prod), model development, testing, documentation. Key output: Working solution in acceptance environment.
Stage 6: Infrastructure
IT infrastructure provisioning + UAT (User Acceptance Testing). 7 activities covering production environment, security hardening, performance testing. Key output: Production-ready infrastructure with UAT sign-off.
Stage 7: Deployment
Production deployment, user onboarding, change management, monitoring activation. Key output: Live system with operational runbook.
Stage 8: Operations
Ongoing monitoring, model performance tracking, drift detection, periodic revalidation. Key output: Continuous operation within defined thresholds.

The 9 Roles

RolePrimary ResponsibilityActive Stages
Initiative SponsorBusiness ownership, funding, strategic alignment1–4, 7–8
Initiative LeadEnd-to-end execution ownership. The pivot role that drives delivery across all stages.1–8 (all)
Subject Matter Expert (SME)Domain knowledge, process understanding, acceptance criteria1–5, 7
Data ScientistModel development, evaluation, prompt engineering2–5, 8
ML EngineerMLOps, pipeline engineering, model deployment infrastructure5–8
Tech ManagerTechnical architecture decisions, platform governance3–6
Cloud DeveloperGCP implementation, API development, integration code5–7
Solution Architect New in v2.0System design, integration patterns, non-functional requirements3–6
Risk ManagerACAA, BIA, NPAP, model risk tier, ongoing risk monitoring4, 8
Stage 5 Reality Check

Stage 5 (Development) carries 13 activities including enterprise registration requirements (STEP ID, 99 numbers, TORAF, Collibra DIC). These are not optional for GCP workloads. Factor 2–4 weeks of governance activities into every delivery timeline — this is the enterprise governance tax that all GBS/GCP use cases must pay. Plan for it; don’t discover it mid-sprint.

Key Principles from RASIC 2.0

Initiative Lead is the Pivot

The Initiative Lead is the only role active across ALL 8 stages. They are the continuity thread. Without a named Initiative Lead, execution stalls at handoff points. This role maps to Product Manager or Technical Lead in practice.

Risk Assessment is a Dedicated Stage

Stage 4 is not a checkbox within another stage — it is a full stage requiring ACAA + BIA + NPAP. This reflects SEB’s learned experience: governance embedded in development creates delays; governance as a dedicated stage creates clarity.

Solution Architect is New

RASIC 2.0 adds Solution Architect as a formal role. This reflects the complexity of GCP + FenX + multi-agent systems. The SA ensures integration patterns are consistent and non-functional requirements (security, performance, resilience) are designed in, not retrofitted.

chapters.title: Navigating Risk & Compliance
chapters.html:
Navigating Risk & Compliance

Compliance is often framed as a constraint. This framing is both inaccurate and counterproductive. In a regulated industry, compliance infrastructure is the foundation that makes sustainable scaling possible. The organisations that move fastest have compliance woven in, not minimised.

Reading scope

Governance explanations record source guidance and working interpretations. Confirm current applicability and decision authority for the actual task. This Hub does not assign a formal legal/risk classification or grant approval.

EU AI Act — Timeline & Implications

The EU AI Act introduces a risk-based classification for AI. Its enforcement timeline is concrete and accelerating:[3]

DateWhat HappensCLM Impact
Feb 2025AI Act enters into forceLegal framework now active. All teams must understand classification obligations.
Aug 2025Prohibited practices (Art. 5) enforceableSocial scoring, manipulative AI, emotion inference at work — banned. No CLM use case should fall here.
Feb 2026GPAI model obligations enforceableGoogle (Gemini provider) must comply with GPAI transparency. SEB as deployer must still assess each use case.
Aug 2026High-risk obligations fully activeCurrent implementation threshold. AI in creditworthiness/risk assessment = high-risk. KAICY and CDD tools likely in scope.
Aug 2027Annex I product safety systemsSystems embedded in regulated products (less relevant for CLM).
OngoingPost-market surveillanceContinuous monitoring, incident reporting, periodic conformity assessment for high-risk systems.

Prohibited AI Practices (Art. 5) — CLM Relevance

These are banned outright. Penalties: up to €35M or 7% of global annual turnover.

  • Social scoring — aggregating client behavioural data for generalised “trustworthiness” outside regulatory mandate. CLM risk assessments are AML/KYC-mandated, not discretionary scoring.
  • Emotion inference in workplaces — using sentiment analysis to evaluate employee performance is prohibited. Call sentiment for KYC purposes (regulatory obligation) is permitted.
  • Biometric categorisation by sensitive attributes — inferring race, religion, or sexual orientation. No CLM application does this.
  • Subliminal/manipulative techniques — distorting behaviour without awareness. CLM tools assist staff, not influence clients.

High-Risk Requirements (Art. 8–15, applicable to Tier 3–4)

  • Art. 9 — Risk management system — identify and mitigate risks throughout the AI lifecycle
  • Art. 10 — Data governance — training data must be relevant, representative, and free from errors
  • Art. 11 — Technical documentation — detailed description of the AI system, its purpose, and performance
  • Art. 12 — Record-keeping — automatic logging of events during operation (min. 6 months)
  • Art. 13 — Transparency — clear information to users about the AI system’s nature and limitations
  • Art. 14 — Human oversight — design for effective human intervention and override
  • Art. 15 — Accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity — appropriate levels maintained throughout lifecycle

Penalty Structure (Art. 99)

ViolationMaximum Fine
Prohibited AI practices€35M or 7% of global annual turnover
High-risk non-compliance€15M or 3% of global annual turnover
Providing incorrect information to authorities€7.5M or 1% of global annual turnover
Practical Implication

Any Tier 3 system should be designed from the outset to meet Art. 8–15 requirements. Building compliance in is a fraction of the cost of retrofitting — or a single fine. The tier model in Section 2 ensures this happens naturally.

Exception from High-Risk (Art. 6(3)) — The KAICY Defence

An Annex III system is not high-risk if it meets any of these conditions:

  • Performs a narrow procedural task
  • Improves the result of a previously completed human activity
  • Detects decision-making patterns without replacing human assessment without proper review
  • Performs a preparatory task to an assessment relevant for the use cases listed in Annex III
⚠️ Critical Exception

A system is always high-risk if it profiles individuals (automated processing of personal data to evaluate aspects of a person’s life). KAICY’s classification argument: it performs a preparatory task (transcription → extraction → FenX mapping) with mandatory human review before any decision. However, because it processes personal data that could be considered profiling, the conservative approach is to treat it as potentially high-risk and apply Art. 8–15 obligations.

Deployer Obligations (Art. 26) — SEB as User

  • Use high-risk AI in accordance with instructions for use
  • Assign competent persons for human oversight
  • Monitor operation and report incidents
  • Keep automatically generated logs (minimum 6 months)
  • Inform workers’ representatives and affected persons

Further Reading

  • EU AI Act — Full Legislative Text (EUR-Lex) ↗
  • EU Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI ↗
  • FSB — Financial Stability Implications of AI (Nov 2024) ↗
  • SEB Risk Instructions & Policies (Intranet) ↗
Reading scope

Governance explanations record source guidance and working interpretations. Confirm current applicability and decision authority for the actual task. This Hub does not assign a formal legal/risk classification or grant approval.

SEB's ACAA Framework

The AI Classification and Assessment Approach provides SEB's internal classification, substantially mirroring the EU AI Act:[4]

Category 1 — Minimal Risk

Category 1 — Minimal Risk

No specific obligations beyond usage guidelines. Maps to Governance Tier 1.

EU AI Act: Minimal risk — unregulated. Spam filters, AI-assisted search, most internal productivity tools.

Examples in CLM:

  • Copilot for drafting internal emails or meeting summaries
  • AI-assisted search across internal policy documents
  • Template generation for standard procedures

Requirements: Usage guidelines, line manager awareness. No formal risk assessment needed. No ACAA portal submission required but recommended for traceability.

Timeline: Days to deploy.

Category 2 — Limited Risk

Category 2 — Limited Risk

Transparency obligations — users must be informed they interact with AI. Maps to Governance Tier 2.

EU AI Act Art. 52: Limited risk systems must ensure people know they interact with AI. Applies to chatbots, deepfakes, and AI-generated content.

Examples in CLM:

  • AI-assisted data extraction from client documents (analyst reviews output)
  • Automated case note drafting from call transcripts
  • KPI dashboard with AI-generated trend analysis
  • Batch processing of internal operational data

Requirements: Model card, ACAA Portal submission, data processing agreement, named owner, Risk & Compliance review, quarterly review cadence.

Key obligations:

  • AI output must be clearly labelled as AI-generated
  • Users must understand system capabilities and limitations
  • Data classification and retention policy required

Timeline: Weeks to deploy.

Category 3 — High Risk

Category 3 — High Risk

Comprehensive requirements including conformity assessment. Maps to Governance Tier 3.

EU AI Act Annex III, §5: AI systems evaluating creditworthiness, risk scoring of natural persons, or used in essential services. High-risk obligations fully enforceable Aug 2, 2026.

Examples in CLM:

  • KAICY — KYC data extraction informing CDD risk classification
  • AI-generated risk scores influencing client treatment
  • Automated EDD trigger recommendations
  • Client segmentation models using personal data

Mandatory requirements (Art. 8–17):

  • Art. 9: Lifecycle risk management system
  • Art. 10: Data governance — training data must be relevant, representative, error-free
  • Art. 11: Full technical documentation (model card + architecture)
  • Art. 12: Automatic logging — min 6 months retention
  • Art. 13: Explainability — SHAP, Vertex Explainable AI, or inherent interpretability
  • Art. 14: Human oversight design — documented escalation path
  • Art. 15: Accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity requirements

Governance: NPAC approval, Group Non-Financial Risk sign-off, bias assessment (80% rule), DPIA, NPA proposal via NAMIS.

Timeline: Months to deploy.

Category 4 — Unacceptable Risk

Category 4 — Unacceptable Risk

Prohibited. Social scoring, manipulative AI, etc. No CLM applications should fall here.

EU AI Act Art. 5 — PROHIBITED. Enforceable since Aug 2, 2025. Penalties: up to €35M or 7% of global annual turnover.

Prohibited practices:

  • Social scoring based on social behaviour or personality traits
  • Subliminal or manipulative techniques distorting behaviour
  • Exploiting vulnerabilities (age, disability, socio-economic)
  • Biometric categorisation inferring race, religion, sexual orientation
  • Emotion inference in workplaces (except medical/safety)
  • Untargeted facial recognition database scraping
  • Criminal risk assessment solely based on profiling

CLM relevance: Any AI that scores clients based on personality traits (vs. legitimate risk factors), uses deceptive nudging in client communications, or infers protected attributes from proxy data would be prohibited.

Action: If a use case falls here, it must be redesigned or killed. The AI Use Case Classifier (Section 12) blocks these at Step 0 before any tier assignment.

The governance tier model is designed to create a single classification exercise — one assessment that satisfies both ACAA and the lifecycle governance requirements, eliminating duplicate processes.

KAICY Classification Analysis

KAICY processes personal data for AML/KYC risk assessment. Under ACAA, it classifies as Category 3 — High Risk because it:

  • Evaluates natural persons for creditworthiness or risk purposes (Annex III, §5)
  • Processes special-category data (PEP status, sanctions)
  • Directly influences regulatory-mandated outcomes (CDD)
  • Integrates with external systems (FenX, SensAIa) creating cross-system dependencies

This means KAICY triggers Governance Tier 3 requirements: formal risk assessment, model card, human oversight design, conformity self-assessment, and periodic validation.

How to Classify

Every new AI use case must complete an ACAA classification before development begins. The classification portal guides you through a structured questionnaire that maps your use case to the appropriate risk category.

Action

Start your ACAA classification at the ACAA Classification Portal ↗. For questions, contact the AI Governance Forum ↗.

Reading scope

Governance explanations record source guidance and working interpretations. Confirm current applicability and decision authority for the actual task. This Hub does not assign a formal legal/risk classification or grant approval.

Governance & Control in Practice

The most useful control questions are operational, not theoretical: what AI services exist, what data they use, what permissions they have, what they produce, what is logged, who owns them, and how they are paused or stopped. This applies to both AI applications and AI agents, and this is where the email discussion should land in the operating model.

Single-home principle

Keep one authoritative control register here in Risk & Compliance, then echo only the essentials in the lifecycle, platform, and portfolio sections. That keeps governance visible without turning the whole Hub into repeated policy text.

A second, complementary axis

The register above governs AI services. A separate question is how trustworthy a knowledge claim feeding those services is — binding law vs. approved interpretation vs. unvalidated AI inference. See CLM Intelligence Model (Section 11) → Authority & Evidence.

Portfolio-informed operating observations

  • Most dependency risk is structural: environment provisioning, data access agreements, and role capacity tend to delay delivery more than use-case definition.
  • Capability reuse matters: document intelligence, data quality, risk reasoning, and knowledge support can be built as reusable layers rather than isolated projects.
  • Parallel tracks are healthier than one queue: low-governance improvements can proceed while regulated workloads complete deeper governance steps.
  • Keep assumptions explicit: legacy time/cost figures are directional and should be updated as FenX-native measurements mature.

GDPR Considerations

CLM data is inherently personal — client identities, financial information, risk assessments, transaction patterns. Every AI application processing this data must comply:[4]

The 7 GDPR Principles Applied to CLM AI

PrincipleWhat It Means for CLM AI
1. Lawfulness, fairness, transparencyLegal basis: "legal obligation" (AML/KYC mandate) or "legitimate interest". Clients informed about AI-assisted processing.
2. Purpose limitationData collected for KYC/CDD may only be used for that purpose — not repurposed for marketing or scoring without separate consent.
3. Data minimisationAI systems process only fields necessary for the task. KAICY uses progressive PD minimisation — full data at ingestion, reduced over lifecycle.
4. AccuracyClient data must be kept up to date. AI outputs (risk scores, flags) must be verifiable and correctable.
5. Storage limitationRetention follows SEB's data retention policy. AI-generated logs and explanations stored for audit, then purged.
6. Integrity & confidentialityEncryption at rest and in transit. Role-based access control. GCP European data residency.
7. AccountabilityThe model owner is the GDPR Controller — responsible for demonstrating compliance at all times.

Key Requirements

  • Lawful basis: "Legal obligation" (AML/KYC compliance) or "legitimate interest" — both well-established for CLM
  • Right to explanation (Art. 22): Where automated processing significantly affects individuals, they can request meaningful information about the logic — reinforces explainability
  • DPIA almost certainly required for KAICY: The AI Risk Instruction states: "The use of AI is a strong indicator that the processing may be considered high-risk and thus require a DPIA." SensAIa's NPAC approval included a DPIA deadline as Condition #1. KAICY processes personal data (KYC) with AI — a DPIA is effectively mandatory, not optional.
  • Data residency: SEB's GCP setup within European regions addresses primary concerns
  • Breach notification: 72-hour reporting obligation to supervisory authority if personal data breach detected

GDPR Controller Responsibilities

The model owner is the GDPR Controller. Before processing any personal data through an AI system, you must consult your local Data Protection Officer Representative (DPOR). The 7 fundamental GDPR principles apply to all AI processing: lawfulness, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, security, and controller accountability.[4]

The NPA process governs how SEB evaluates new products, services, and significant changes. It ensures approved products are consistent with Group Risk Policy, the CRO Function instruction, and the Risk Appetite approved by the Board of Directors.

The NPA Process (3 Steps)

1. Proposal Submission
Scope description and Risk Assessment — the proposing unit documents the change and assesses associated risks.
2. Risk Quality Control
2nd line control functions review the proposal for completeness and risk alignment.
3. Approval

NPA Scope

NPA covers:

  • Significant changes to existing products/services

SEB AI Ethics Policy

Four principles and seven requirements govern all AI at SEB:[4]

Four Principles

Autonomy

Human agency preserved. People retain meaningful control over AI-assisted decisions.

Harm Prevention

Do no harm through algorithmic decisions. Safeguards against adverse outcomes.

Fairness

Non-discrimination. Operationalised through the 80% rule: selection rates for any group ≥ 80% of the highest-performing group.

Explainability

Transparency in decision logic. Every AI recommendation traceable to inputs and reasoning.

Seven Requirements

  1. Human oversight
  2. Technical robustness and safety
  3. Privacy and data governance
  4. Transparency
  5. Diversity and non-discrimination
  6. Societal and environmental wellbeing
  7. Accountability

For CLM, the most operationally relevant: fairness (bias-free risk assessments) and explainability (every recommendation traceable). Tools: Vertex Explainable AI, SHAP values.[4]

Bias & Fairness in Practice

The 80% rule (four-fifths rule) requires that the selection rate for any protected group be at least 80% of the highest-performing group (disparate ratio 0.8–1.25). There is no universal fairness metric — the appropriate measure depends on context and requires domain knowledge.[4]

Three intervention points for mitigating bias:

  • Pre-processing — address bias in training data before model training
  • In-processing — apply fairness constraints during model training
  • Post-processing — adjust model predictions to meet fairness thresholds

Explainability Approaches

The EU AI Act (Article 13) and GDPR both require meaningful explanation of AI logic. Two technical paths:[4]

  1. Inherently interpretable models — decision trees, logistic regression (transparent by design)
  2. External frameworks — Vertex Explainable AI (integrated with AutoML), SHAP/Shapley Values (feature-level attribution)

For CLM: CDD risk-scoring models should use SHAP to provide per-decision explanations showing which risk factors contributed most to a given classification.

GenAI & LLM-Specific Ethics Considerations

Generative AI introduces unique ethical risks beyond traditional ML. The following apply to all CLM agents and LLM-based tools:

RiskMitigation
HallucinationNever use LLM output as sole basis for regulatory decisions. Human-in-the-loop mandatory for Tier 2+.
Data leakageNo client PII in prompts to general-purpose models. Use SEB-provisioned endpoints with data processing agreements.
Prompt injectionInput sanitisation, output validation, and separation of system/user instructions in agent architectures.
Opacity of reasoningChain-of-thought logging for audit trail. Agent decisions logged with full prompt context.
Bias amplificationLLMs can amplify biases present in training data. Monitor outputs for demographic patterns. Apply fairness checks.
Over-relianceTraining programs to ensure staff maintain critical judgement. Periodic manual-only exercises.

Customer-Facing AI Ethics Checklist

  • ☐ Client informed they are interacting with or assisted by AI
  • ☐ Client can request human review of any AI-influenced decision
  • ☐ No emotional manipulation or dark-pattern nudging
  • ☐ Outputs do not reveal internal risk thresholds or model logic
  • ☐ Adverse decisions explained in plain language
