chapters.title: AI, Agents & MCP in CLM
chapters.html:
AI, Agents & MCP in CLM

This section is your educational deep-dive into how AI transforms Client Lifecycle Management — from practical use cases anyone can imagine, to the agentic architectures that coordinate specialised AI workers, to the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that connects AI to your systems. Whether you are a business analyst, compliance officer, developer, or product manager, start here to see what is possible.

How AI Can Transform CLM

AI is not a single tool — it is a capability layer that can be applied across every stage of the client lifecycle. The key is to think in terms of patterns, not individual products. Once you recognise the pattern, you can see dozens of use cases from your own perspective and domain expertise.

The Seven AI Capability Patterns

Every AI application in CLM falls into one or more of these fundamental patterns:

🔍 Pattern Recognition

AI excels at finding signals in noise — anomalous transactions, unusual relationship structures, emerging risk indicators across thousands of clients that no human could manually review.

Imagine: A system that continuously scans your entire client portfolio and surfaces the 15 cases that need attention today — before anyone asks.

📄 Document Intelligence

Extracting structured data from unstructured documents — passports, financial statements, corporate registries, tax returns, annual reports — and cross-referencing across sources automatically.

Imagine: Dropping a stack of onboarding documents into a system and getting a pre-filled client profile with flagged inconsistencies in minutes, not hours.

✍️ Narrative Generation

AI can draft case summaries, risk assessments, compliance reports, and client communications — producing first drafts that analysts review and refine rather than write from scratch.

Imagine: Every periodic KYC review starts with an AI-drafted narrative that captures all data changes since the last review — the analyst edits rather than creates.

📊 Dashboards & Analytics

Real-time visualisation of portfolio health, KPI tracking, workload distribution, compliance status, and trend analysis — turning raw data into actionable insight for managers and teams.

Imagine: A dashboard where every team lead sees their team's KYC backlog, average review time, upcoming deadlines, and quality scores — updated in real-time.

⚡ Task Automation

Repetitive, rule-based tasks that consume analyst time — data entry, status updates, notification routing, deadline tracking, document requests — can be fully or partially automated.

Imagine: When a client's corporate structure changes in a registry, the system automatically triggers a review, pulls updated data, and notifies the assigned analyst.

🧠 Decision Support

AI provides recommendations with evidence and confidence levels — risk scores, classification suggestions, next-best-action guidance — while the human retains final authority.

Imagine: A risk scoring engine that explains why it scored a client as high-risk, citing the specific data points, so the analyst can agree, adjust, or override with full context.

Where to Start: Low-Hanging Fruit

The most impactful AI applications share a common trait: they eliminate work that is high-volume, repetitive, and time-consuming while being low-risk and verifiable. Start here:

Use CasePatternImpactComplexity
Meeting transcription & summarisationNarrative GenerationSave 30–60 min per meetingLow
Document data extraction (passports, IDs)Document Intelligence80%+ time reduction on data entryMedium
Periodic review pre-populationTask Automation + NarrativeFirst draft in minutes vs. hoursMedium
KPI dashboards & reportingDashboards & AnalyticsReal-time visibility for managersLow
Anomaly detection in transactionsPattern RecognitionEarlier risk detection, fewer false positivesHigh
Source of Wealth corroborationDecision Support + Document Intel67% review time reduction (Deloitte benchmark)High
Key Insight

The most powerful insight about AI in CLM is this: you do not need to be technical to identify use cases. If you find yourself doing the same thing repeatedly, copying data between systems, or wishing you had a summary of something — that is a use case. The technology exists. The bottleneck is imagination and prioritisation, not capability.

The Transformation Spectrum

AI adoption in CLM follows a natural progression — each stage builds confidence and infrastructure for the next:

Stage 1: Assist
AI helps individuals work faster — copilots, search assistants, meeting summaries. Human does the work, AI provides inputs. Low risk, fast deployment, builds trust.
Stage 2: Augment
AI produces draft outputs that humans review — pre-filled forms, draft narratives, risk pre-scores. AI does first pass, human validates and edits. Medium risk, requires quality monitoring.
Stage 3: Automate
AI handles end-to-end processes with human oversight at gates — document processing pipelines, automated screening. AI executes, human supervises and intervenes. Higher risk, requires robust governance.
Stage 4: Orchestrate
Multiple AI agents coordinate complex workflows — full KYC reviews, cross-system data reconciliation. AI systems collaborate, human oversees the outcome. Highest complexity, requires the agentic architectures described in this section.

What Are AI Agents?

An AI agent is a system that can perceive its environment, make decisions, and take actions to achieve a goal — autonomously, without step-by-step human instruction. Unlike a chatbot that responds to prompts, an agent can plan multi-step workflows, use tools, call APIs, and adapt when things go wrong.

The Simple Analogy

A chatbot is like asking a colleague a question — you get an answer. An agent is like delegating a task to a colleague — they figure out the steps, gather what they need, do the work, and come back with the result. The shift is from question-answering to task-completion.

Agent Anatomy

Every AI agent, whether simple or complex, has the same fundamental components:

🧠 Reasoning Engine

The LLM at the core — interprets instructions, plans steps, makes decisions. Powered by models like Gemini, Claude, or GPT. The "brain" that decides what to do next.

🔧 Tools

Executable functions the agent can invoke — database queries, API calls, file operations, web searches, calculations. Tools are how agents act on the world.

💾 Memory

Context the agent carries — conversation history, task state, retrieved documents, intermediate results. Memory enables multi-step reasoning across a complex workflow.

📋 Instructions

The system prompt defining the agent's role, constraints, output format, and guardrails. In CLM, this includes regulatory boundaries, data access permissions, and escalation rules.

Agents need roads, not just engines

An agent is only as capable as the systems it can reach. Think of your connected systems — FenX APIs, policy databases, screening providers, document stores — as roads. Without roads, an agent faces the same bottlenecks as a human: switching between screens, copy-pasting between applications, waiting for responses. An agent with access to structured data via MCP servers can complete in minutes what takes an analyst hours. The same agent without those connections is a powerful engine parked in a garage.

This is why infrastructure comes before agents in any pragmatic portfolio. GCP access, FenX APIs, MCP servers, data access layers, and policy corpus — these are the roads. Equally important: good data quality. An agent driving on broken roads — inconsistent fields, missing identifiers, stale records — produces unreliable outputs no matter how sophisticated the model. Roads and data quality first, agents second.

Types of Agents in CLM

Based on Deloitte's agentic architecture for CLM[2] and industry patterns:

Orchestrator Agents
Coordinate end-to-end processes. Receive a goal (e.g., "complete periodic review for Client X"), decompose it into sub-tasks, assign to functional agents, aggregate results, manage exceptions. CLM example: A KYC review orchestrator that sequences document collection, data verification, risk scoring, and narrative generation.
Functional Agents
Execute specific business tasks — CDD evaluation, SoW corroboration, document extraction, name screening, adverse media search. Each has domain-specific prompts, tool access, and output schemas. CLM example: A Source of Wealth agent that verifies declared wealth against external registries and financial data.
Helper Agents
Provide cross-cutting services reusable by any functional agent — translation, summarisation, citation tracking, data formatting, template compilation. CLM example: A narrative generation helper that any functional agent calls to produce human-readable summaries from structured data.
Utility Agents
Non-AI microservices that agents call as tools — database connectors, API gateways, file storage, logging, audit trail services. High reusability, no intelligence required. CLM example: A FenX data connector that any agent uses to read/write client records.

Why Multi-Agent Over Single-Agent?

A single monolithic agent attempting a full KYC review would quickly hit context limits, mix concerns, and become impossible to debug. Multi-agent architectures solve this:

ChallengeSingle AgentMulti-Agent
Context windowOverloaded with all data and instructionsEach agent has focused, manageable context
DebuggingOpaque — hard to trace where errors occurClear chain — trace exactly which agent failed
ReusabilityNothing is reusableHelper and utility agents serve multiple workflows
ScalingBottleneck at one LLM callParallel execution — multiple agents work simultaneously
GovernanceAll-or-nothing permissionsEach agent has precisely scoped data access
Model flexibilityOne model for everythingRight model per task — powerful for reasoning, fast for extraction

Goose — An Open-Source Agent Framework

Goose ↗ (Agentic AI Foundation / Linux Foundation) is a general-purpose open-source AI agent — available as desktop app, CLI, and API. It illustrates the agent paradigm well:

  • Provider-agnostic: Works with 15+ LLM providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama, Azure, Bedrock)
  • MCP-native: Connects to 70+ extensions via the Model Context Protocol — the open standard described in the MCP tab
  • Not just code: Research, writing, automation, data analysis — demonstrating that agents are general-purpose task-completion systems
  • Built in Rust: Performance and portability, 43k+ stars on GitHub, 467+ contributors

The relevance to CLM: Goose demonstrates that agents can connect to any system via standardised protocols (MCP), use any LLM, and perform any task — the same pattern CLM agents would follow when connecting to FenX, CRM, sanctions databases, and document stores.

Key Insight

Agents are not a future technology. They are shipping today — in developer tools (Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code), in customer service (Salesforce Einstein), and increasingly in financial services. The question for CLM is not whether to adopt agents, but how to architect them within our regulatory and governance constraints.

Agent Safety & Maintenance Principles

Building agents in a regulated environment requires deliberate safety architecture. These principles — derived from leading AI companies (Anthropic, Google, OpenAI) and adapted for financial services — should guide every agent built within CLM:

1. Reversibility Awareness
Agents must consider the impact and reversibility of their actions. Read-only operations (data retrieval, analysis, summarisation) execute freely. Write operations (updating records, triggering workflows, sending communications) require explicit human approval. Hard-to-reverse actions always pause for confirmation.
2. Confidence Disclosure
Every agent output must disclose its confidence level. Low-confidence outputs are flagged for deeper human review. High-confidence outputs receive lighter review. The system — not the human — determines which outputs need attention. This prevents automation bias at scale.
3. Structured Outputs as Guardrails
Agent responses should be structured (JSON schemas, typed fields, enumerated categories) rather than free-text wherever possible. Structured outputs are validatable, auditable, and reduce hallucination surface. Free-text narratives are the exception, not the default.
4. Graceful Degradation
When an agent fails — model timeout, API error, unexpected input — the system must degrade gracefully: checkpoint state, escalate to human, and never corrupt upstream data. Idempotent design ensures partial failures don’t create inconsistent states. The system loses time, never data.
5. Version-Controlled Behaviour
Agent instructions (system prompts), model IDs, and tool configurations are versioned in Git. Semantic versioning applies: major changes (new capabilities, changed scope) require revalidation; minor changes (quality improvements) require regression testing; patches (typos, formatting) require no action.
6. Operational Monitoring
Every agent in production must track: invocation count, latency, error rates, override rates, output quality samples, and cost. Override rates >15–20% trigger investigation. These metrics feed into the MRM monitoring requirement — not as separate work, but as the same process.

Agent Maintenance Lifecycle

Agents are not “set and forget” systems. They require ongoing maintenance proportionate to their tier:

ActivityTier 1Tier 2Tier 3
Model ID pinning & update testingOn changeQuarterlyMonthly
Prompt regression testingOn changeMonthlyBi-weekly
Output quality samplingSpot checksMonthly (20+ samples)Weekly (50+ samples)
Bias & fairness audit—AnnualSemi-annual
Formal model validation (MRM)—Biennial (by owner)Annual (by CRO)
Cost monitoringAwarenessMonthly budget checkPer-invocation tracking
Canary testing (inject known-incorrect inputs)—QuarterlyMonthly

Named ownership is mandatory: every agent has a Model Owner (responsible for performance and compliance) and a System Owner (responsible for infrastructure and availability). No ownerless agents in production.

Model Context Protocol (MCP)

MCP is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems — data sources, tools, and workflows. Think of it as the "USB-C port for AI": just as USB-C provides a standardised way to connect devices, MCP provides a standardised way to connect AI to everything else.

Why MCP Matters for CLM

CLM processes require AI to interact with many different systems — client databases, document stores, sanctions lists, corporate registries, CRM platforms, policy engines. Without MCP, each integration is a custom, fragile point-to-point connection. With MCP, you build a connector once and any AI application can use it.

1×Build once
N×Use everywhere
0Custom glue code

MCP Architecture

MCP follows a clean client-server model with three participants:

MCP Host
The AI application that needs context — an AI agent, chatbot, copilot, or orchestrator. The host manages one or more MCP clients. CLM example: A KYC review agent that needs to pull data from FenX, check sanctions lists, and read policy documents.
MCP Client
A component within the host that maintains a dedicated connection to one MCP server. Each client handles the protocol — initialisation, capability negotiation, request routing. Think of it as: The "plug" that connects one host to one server.
MCP Server
A program that exposes data, tools, or workflows to AI applications. Can run locally (same machine) or remotely (cloud service). CLM example: A FenX MCP server that exposes client records as resources and KYC operations as tools.

The Three Primitives

MCP servers expose exactly three types of capabilities. This simplicity is the power — three building blocks compose into unlimited functionality:

🔧 Tools

Executable functions that AI applications can invoke to perform actions — file operations, API calls, database queries, calculations, system commands.

CLM examples:

  • fenx_get_client(client_id) — retrieve client record
  • sanctions_screen(name, dob) — run sanctions check
  • create_review_case(client_id) — initiate periodic review

📂 Resources

Data sources that provide contextual information — file contents, database records, API responses, configuration data. Resources give AI the information it needs to reason.

CLM examples:

  • Client onboarding documents (PDFs, scans)
  • KYC policy documents and thresholds
  • Transaction history and patterns

💬 Prompts

Reusable templates that structure interactions with language models — system prompts, few-shot examples, role definitions. Prompts ensure consistent, high-quality AI behaviour.

CLM examples:

  • SoW narrative template with required sections
  • Risk assessment prompt with SEB's taxonomy
  • Client communication templates by language

MCP in a CLM Architecture

Here is how MCP would connect a CLM AI agent to SEB's ecosystem:

Scenario: AI-Assisted Periodic KYC Review
Scenario: AI-Assisted Periodic KYC Review

A KYC analyst triggers a periodic review. The orchestrator agent connects to multiple systems via MCP:

MCP ServerProvidesAgent Uses It To
FenX ServerClient records, KYC data (Resources + Tools)Pull current client profile, update fields after review
Document Store ServerOnboarding documents, financial statements (Resources)Extract data from uploaded documents
Sanctions ServerScreening results (Tools)Run real-time sanctions and PEP checks
Registry ServerCorporate registry data (Resources + Tools)Verify company structure, UBOs, financial data
Policy ServerKYC policies, risk thresholds (Resources + Prompts)Apply correct policy rules to the assessment
CRM ServerRM notes, interaction history (Resources)Context for relationship understanding

The agent discovers available tools at startup via tools/list, negotiates capabilities, and dynamically adapts to what each server offers. If a server is updated (e.g., new sanctions list format), it sends a notification and the agent refreshes — no code changes needed.

Transport Layer

MCP supports two transport mechanisms — both using the same JSON-RPC 2.0 message format:

TransportHow It WorksBest For
StdioStandard input/output streams between local processesLocal development, same-machine integrations, testing
Streamable HTTPHTTP POST + Server-Sent Events for streamingRemote servers, cloud services, production deployments

Ecosystem Support

MCP is not a niche protocol — it has broad industry adoption:

  • AI assistants: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini
  • Development tools: VS Code (Copilot), Cursor, Windsurf
  • Agent frameworks: Goose (70+ MCP extensions), LangChain, CrewAI
  • Open governance: Linux Foundation project, open specification, SDKs for Python, TypeScript, Java, Kotlin, C#
Strategic Implication

Investing in MCP servers for CLM systems (FenX, document stores, sanctions databases) creates reusable AI infrastructure. Any future AI application — whether built internally or by vendors — can immediately connect to these systems. This is the difference between building one integration and building a platform.

Further Reading

  • What is MCP? — Official Introduction ↗
  • MCP Architecture Overview ↗
  • MCP Reference Server Implementations (GitHub) ↗
  • Goose — Open-Source AI Agent with MCP Support ↗
Reading scope

FenX Integration — Connecting AI Agents to CLM

The MCP tab explains the protocol. This tab explains the target system. FenX (Fenergo SaaS) is the CLM platform SEB is onboarding for KYC/CDD. Understanding its architecture is essential for anyone building or specifying AI integrations — because agents can only act on systems they can reach, and FenX has specific patterns for how external systems connect.

Why This Matters

Every AI agent that reads client data, triggers a review, or updates a KYC record will go through FenX APIs. This is not optional infrastructure — it is the road. The architecture below determines what is technically possible for KAICY and every future CLM agent.

Platform Architecture

FenX is an Event Sourced, CQRS, API-first platform. Three facts shape every integration:

CQRS
Command APIs (write operations) are separated from Query APIs (read operations). You write to one endpoint and read from another. This means: after creating a record, you may need to wait briefly before it appears in queries.
Event Sourced
Every state change is an immutable event. Nothing is overwritten — history is preserved. This gives you a full audit trail by design, which aligns with EU AI Act Article 12 record-keeping requirements.
API-First
"Whatever you can do through the Fenergo User Interface, you can do through the APIs." — This is the principle that makes AI agents viable. Every human workflow has a programmatic equivalent.

Authentication

All API access uses Client Credential Flow → Bearer Token:

  • Token TTL: 15 minutes (must be cached — auth endpoint is throttled)
  • Required headers: x-tenant-id + authorization: Bearer <token>
  • Tokens are bearer-only — any client presenting a valid token gets access (no additional identity binding)

Eventual Consistency — The Critical Caveat

FenX Command responses return before data is committed to the Data Store. This means:

  • A Query immediately after a Command may return HTTP 404
  • Recommended: 2-5 second retry with exponential backoff
  • Same applies to webhook events — there is a minuscule chance of stale data

For AI agents, this means: never assume immediate read-after-write consistency. Build retry logic into every agent that writes then reads.

Five Integration Patterns

FenX supports five standard patterns for connecting external systems. Each has a specific use case — choosing the right one determines whether your integration is clean or fragile:

PatternDirectionWhen to UseCLM Agent Example
1. Direct API (CQRS)External → FenX (bidirectional)Any direct read/write — client data, journey management, field updatesKAICY reads client profile, updates data fields after call transcription extraction
2. Event NotificationFenX → ExternalReact to changes inside FenX — new client, journey completed, risk score changedAgent triggers periodic review preparation when FenX emits "review due" event
3. Data SyncFenX → External (persist)Keep an external system updated with FenX data (e.g., BigQuery analytics layer)Data Layer receives all client updates for portfolio dashboards and AI training
4. External AdapterFenX → Your System (callback)FenX needs data from an external source during a journey (screening, registry lookups)Custom screening adapter connects FenX to SEB's internal sanctions database
5. Event IngressExternal → FenX (one call triggers workflow)Kick off an entire FenX business process from outside — data import, create entity, alertUpstream system detects ownership change → sends Event Ingress → FenX auto-starts review

External Adapters — Three Types

When FenX needs data from an external system during a journey (rather than the other way around), it uses External Adapters. FenX calls your hosted endpoint:

📡 External Data Adapter

Async pattern. FenX sends a data request to your adapter. Your system processes it, then calls back to FenX's Receptor API with the result. Used for corporate registry lookups, external database enrichment, or any data source FenX doesn't natively connect to.

Key detail: The callback uses a Receptor endpoint — your adapter must store the callback URL from the initial request.

🛡️ Custom Screening Adapter

Async + encrypted PII. Same callback pattern as Data Adapter, but handles personally identifiable information with additional encryption. Used for sanctions screening, PEP checks, adverse media. PII is encrypted in transit even within the platform boundary.

Key detail: Screening results return via a dedicated Screening Receptor endpoint — separate from the data receptor.

⚡ Policy Field Provider

Synchronous. Unlike the other two, this adapter responds in real-time. FenX calls your endpoint during form rendering — your system returns field suggestions or auto-populated values. Used for real-time policy lookups, dynamic form behaviour, or AI-powered field suggestions.

Key detail: Must respond within FenX's timeout window — latency-sensitive. Ideal for lightweight AI inference (classification, suggestion).

Event Notification — Push vs. Pull

ModeHow It WorksReliabilityBest For
Push (Webhooks)FenX delivers events to your endpoint in real-time. Delivery confirmed on HTTP < 400.Back-off retry: 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 min. Webhook disabled after max retries. Must re-enable to resume.Real-time reactions — trigger agent workflows immediately when something happens in FenX
Pull (Polling)Your system polls a notification queue. Messages removed only after you confirm "handled."Messages persist up to 30 days. Guaranteed delivery to queue. Your system controls consumption pace.Batch processing, systems with intermittent connectivity, guaranteed-delivery requirements

API Catalogue — Key Domains

FenX exposes 30+ API domains at api.fenergox.com, all with OpenAPI/Swagger specifications. The most relevant for CLM AI agents:

DomainWhat It ProvidesAgent Use Case
Entity DataClient records, legal entities, corporate structuresRead/write client profiles, extract relationship graphs
JourneyOnboarding and review workflow managementStart reviews, check progress, move stages
Document ManagementUpload, retrieve, classify documentsIngest extracted documents, attach AI outputs
Policy EngineRules, requirements, risk thresholdsDetermine what data is required for a given client type
Risk & ScreeningRisk scores, screening results, alertsFeed screening data into AI risk assessment
Event NotificationsSubscribe to and consume platform eventsTrigger agent workflows on state changes
External OutreachClient-facing data collection via secure linksOrchestrate automated client outreach for missing data
The MCP Connection

Each FenX API domain is a candidate for an MCP Server. A FenX MCP Server would wrap these APIs and expose them as Tools (write operations), Resources (read operations), and Prompts (templates for structuring queries). Build the MCP server once — every future AI agent can use it. This is how the "build once, use everywhere" principle from the MCP tab becomes concrete.

What This Means for CLM Builders

Available now
Full API documentation publicly available at docs.fenergox.com. OpenAPI specs downloadable. No NDA required to read integration docs. Prototype integrations possible in any GCP development environment.
Requires coordination
Tenant credentials, IP whitelisting (FenX requires your egress IPs), webhook registration, adapter endpoint hosting. Coordinate with FenX onboarding team and SEB infrastructure.
Strategic decision
Which integration pattern to use for each agent capability. Direct API vs. Event-driven vs. Adapter pattern — this is an architecture decision that should be made once and documented, not discovered per-project.

Source-First Data Access — Architecture Decision (May 2026)

Architecture Decision Record

All new CLM AI use cases use source-first data access. This means agents go to the authoritative data source — not cached copies. KycStore is explicitly excluded from new use cases.

Access ModeSource SystemWhen to Use
Real-timeFenX APIs (CQRS) + CSS GraphQL + IPD/DnbPlusFacadeAgent needs current client data during a workflow (e.g., field lookup, enrichment check)
Batch/AnalyticsGroup Involved Party (GIP) in BigQuery (full_group_involved_party)Portfolio-level analysis, training data, cross-client pattern detection, reporting
ExcludedKycStoreLegacy system — not used for new AI use cases. Stale data, no real-time guarantees.

Rationale: As of May 2026, GCP is the boundary where C4 data + Gemini + VPC-SC + IAM + GIP + FenX APIs coexist without cross-platform complexity. This makes it the strongest current candidate for CLM AI workloads. The assessment should be revisited if material constraints change (e.g., approved LLMs in other environments, cross-cloud GIP federation).

Data Governance — Source Tiering for AI Enrichment

When AI agents propose data changes to client records, the changes follow a strict source tiering hierarchy. AI-generated data is never written directly to golden fields — it always goes through a human-gated proposal mechanism.

T1 — Analyst Verified
Human analyst has personally verified against primary source. Highest trust. Cannot be overwritten by any automated process.
T2 — Client Attested
Client self-declared via portal or signed document. High trust but unverified against external source.
T3 — Registry
Government or commercial registry (D&B, Bolagsverket, Companies House). Authoritative for structured data.
T4 — System Calculated
Deterministic rules or formulas (e.g., risk score from indicator weights). Reproducible and auditable.
T5 — AI Inferred
AI-generated enrichment. Probabilistic. Always enters as “proposed” — never overwrites verified data. Requires human acceptance to promote to golden record.
T6 — Legacy/Untagged
Historical data without source provenance. Lowest trust. Target for systematic re-verification.

Survivorship rule: Higher tier ALWAYS wins. AI (T5) never overwrites analyst-verified (T1) or client-attested (T2) data. Verified data is immutable during an active journey.

FenX Journey Architecture — What AI Agents Actually Touch

The FenX Integration tab shows how to connect. This tab shows what is inside — the actual onboarding journey structure, field architecture, data paths, and where AI creates the most value. Based on the PWM&FO journey mapping by Alexander da Silva Villalba (CLM Development).

450+ numbered fields · 10 stages · 29 processes · 62 tasks

This is the real scale of a single FenX onboarding journey for Natural Persons. Every field has a unique number, a data type, and an actor who enters it. AI agents must know which field path to read or write — analyst-entered, client-submitted, and system-generated data live in parallel paths with different field IDs.

The 10 Onboarding Stages

Each stage has a distinct purpose, actor, and set of FenX tasks. The journey reads left to right — and AI opportunity increases as you move deeper.

Stage 1
New Request — Capture basic client details (10 fields: name, DoB, client type, country, GIP, entity, BU, booking location). Actor: KYC Analyst. This is the intake gate.
Stage 2
Initial Client Enrichment — The heaviest data capture stage. 13 categories covering identity, addresses, employment, source of wealth & funds, purpose & nature, cash transactions, international transactions, and relationship linking. Actor: KYC Analyst. Also produces initial risk score and outreach decision.
Stage 3
Internal Outreach — Welcome Team prepares client-facing outreach. Same data categories as Stage 2 but rephrased as client-facing questions. Includes portal preparation: outreach scoping, magic link generation (IntegrationsDataPublishTask), and portal quick links.
Stage 4
Client Outreach — Client self-service via FenX portal. 7 data tasks all assigned to Client: identity, occupation, tax, wealth/funds, domestic payments, cash, international transfers. Plus related party management and document upload. Outreach snapshot imported back to FenX on completion.
Stage 5
Review Client Outreach — KYC Analyst reviews all client-submitted data. Compares portal responses against analyst expectations. This is where discrepancies surface.
Stage 6
Client Enrichment — Final enriched version. Analyst merges all data sources into the authoritative record. Also includes Screening and ID&V tasks.
Stage 7
Screening — PEP/sanctions screening resolution and identity verification. Uses ScreeningTask and IDVTask FenX task types.
Stage 8
KYC Assessment — Risk model execution, risk score calculation, KYC level determination, and the critical Overall AML Risk Assessment narrative. If EDD triggered: enhanced SoW/SoF deep dive. The most complex stage for AI.
Stage 9
Review & Approval — KYC Manager reviews entire case (18 categories). Can escalate to CAC Specialist (Client Acceptance Forum). Includes journey blocking and cancellation paths.
Stage 10
Verify & Complete — System-automated verification of related parties, entity data, and KYC due date calculation. No human actor — purely system tasks.

Parallel Data Paths — The Hidden Architecture

The same data (e.g., “First Name”) has different FenX field IDs depending on who enters it. This is not a bug — it is how FenX tracks provenance and enables reconciliation:

Data PathField RangeActorStage
Analyst intake#1 – #10KYC AnalystStage 1 (New Request)
Analyst enrichment#58 – #149KYC AnalystStage 2 (Initial Enrichment)
Welcome Team outreach#153 – #226Welcome TeamStage 3 (Internal Outreach)
Client portal#227 – #300Client (self-service)Stage 4 (Client Outreach)
Post-outreach enrichment#301 – #370KYC AnalystStage 6 (Client Enrichment)
Assessment & review#405 – #450KYC Analyst / ManagerStages 8–9 (Assessment & Approval)
Why this matters for AI agents

An AI agent that pre-fills client data must write to the correct field path. Writing to analyst fields (#58–#149) when the data came from a client portal response (#227–#300) would break the audit trail and reconciliation logic. Understanding this architecture is a prerequisite for any FenX automation.

FenX Task Types

FenX uses specialised task types for different workflow actions. Each maps to specific agent capabilities:

IntegrationsDataPublishTaskIntegration/API trigger (portal link)Orchestration hook for agent workflows

AI Opportunity Map

Where AI creates the most value in the journey, mapped to specific stages and field ranges:

⚡ Stage 2 — Pre-fill from External Sources

AI pulls data from GIP, D&B, previous reviews to pre-populate the 13-category enrichment. Targets fields #58–#149. Reduces analyst data entry from hours to minutes.

Tier: Augment (T2) · Prerequisite: IPD API / GIP data product access

🔍 Stage 5 — Outreach Anomaly Detection

AI compares client-submitted portal data (#227–#300) against analyst-entered data (#58–#149) and flags discrepancies. Nationality changed? Income figure doubled? Address moved country?

Tier: Augment (T2) · Prerequisite: Read access to both field paths

📄 Stage 8 — Risk Narrative Generation

AI drafts the Overall AML Risk Assessment (field #412, textArea) from risk factors, screening results, and enrichment data. The analyst reviews and edits rather than writing from scratch.

Tier: Augment (T2–T3) · Prerequisite: Risk model output + enrichment data access

📝 Stage 3 — Outreach Scope Suggestion

AI assists the Welcome Team in deciding which data gaps to prioritise for client outreach (fields #435–#437) based on risk profile and missing data patterns.

Tier: Assist (T1) · Prerequisite: Stage 2 data + risk score

📃 Stage 6 — Data Reconciliation

AI merges analyst, Welcome Team, and client data into the final enrichment, flagging conflicts and suggesting resolutions. Three sources, one authoritative record.

Tier: Augment (T2) · Prerequisite: All three field paths readable

✅ FATCA/CRS Classification

Decision tree logic is fully deterministic — ideal for rule-based automation. AI handles edge cases where classification is ambiguous (e.g., Central Bank with no direct FATCA label).

Tier: Assist/Automate (T1) · Prerequisite: Entity type + FI status data

Treatment Actions — FenX Is the Single Target

Two open BWRA treatment actions confirm the strategic direction:

TA 69:2025
Enhance CRS in FenX — Evaluate and incorporate additional risk indicators into the FenX customer risk scoring model. Active development.
TA 70:2025
Sunset ALL Legacy CRS — Decommission every local customer risk scoring model across PWM&FO sites. FenX Risk Model is the only survivor. No point building AI on platforms that are being sunset.

Source: PWM&FO Journey Mapping, Risk Model Engine, Treatment Actions, FATCA & CRS Classification Tool — Alexander da Silva Villalba, CLM Development. Collected May 2026.

Agent Orchestration Patterns

When you move beyond a single agent to multiple agents working together, you need orchestration — the discipline of coordinating, routing, and managing agent workflows. This is where the real complexity (and power) emerges.

Core Orchestration Concepts

🎯 Task Decomposition

Break complex goals into discrete, manageable sub-tasks. A "complete KYC review" becomes: collect documents → extract data → verify identity → screen sanctions → assess risk → generate narrative → route for approval.

🔀 Routing & Dispatch

The orchestrator decides which agent handles which task based on the task type, required capabilities, and current workload. Smart routing can parallelise independent tasks for speed.

🔄 State Management

Track where each workflow stands — which steps are complete, which are blocked, what data has been produced. Essential for resuming after failures and providing audit trails.

🚦 Quality Gates

Checkpoints where outputs are validated before proceeding — human approval, automated quality checks, compliance verification. In CLM, every high-risk decision is a gate.

🔁 Error Recovery

When an agent fails (bad output, timeout, API error), the orchestrator retries, routes to a fallback agent, or escalates to a human. Graceful degradation, not catastrophic failure.

📊 Observability

Logging, metrics, and tracing across all agents — who did what, when, with what inputs and outputs. Critical for debugging, compliance audit, and performance optimisation.

Orchestration Patterns

Different workflow shapes suit different CLM processes:

Sequential Chain
Agents execute in order — output of one feeds input of the next. Simple, predictable, easy to audit. Best for: Document processing pipelines (extract → classify → validate → store).
Parallel Fan-Out
Multiple agents work simultaneously on independent tasks, results merged by orchestrator. Best for: KYC data collection (sanctions check + registry lookup + adverse media search happening in parallel).
Hierarchical
Supervisor agents manage groups of worker agents, escalating only exceptions. Multiple levels possible. Best for: Large-scale periodic review campaigns (supervisor assigns cases, workers execute, supervisor reviews quality).
Workflow Molecules
Pre-defined workflow templates (inspired by Steve Yegge's MEOW stack) — chained task sequences that agents follow step-by-step. Durable across agent restarts. Best for: Complex multi-day processes like EDD investigations where state must persist.

The 7 Composable Architecture Patterns (Anthropic, May 2026)

Source: “Building Effective Agents” — Anthropic’s distilled experience from dozens of production agent deployments. Core principle: “The most successful implementations weren’t using complex frameworks. They were building with simple, composable patterns.”

Why This Matters for SEB

These 7 patterns are not theory — they are the industry-standard architecture vocabulary for production agents. Google’s ADK 2.0 (GA 19 May 2026) implements each pattern as a first-class primitive. SEB’s approved platform now has native support for the full pattern set. Every CLM use case maps to one or more of these patterns.

1. Augmented LLM

What: LLM enhanced with retrieval, tools, and memory. The building block for everything else.

CLM: Every use case starts here — Gemini + FenX tools + knowledge retrieval. Single model with structured access to CLM data.

ADK 2.0: Base agent with tool declarations + memory store.

2. Prompt Chaining

What: Decompose task into fixed sequential steps. Each LLM call processes output of previous one. Programmatic gates between steps.

CLM: CDD Completeness: check field → classify gap → generate recommendation. KAICY: ingest → score → generate narrative.

ADK 2.0: Workflow primitive with sequential step execution.

3. Routing

What: Classify input, direct to specialised followup task. Separation of concerns.

CLM: BO Cross-Check: route by entity type (NP / LE / Trust) → specialised verification logic. P&N Classifier: route by business relationship type.

ADK 2.0: Routing Nodes — classify and direct to specialised agent paths.

4. Parallelization

What: Multiple LLMs work simultaneously, outputs aggregated. Variants: sectioning (split task) or voting (same task, multiple perspectives).

CLM: BWRA: parallel risk factor assessment. Screening: voting — multiple prompts evaluate same hit; majority “false positive” = auto-resolve.

ADK 2.0: Task API with fan-out/fan-in aggregation.

5. Orchestrator-Workers

What: Central LLM dynamically breaks down tasks, delegates to workers, synthesizes. Key difference from parallelization: subtasks NOT pre-defined.

CLM: RM Client Intelligence: orchestrator analyses portfolio → dispatches workers per client → synthesizes action list. PEP Network: map connections → synthesize risk.

ADK 2.0: Multi-Agent coordinator with specialist sub-agents.

6. Evaluator-Optimizer

What: One LLM generates, another evaluates and provides feedback in a loop. Iterates until quality threshold met.

CLM: STR Narrative: draft assessment → evaluate against Art. 69/70 → refine until regulatory-quality. KAICY: score → check → loop.

ADK 2.0: Loop Nodes with exit conditions.

7. Autonomous Agent

What: LLM dynamically directs its own process: plan → act → observe → assess → repeat. Pauses for human feedback at checkpoints.

CLM: EDD Enrichment: full autonomous research — searches, reads, extracts, synthesizes SoW/SoF dossier. PEP Network: autonomous graph exploration.

ADK 2.0: Full agent loop with tool access + stopping conditions.

Decision Framework: When to Use What

ComplexityPatternWhen to ChooseCLM Example
LowestAugmented LLMSingle model call with good prompt + retrieval is ENOUGHCopilot answering policy questions
LowPrompt ChainingTask cleanly decomposes into fixed subtasks; accuracy > latencyCDD field completeness scoring
LowRoutingDistinct categories better handled separatelyEntity-type routing (NP vs LE vs Trust)
MediumParallelizationIndependent subtasks can run simultaneously; or voting neededMulti-source screening
MediumEvaluator-OptimizerClear evaluation criteria exist; iterative refinement adds valueRegulatory narrative generation
HighOrchestrator-WorkersCan’t predict subtasks in advance; dynamic decomposition neededFull periodic review orchestration
HighestAutonomous AgentOpen-ended problems; trusted environment; human checkpointsEDD autonomous research
Critical Principle

Start with the simplest solution. Add complexity ONLY when it measurably improves outcomes. For many CLM applications, optimising a single LLM call with good retrieval and in-context examples is enough. Agentic systems trade latency and cost for better task performance — ensure the trade-off is justified.

Lessons from the Frontier

The most advanced agent orchestration systems (Gas Town, Temporal, Kubernetes) reveal patterns directly applicable to CLM:

Persistent Agent Identities
Persistent Agent Identities

Agents are not ephemeral sessions — they have persistent identities with histories, performance records, and specialisations. In CLM, this means a "SoW Corroboration Agent" has a track record of accuracy, a known set of capabilities, and a documented decision history that compliance can audit.

Nondeterministic Idempotence
Nondeterministic Idempotence

Even though AI agents are nondeterministic (same input can produce different outputs), workflows can be made effectively idempotent — if an agent crashes mid-workflow, another picks up where it left off, and the end result is functionally equivalent. Critical for CLM where a KYC review might span hours and multiple system calls.

Merge Queues & Conflict Resolution
Merge Queues & Conflict Resolution

When multiple agents produce outputs that need to be consolidated (e.g., different agents enriching the same client profile), a merge process ensures consistency. In software this is a merge queue; in CLM it is a reconciliation step where conflicting data is flagged for human review.

Graceful Degradation
Graceful Degradation

The best orchestration systems work even when parts fail. Each agent can operate independently, in small groups, or as part of the full system. In CLM: if the automated SoW agent is down, the process continues manually. If the orchestrator is down, individual agents still work. AI accelerates; it never becomes a single point of failure.

Further Reading

Steve Yegge — "Welcome to Gas Town" ↗ — A deep exploration of agent orchestration patterns: MEOW stack (Molecular Expression of Work), persistent identities, convoy-based work tracking, and "Kubernetes for agents" thinking. While focused on software development, the orchestration principles map directly to CLM workflows.

Agent Security — Threat Model for CLM

Regulatory compliance (covered in Section 5) is necessary but not sufficient. AI agents operating in CLM introduce technical attack surfaces that traditional security controls were not designed for. This section equips readers to think about agent security as a first-class concern — not an afterthought.

The New Attack Surface

"We cannot secure what we do not understand." — SANS Institute. As AI agents become autonomous decision-makers with tool access, the attack surface shifts from data-at-rest to decisions-in-motion. A compromised agent doesn't just leak data — it can take actions: approve cases, route workflows, generate outputs that humans trust by default.

Agent-Specific Threat Vectors

These threats are unique to agentic systems — they don't exist in traditional software and require new defensive thinking:

ThreatWhat It IsCLM ImpactMitigation
Prompt InjectionMalicious instructions hidden in documents, emails, or data fields that override agent behaviour when processedA document submitted for KYC review contains hidden instructions that manipulate the agent's risk assessmentInput sanitisation, content separation (data vs. instructions), Constitutional Classifiers, output validation against policy rules
Tool PoisoningA compromised or malicious MCP server returns manipulated data when agents query itA screening MCP server returns "no match" for a sanctioned entity — agent proceeds without flaggingTool verification, response validation against known-good sources, anomaly detection on tool outputs
Rug PullsAn MCP server behaves correctly during testing but changes behaviour in production (after trust is established)External data adapter passes all integration tests, then starts returning manipulated corporate registry dataContinuous monitoring, canary queries with known answers, integrity hashing of tool responses
Privilege EscalationAgent exploits broad permissions to access data or perform actions beyond its intended scopeA document extraction agent uses its FenX API token to read client records it shouldn't accessLeast-privilege token scoping, per-agent API credentials, action logging, scope-limited MCP servers
Reasoning ManipulationAdversarial inputs that cause the agent to reason incorrectly while appearing confident in its outputCarefully crafted client data patterns that consistently lead the agent to under-score riskConfidence calibration, adversarial testing (red-teaming), human review of edge cases, bias monitoring

The Four-Pillar Security Strategy

Based on the SANS/AWS framework for securing agentic AI systems, adapted for CLM:

🔐 1. Identity & Access

Every agent gets a unique identity. On GCP, this means a dedicated service account per agent with minimum-viable permissions. Agent tokens should be short-lived (align with FenX's 15-min TTL). OAuth delegation chains must be explicit — no inherited broad permissions.

CLM implementation: Any production CLM agent (e.g. KAICY) would get its own GCP service account. Sub-agents would each get scoped credentials limiting which FenX API domains they can reach.

🛡️ 2. Input Validation

Treat all external data as untrusted. Documents, API responses, user inputs — everything entering the agent's context must be validated. Separate the instruction channel (system prompt) from the data channel (user content). Never allow data to be interpreted as instructions.

CLM implementation: Documents uploaded for KYC review go through content sanitisation before agent processing. FenX API responses are schema-validated before agent consumption.

📊 3. Runtime Monitoring

Watch what agents do, not just what they produce. Log every tool invocation, every API call, every decision point. Use anomaly detection to flag unusual patterns — an agent that suddenly queries 100x more records, or one that starts approving cases 3x faster.

CLM implementation: GCP Cloud Trace for agent execution paths. Alert on: override rate spikes, unusual API call patterns, processing time anomalies, confidence score distribution shifts.

🧪 4. Continuous Testing

Agents drift. Test continuously, not just at deployment. Inject known-incorrect inputs (canary testing) to verify agents still reject bad data. Run adversarial prompts monthly. Compare outputs against gold-standard cases. Track accuracy over time, not just at launch.

CLM implementation: Monthly canary tests with known sanctioned entities. Quarterly adversarial prompt injection testing. Continuous comparison against human-reviewed baseline cases.

MCP-Specific Security Controls

The Model Context Protocol introduces specific security considerations because it standardises how agents connect to tools:

ControlPurposeImplementation
Server authenticationVerify MCP servers are who they claim to bemTLS between MCP client and server, certificate pinning for critical servers (FenX, sanctions)
Tool allowlistingAgents can only invoke pre-approved toolsAgent Gateway enforces tool manifest — unknown tools rejected. Aligns with GCP Agent Registry.
Response validationDetect manipulated tool responsesSchema validation on every MCP response. Integrity checks for critical data (screening results, risk scores).
Scope limitationEach MCP server exposes only what the agent needsBuild narrow MCP servers (e.g., "FenX Read-Only" vs "FenX Write") rather than one broad server.
Audit loggingFull trail of agent-tool interactionsEvery MCP request/response logged with timestamps, agent ID, and correlation ID for traceability.

Security by Tier

Agent security requirements scale with the governance tier (Section 2):

Tier 1 (Assist)
Standard SEB security controls. No autonomous actions. Human initiates every interaction. Low risk — but still requires input sanitisation and output validation. Example: Policy Q&A agent that only reads documents.
Tier 2 (Augment)
Dedicated agent identity. Tool-level access controls. Continuous monitoring with anomaly detection. Monthly adversarial testing. Output validation against policy rules before presenting to users. Example: KAICY extracting and pre-populating data for analyst review.
Tier 3 (Orchestrate)
Per-agent cryptographic identity (SPIFFE). Multi-agent interaction logging. Real-time anomaly detection. Formal red-team exercises quarterly. Agent Gateway enforcement. Human approval gates at every consequential decision. Example: Multi-agent periodic review workflow.
Practical Priority

Start with the basics: unique agent identities, least-privilege access, and comprehensive logging. These three controls address 80% of the attack surface. Advanced controls (anomaly detection, adversarial testing, MCP-level security) layer on as you move to Tier 2-3 agents. Don't let security perfection delay Tier 1 delivery.

Source: SANS Institute / AWS — "Navigating modern application security challenges with evolved reliance on AI-based applications" (2025) + Anthropic "Trustworthy Agents in Practice" (April 2026) + Google Agent Platform security documentation (May 2026)

Deloitte's Agentic Architecture for CLM[2]

Deloitte's March 2026 presentation to SEB outlined a production-tested four-layer agentic architecture specifically designed for KYC/AML processes. Their benchmarks show transformative results: periodic review time from 90 to <30 minutes (-67%), onboarding time from 14 to <5 days (-65%), and file revisit rates from 49% to <5% (-90%).

The Four-Layer Pattern

Based on SEB's own ADK exploration[5] and Deloitte's framework:

Orchestrator
Receives user intent, decomposes into sub-tasks, routes to functional agents, aggregates results, manages workflow state. CLM analogy: The senior analyst who receives a complex case and decides what happens in what order. Tech: ADK on Gemini 2.5 Pro.
Functional Agents
Specialised domain agents — CDD Evaluation, SoW Corroboration, Document Extraction, Regulatory Mapping. Each has its own system prompt, tool access, and output schema. CLM analogy: The specialist team — sanctions screener, document reviewer, risk scorer. Tech: Gemini 2.5 Flash or Pro.
Helper Agents
Cross-cutting shared services — Translation, Summarisation, Citation (tracking provenance). Reusable across functional agents. CLM analogy: Shared services — QA, translation, formatting. Tech: Gemini 2.0 Flash (bounded tasks).
Utility Layer
Non-AI services agents call — database lookups, API integrations (sanctions lists, registries, credit bureaus), file storage, logging, audit trail. CLM analogy: The systems and databases everyone accesses. Tech: Standard APIs, GCP services.

Case Studies

Source of Wealth Corroboration Agent

Decomposes declared SoW into verifiable claims, searches external sources for corroborating or contradicting evidence, produces a structured report with confidence levels and evidence links.

Agent chain: Document Classifier → Extractor → Income Calculators (Employment, Business Profit, Investment, Inheritance) → Net Wealth Estimator → Discrepancy Analyser → Benchmark Lookup → Risk Flag Identifier → SoW Narrator → Final Narrative

Human gate: Analyst reviews every corroboration report, approves or rejects with rationale, before it enters the client record. AI write-ups shown in teal — can be accepted, adjusted, or re-written at each level.

CDD Evaluation Agent

Assesses client risk profile against SEB's risk taxonomy, pulls data from multiple internal and external sources, produces a draft risk score with itemised rationale.

Agent chain: Document Classifier → OCR Extractor → Information Extractor → News Summarizer → Web Scraper → Match Analyzer → Discrepancy Analyser → Net Wealth Estimator → Consistency Checker → Summary Writer → AML Final Assessment → Template Compiler → CDD Report

Human gate: Analyst reviews every evaluation, adjusts scores where judgement differs, and signs off before classification becomes official.

Design Principle

The architecture should be designed so that removing the AI layer would leave a functional (if slower) manual process. AI accelerates and augments; it does not become a single point of failure. This also ensures regulatory resilience — if a model is withdrawn, the business continues.

Human-in-the-Loop Requirements

In CLM, human oversight is a regulatory and ethical necessity, not merely a preference. The role of the human shifts from "doing" to "supervising" — maintaining control consistent with the risk of KYC/AML processes.[4][2]

The Three Paradigms

Human-in-the-Loop
Humans make final decisions based on pre-population, pre-checks, and pre-approvals by agents within guardrails. This is the appropriate paradigm for CLM. Agents do the preparation; humans own the decision.
Human-on-the-Loop
Agents make decisions autonomously, humans monitor and can intervene. Not appropriate for high-risk KYC/AML in the foreseeable future. Could apply to low-risk, high-volume screening with established accuracy.
Human-out-of-the-Loop
Fully autonomous AI with no human involvement. Unwise and likely non-compliant for any consequential CLM process. Reserved for purely internal, non-customer-facing utility tasks.

Process Stage Requirements

Process StageAgent ActionHuman RoleOverride
Document extractionExtract & classify dataSpot-check (sample-based)Analyst corrects any extraction
Risk pre-scoringCalculate preliminary indicatorsReview every scoreOverride with documented rationale
SoW corroborationCross-reference against sourcesReview flagged discrepanciesFull override — human is final word
EDD triggerIdentify EDD-required clientsApprove every triggerCan add or remove triggers
Case summaryGenerate narrative findingsEdit and sign offFull editorial control

Monitoring Agent Effectiveness

Continuous monitoring on human adjustments is necessary to ensure agents remain effective and do not "drift":

  • Override rate tracking: If analysts override agent recommendations more than 15–20%, investigate — the agent may be drifting or the policy may have changed
  • Quality scoring: Compare agent outputs against expert-reviewed gold standard cases
  • Benefit tracking: Measure time savings, accuracy improvements, and throughput per analyst
  • Bias monitoring: Ensure agent decisions are not systematically skewed by client demographics, geography, or industry
Organisational Change

Substantial change effort is needed to optimise staff effectiveness as their role shifts from operator to expert, reviewer, and supervisor. This is not just a technology deployment — it is a fundamental redesign of how KYC work is done, requiring training, new performance metrics, and cultural adaptation.

How AI Can Transform CLM

AI is not a single tool — it is a capability layer that can be applied across every stage of the client lifecycle. The key is to think in terms of patterns, not individual products. Once you recognise the pattern, you can see dozens of use cases from your own perspective and domain expertise.

The Seven AI Capability Patterns

Every AI application in CLM falls into one or more of these fundamental patterns:

🔍 Pattern Recognition

AI excels at finding signals in noise — anomalous transactions, unusual relationship structures, emerging risk indicators across thousands of clients that no human could manually review.

Imagine: A system that continuously scans your entire client portfolio and surfaces the 15 cases that need attention today — before anyone asks.

📄 Document Intelligence

Extracting structured data from unstructured documents — passports, financial statements, corporate registries, tax returns, annual reports — and cross-referencing across sources automatically.

Imagine: Dropping a stack of onboarding documents into a system and getting a pre-filled client profile with flagged inconsistencies in minutes, not hours.

✍️ Narrative Generation

AI can draft case summaries, risk assessments, compliance reports, and client communications — producing first drafts that analysts review and refine rather than write from scratch.

Imagine: Every periodic KYC review starts with an AI-drafted narrative that captures all data changes since the last review — the analyst edits rather than creates.

📊 Dashboards & Analytics

Real-time visualisation of portfolio health, KPI tracking, workload distribution, compliance status, and trend analysis — turning raw data into actionable insight for managers and teams.

Imagine: A dashboard where every team lead sees their team's KYC backlog, average review time, upcoming deadlines, and quality scores — updated in real-time.

⚡ Task Automation

Repetitive, rule-based tasks that consume analyst time — data entry, status updates, notification routing, deadline tracking, document requests — can be fully or partially automated.

Imagine: When a client's corporate structure changes in a registry, the system automatically triggers a review, pulls updated data, and notifies the assigned analyst.

🧠 Decision Support

AI provides recommendations with evidence and confidence levels — risk scores, classification suggestions, next-best-action guidance — while the human retains final authority.

Imagine: A risk scoring engine that explains why it scored a client as high-risk, citing the specific data points, so the analyst can agree, adjust, or override with full context.

Where to Start: Low-Hanging Fruit

The most impactful AI applications share a common trait: they eliminate work that is high-volume, repetitive, and time-consuming while being low-risk and verifiable. Start here:

Use CasePatternImpactComplexity
Meeting transcription & summarisationNarrative GenerationSave 30–60 min per meetingLow
Document data extraction (passports, IDs)Document Intelligence80%+ time reduction on data entryMedium
Periodic review pre-populationTask Automation + NarrativeFirst draft in minutes vs. hoursMedium
KPI dashboards & reportingDashboards & AnalyticsReal-time visibility for managersLow
Anomaly detection in transactionsPattern RecognitionEarlier risk detection, fewer false positivesHigh
Source of Wealth corroborationDecision Support + Document Intel67% review time reduction (Deloitte benchmark)High
Key Insight

The most powerful insight about AI in CLM is this: you do not need to be technical to identify use cases. If you find yourself doing the same thing repeatedly, copying data between systems, or wishing you had a summary of something — that is a use case. The technology exists. The bottleneck is imagination and prioritisation, not capability.

The Transformation Spectrum

AI adoption in CLM follows a natural progression — each stage builds confidence and infrastructure for the next:

Stage 1: Assist
AI helps individuals work faster — copilots, search assistants, meeting summaries. Human does the work, AI provides inputs. Low risk, fast deployment, builds trust.
Stage 2: Augment
AI produces draft outputs that humans review — pre-filled forms, draft narratives, risk pre-scores. AI does first pass, human validates and edits. Medium risk, requires quality monitoring.
Stage 3: Automate
AI handles end-to-end processes with human oversight at gates — document processing pipelines, automated screening. AI executes, human supervises and intervenes. Higher risk, requires robust governance.
Stage 4: Orchestrate
Multiple AI agents coordinate complex workflows — full KYC reviews, cross-system data reconciliation. AI systems collaborate, human oversees the outcome. Highest complexity, requires the agentic architectures described in this section.
panels.arch-agents:
What Are AI Agents?

An AI agent is a system that can perceive its environment, make decisions, and take actions to achieve a goal — autonomously, without step-by-step human instruction. Unlike a chatbot that responds to prompts, an agent can plan multi-step workflows, use tools, call APIs, and adapt when things go wrong.

The Simple Analogy

A chatbot is like asking a colleague a question — you get an answer. An agent is like delegating a task to a colleague — they figure out the steps, gather what they need, do the work, and come back with the result. The shift is from question-answering to task-completion.

Agent Anatomy

Every AI agent, whether simple or complex, has the same fundamental components:

🧠 Reasoning Engine

The LLM at the core — interprets instructions, plans steps, makes decisions. Powered by models like Gemini, Claude, or GPT. The "brain" that decides what to do next.

🔧 Tools

Executable functions the agent can invoke — database queries, API calls, file operations, web searches, calculations. Tools are how agents act on the world.

💾 Memory

Context the agent carries — conversation history, task state, retrieved documents, intermediate results. Memory enables multi-step reasoning across a complex workflow.

📋 Instructions

The system prompt defining the agent's role, constraints, output format, and guardrails. In CLM, this includes regulatory boundaries, data access permissions, and escalation rules.

Agents need roads, not just engines

An agent is only as capable as the systems it can reach. Think of your connected systems — FenX APIs, policy databases, screening providers, document stores — as roads. Without roads, an agent faces the same bottlenecks as a human: switching between screens, copy-pasting between applications, waiting for responses. An agent with access to structured data via MCP servers can complete in minutes what takes an analyst hours. The same agent without those connections is a powerful engine parked in a garage.

This is why infrastructure comes before agents in any pragmatic portfolio. GCP access, FenX APIs, MCP servers, data access layers, and policy corpus — these are the roads. Equally important: good data quality. An agent driving on broken roads — inconsistent fields, missing identifiers, stale records — produces unreliable outputs no matter how sophisticated the model. Roads and data quality first, agents second.

Types of Agents in CLM

Based on Deloitte's agentic architecture for CLM[2] and industry patterns:

Orchestrator Agents
Coordinate end-to-end processes. Receive a goal (e.g., "complete periodic review for Client X"), decompose it into sub-tasks, assign to functional agents, aggregate results, manage exceptions. CLM example: A KYC review orchestrator that sequences document collection, data verification, risk scoring, and narrative generation.
Functional Agents
Execute specific business tasks — CDD evaluation, SoW corroboration, document extraction, name screening, adverse media search. Each has domain-specific prompts, tool access, and output schemas. CLM example: A Source of Wealth agent that verifies declared wealth against external registries and financial data.
Helper Agents
Provide cross-cutting services reusable by any functional agent — translation, summarisation, citation tracking, data formatting, template compilation. CLM example: A narrative generation helper that any functional agent calls to produce human-readable summaries from structured data.
Utility Agents
Non-AI microservices that agents call as tools — database connectors, API gateways, file storage, logging, audit trail services. High reusability, no intelligence required. CLM example: A FenX data connector that any agent uses to read/write client records.

Why Multi-Agent Over Single-Agent?

A single monolithic agent attempting a full KYC review would quickly hit context limits, mix concerns, and become impossible to debug. Multi-agent architectures solve this:

ChallengeSingle AgentMulti-Agent
Context windowOverloaded with all data and instructionsEach agent has focused, manageable context
DebuggingOpaque — hard to trace where errors occurClear chain — trace exactly which agent failed
ReusabilityNothing is reusableHelper and utility agents serve multiple workflows
ScalingBottleneck at one LLM callParallel execution — multiple agents work simultaneously
GovernanceAll-or-nothing permissionsEach agent has precisely scoped data access
Model flexibilityOne model for everythingRight model per task — powerful for reasoning, fast for extraction

Goose — An Open-Source Agent Framework

Goose ↗ (Agentic AI Foundation / Linux Foundation) is a general-purpose open-source AI agent — available as desktop app, CLI, and API. It illustrates the agent paradigm well:

  • Provider-agnostic: Works with 15+ LLM providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama, Azure, Bedrock)
  • MCP-native: Connects to 70+ extensions via the Model Context Protocol — the open standard described in the MCP tab
  • Not just code: Research, writing, automation, data analysis — demonstrating that agents are general-purpose task-completion systems
  • Built in Rust: Performance and portability, 43k+ stars on GitHub, 467+ contributors

The relevance to CLM: Goose demonstrates that agents can connect to any system via standardised protocols (MCP), use any LLM, and perform any task — the same pattern CLM agents would follow when connecting to FenX, CRM, sanctions databases, and document stores.

Key Insight

Agents are not a future technology. They are shipping today — in developer tools (Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code), in customer service (Salesforce Einstein), and increasingly in financial services. The question for CLM is not whether to adopt agents, but how to architect them within our regulatory and governance constraints.

Agent Safety & Maintenance Principles

Building agents in a regulated environment requires deliberate safety architecture. These principles — derived from leading AI companies (Anthropic, Google, OpenAI) and adapted for financial services — should guide every agent built within CLM:

1. Reversibility Awareness
Agents must consider the impact and reversibility of their actions. Read-only operations (data retrieval, analysis, summarisation) execute freely. Write operations (updating records, triggering workflows, sending communications) require explicit human approval. Hard-to-reverse actions always pause for confirmation.
2. Confidence Disclosure
Every agent output must disclose its confidence level. Low-confidence outputs are flagged for deeper human review. High-confidence outputs receive lighter review. The system — not the human — determines which outputs need attention. This prevents automation bias at scale.
3. Structured Outputs as Guardrails
Agent responses should be structured (JSON schemas, typed fields, enumerated categories) rather than free-text wherever possible. Structured outputs are validatable, auditable, and reduce hallucination surface. Free-text narratives are the exception, not the default.
4. Graceful Degradation
When an agent fails — model timeout, API error, unexpected input — the system must degrade gracefully: checkpoint state, escalate to human, and never corrupt upstream data. Idempotent design ensures partial failures don’t create inconsistent states. The system loses time, never data.
5. Version-Controlled Behaviour
Agent instructions (system prompts), model IDs, and tool configurations are versioned in Git. Semantic versioning applies: major changes (new capabilities, changed scope) require revalidation; minor changes (quality improvements) require regression testing; patches (typos, formatting) require no action.
6. Operational Monitoring
Every agent in production must track: invocation count, latency, error rates, override rates, output quality samples, and cost. Override rates >15–20% trigger investigation. These metrics feed into the MRM monitoring requirement — not as separate work, but as the same process.

Agent Maintenance Lifecycle

Agents are not “set and forget” systems. They require ongoing maintenance proportionate to their tier:

ActivityTier 1Tier 2Tier 3
Model ID pinning & update testingOn changeQuarterlyMonthly
Prompt regression testingOn changeMonthlyBi-weekly
Output quality samplingSpot checksMonthly (20+ samples)Weekly (50+ samples)
Bias & fairness audit—AnnualSemi-annual
Formal model validation (MRM)—Biennial (by owner)Annual (by CRO)
Cost monitoringAwarenessMonthly budget checkPer-invocation tracking
Canary testing (inject known-incorrect inputs)—QuarterlyMonthly

Named ownership is mandatory: every agent has a Model Owner (responsible for performance and compliance) and a System Owner (responsible for infrastructure and availability). No ownerless agents in production.
panels.arch-mcp:
Model Context Protocol (MCP)

MCP is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems — data sources, tools, and workflows. Think of it as the "USB-C port for AI": just as USB-C provides a standardised way to connect devices, MCP provides a standardised way to connect AI to everything else.

Why MCP Matters for CLM

CLM processes require AI to interact with many different systems — client databases, document stores, sanctions lists, corporate registries, CRM platforms, policy engines. Without MCP, each integration is a custom, fragile point-to-point connection. With MCP, you build a connector once and any AI application can use it.

1×Build once
N×Use everywhere
0Custom glue code

MCP Architecture

MCP follows a clean client-server model with three participants:

MCP Host
The AI application that needs context — an AI agent, chatbot, copilot, or orchestrator. The host manages one or more MCP clients. CLM example: A KYC review agent that needs to pull data from FenX, check sanctions lists, and read policy documents.
MCP Client
A component within the host that maintains a dedicated connection to one MCP server. Each client handles the protocol — initialisation, capability negotiation, request routing. Think of it as: The "plug" that connects one host to one server.
MCP Server
A program that exposes data, tools, or workflows to AI applications. Can run locally (same machine) or remotely (cloud service). CLM example: A FenX MCP server that exposes client records as resources and KYC operations as tools.

The Three Primitives

MCP servers expose exactly three types of capabilities. This simplicity is the power — three building blocks compose into unlimited functionality:

🔧 Tools

Executable functions that AI applications can invoke to perform actions — file operations, API calls, database queries, calculations, system commands.

CLM examples:

  • fenx_get_client(client_id) — retrieve client record
  • sanctions_screen(name, dob) — run sanctions check
  • create_review_case(client_id) — initiate periodic review

📂 Resources

Data sources that provide contextual information — file contents, database records, API responses, configuration data. Resources give AI the information it needs to reason.

CLM examples:

  • Client onboarding documents (PDFs, scans)
  • KYC policy documents and thresholds
  • Transaction history and patterns

💬 Prompts

Reusable templates that structure interactions with language models — system prompts, few-shot examples, role definitions. Prompts ensure consistent, high-quality AI behaviour.

CLM examples:

  • SoW narrative template with required sections
  • Risk assessment prompt with SEB's taxonomy
  • Client communication templates by language

MCP in a CLM Architecture

Here is how MCP would connect a CLM AI agent to SEB's ecosystem:

Scenario: AI-Assisted Periodic KYC Review
Scenario: AI-Assisted Periodic KYC Review

A KYC analyst triggers a periodic review. The orchestrator agent connects to multiple systems via MCP:

MCP ServerProvidesAgent Uses It To
FenX ServerClient records, KYC data (Resources + Tools)Pull current client profile, update fields after review
Document Store ServerOnboarding documents, financial statements (Resources)Extract data from uploaded documents
Sanctions ServerScreening results (Tools)Run real-time sanctions and PEP checks
Registry ServerCorporate registry data (Resources + Tools)Verify company structure, UBOs, financial data
Policy ServerKYC policies, risk thresholds (Resources + Prompts)Apply correct policy rules to the assessment
CRM ServerRM notes, interaction history (Resources)Context for relationship understanding

The agent discovers available tools at startup via tools/list, negotiates capabilities, and dynamically adapts to what each server offers. If a server is updated (e.g., new sanctions list format), it sends a notification and the agent refreshes — no code changes needed.

Transport Layer

MCP supports two transport mechanisms — both using the same JSON-RPC 2.0 message format:

TransportHow It WorksBest For
StdioStandard input/output streams between local processesLocal development, same-machine integrations, testing
Streamable HTTPHTTP POST + Server-Sent Events for streamingRemote servers, cloud services, production deployments

Ecosystem Support

MCP is not a niche protocol — it has broad industry adoption:

  • AI assistants: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini
  • Development tools: VS Code (Copilot), Cursor, Windsurf
  • Agent frameworks: Goose (70+ MCP extensions), LangChain, CrewAI
  • Open governance: Linux Foundation project, open specification, SDKs for Python, TypeScript, Java, Kotlin, C#
Strategic Implication

Investing in MCP servers for CLM systems (FenX, document stores, sanctions databases) creates reusable AI infrastructure. Any future AI application — whether built internally or by vendors — can immediately connect to these systems. This is the difference between building one integration and building a platform.
