Google Cloud Platform — The Strategic AI Surface

GCP is SEB’s strategic platform for AI — not by preference, but by elimination. It is the only boundary where all required capabilities coexist:[6]

Platform Decision Rationale (as of May 2026)

The source records a GCP/Vertex AI direction for controlled CLM workloads. Its claim that the required data, interfaces and controls coexist is a dated architecture assessment, not verification of a current working interface or workload permission.

Why GCP Today — Six Constraints Compared

ConstraintGCPAzure/M365On-prem
C4 data processing✅ VPC-SC perimeter, data residency controls⚠️ Copilot sees workspace data (C1-C3 only)✅ But no AI models
Gemini models (approved)✅ 27 models, provisioned throughput❌ Not available❌ Not available
VPC Service Controls✅ Network isolation for AI workloads⚠️ Different isolation model✅ Physical isolation
IAM + Identity✅ Google Groups, service accounts, workload identity✅ Entra ID✅ AD
GIP data (BigQuery)✅ Native access, same boundary⚠️ Cross-cloud federation possible but adds latency + governance complexity⚠️ Requires export pipeline
FenX API egress✅ Whitelisted egress IPs, Cloud Run hosting⚠️ Possible but requires separate infra⚠️ Complex networking

Platform Capabilities

Vertex AI + ADK 2.0

Model deployment, serving, and agent orchestration. ADK 2.0 GA (May 2026) provides production-grade agent primitives. Versioning, A/B testing, monitoring, explainability.

Cloud Run

Serverless container hosting — already used by SensAIa and Team SPARK. Suitable for API services, agents, and lightweight web apps.

BigQuery + GIP

Analytical querying and batch data access. Group Involved Party (full_group_involved_party) provides portfolio-level client data for AI training and cross-client analysis.

VPC-SC + IAM + Secret Manager

Network isolation perimeter, role-based access control, credential management. The security boundary that makes C4 data processing possible.

Current GCP Agent Stack

Google’s current stack is more than raw model calls: ADK 2.0 builds the agent, Vertex AI Agent Engine hosts it, A2A supports inter-agent interoperability, and Agentspace is the employee-facing layer. That makes GCP the governed execution surface, not just the model endpoint.

Platform Economics — Compounding Cost Model

The first use case carries the full infrastructure cost. Subsequent use cases are incremental.

Note: the three rows below are a static readout (not expandable).

Use case 1
GCP project setup + VPC-SC + IAM + provisioned throughput + Cloud Run + monitoring = full platform investment (~2,700 USD/month base)
Use case 2–5
Incremental: additional Cloud Run service + model calls. Infrastructure already exists. Marginal cost per use case drops 60–80%.
Use case 6–15
Near-zero marginal infrastructure cost. All agents share platform, monitoring, security. Investment amortizes across portfolio.

This is why the portfolio approach matters. We’re not funding one project — we’re funding a capability that serves 15 use cases.

Honest Caveat

This assessment reflects May 2026 constraints. If Azure gains approved LLM access for C4 data, or if GIP data becomes accessible cross-cloud with acceptable governance, the calculus changes. Platform decisions should be revisited when material constraints shift — not treated as permanent.

Model Selection Guidance

Use Gemini 2.5 Flash for 80% of CLM tasks — classification, extraction, templated generation, routing. Lower latency, lower cost, sufficient accuracy for well-scoped tasks.
Upgrade: Pro
Use Gemini 2.5 Pro when the task requires multi-step reasoning, complex narrative generation, orchestration decisions, or 1M+ context window. The orchestrator agent justifies premium cost.

panels.tech-quickstart:
Builder's Quickstart — From Idea to Running Agent

This tab is for the person who has read the architecture sections and wants to know: "How do I actually start building?" — practical guidance for CLM builders, not theory.

Model Selection for CLM Tasks

Not every task needs the most powerful model. Match model to task based on complexity, latency requirements, and cost:

CLM Task TypeRecommended ModelWhyCost Tier
Document classification (passport vs. financial statement vs. registry extract)Gemini 2.5 FlashFast, cheap, accurate for classification tasks. Process thousands of documents at low cost.Low
Data extraction (pull structured fields from unstructured documents)Gemini 2.5 ProBetter reasoning for complex table/form extraction. Worth the cost for accuracy on financial statements.Medium
Risk narrative generation (draft case summaries, SoW explanations)Gemini 2.5 ProRequires nuance, regulatory language awareness, and multi-source reasoning.Medium
Policy Q&A / search (find relevant policy for a given scenario)Gemini 2.5 Flash + EmbeddingsRAG pattern: embed policies, retrieve relevant chunks, generate answer with Flash.Low
Multi-agent orchestration (coordinator agent that delegates tasks)Gemini 2.5 ProComplex reasoning about task decomposition and result synthesis. The orchestrator justifies premium model cost.Medium
Simple automation (field mapping, format conversion, status routing)Gemini 2.5 FlashDeterministic-enough tasks where speed and cost matter more than deep reasoning.Low
Cost Principle

Use Flash by default, Pro when the task demands it. Most CLM tasks are classification, extraction, or templated generation — Flash handles these well. Reserve Pro for multi-step reasoning, complex narratives, and orchestration decisions. This isn't about being cheap — it's about being fast (Flash is significantly lower latency) and reserving expensive reasoning for where it adds value.

Prompt Patterns for KYC/CDD

Proven patterns for CLM-specific AI tasks. These are starting points — refine based on evaluation results:

📄 Document Extraction Pattern

Structure: Role → Context → Task → Output Schema → Constraints

You are a KYC data extraction specialist at a Nordic bank. Given this [document_type], extract the following fields into the exact JSON schema provided. If a field is not clearly present, return null — never guess. Flag any fields where confidence is below 90%. Schema: {name, reg_number, address, UBOs: [{name, ownership_pct}], ...}

Key: Explicit schema prevents hallucination. "Never guess" constraint is critical for regulated environments.

✍️ Narrative Generation Pattern

Structure: Role → Context → Source Data → Template → Regulatory Constraints

You are drafting a Source of Wealth narrative for periodic KYC review. Use ONLY the data provided below — do not infer or add information. Structure: [1] Client overview, [2] Income sources with evidence, [3] Wealth accumulation, [4] Gaps or concerns. Flag any section where evidence is insufficient.

Key: "ONLY the data provided" prevents hallucination. Explicit structure ensures regulatory completeness.

🔍 Gap Analysis Pattern

Structure: Policy Requirements → Available Data → Compare → Output Missing Items

Given the KYC policy requirements for a [client_type] in [jurisdiction]: Required fields: [policy_fields_list] Available data: [current_client_data] Identify: (1) fields that are missing, (2) fields that are stale (>12 months), (3) fields with conflicting sources. Output as actionable checklist for the analyst.

Key: This is KAICY's core pattern — compare what's needed against what's available, output the delta.

Evaluation — How to Know If It's Working

Before deploying any agent, establish measurable success criteria. These metrics apply across CLM AI use cases:

MetricWhat It MeasuresTarget (Tier 1-2)How to Measure
Extraction accuracy% of fields correctly extracted vs. human baseline>95% on core fieldsCompare agent output against 50+ human-reviewed gold standard cases
Hallucination rate% of outputs containing information not in source data<2%Automated check: every agent output field must trace to a source document line
Human override rate% of agent decisions changed by analyst<15%Track in production — high override = agent drift or policy change
Time-to-decisionAnalyst time from receiving agent output to final decision50% reduction vs. manualCompare pre/post agent deployment workflow timings
Coverage% of cases where agent can produce useful output>80%Track "agent unable to process" cases — are edge cases systematic?

What You Can Use at SEB Today

Ready now
GCP Vertex AI (27 approved models), GitHub Copilot for development, Cloud Run for hosting, BigQuery for logging/analytics, ADK 2.0 (GA) for agent orchestration, docs.fenergox.com for API specifications
Check first
Agent Runtime (managed hosting), Sessions & Memory Bank (state management), managed MCP servers, Evaluation Service — check SEB's activated services list before assuming availability
Needs approval
Partner models (Claude via Vertex), new tooling via Digital Workplace intake (JIRA portal 1017), production FenX API credentials (coordinate with FenX onboarding team)

First Steps — The Pragmatic Path

  1. Pick a Tier 1 use case from the Portfolio (Section 8) — something with clear inputs, clear outputs, and no autonomous actions
  2. Set up your builder workstation — VS Code + GitHub Copilot + GCP project access (see Builder tab)
  3. Start with a prompt, not a system — test your prompt pattern against 10 real examples in Vertex AI Studio before writing any code
  4. Build evaluation first — create your gold-standard test set before building the agent. You cannot improve what you cannot measure.
  5. Wrap in ADK only when needed — if your use case requires tool access, multi-step reasoning, or state management, structure it as an ADK agent. Otherwise, a simple API call with a good prompt may be enough.
  6. Deploy to Cloud Run for prototype — cheap, serverless, easy to iterate. Move to Agent Runtime later if it becomes available and adds value.

Power Platform — The Business Builder Stack

Microsoft Power Platform is SEB’s approved low-code automation platform — the operational answer to “Business Builders (Tier 1–2)” from Section 2. Copilot Studio is one product inside that stack, not the whole stack. While Vertex AI serves technical builders engineering Tier 3 systems, Power Platform enables CLM analysts, process owners, and domain experts to build and ship governed AI solutions themselves — in days, not months.

15 production applications already run on Power Platform at SEB. This is not theoretical — it is proven at scale.

Why This Matters for CLM

The Knowledge Hub’s Executive Summary promises two tracks: Business Builders (Tier 1–2) and Technical Builders (Tier 2–4). GCP/Vertex AI serves the technical track. Power Platform is the missing operational layer for the business track. Without it, the Business Builder promise is aspirational. With it, CLM analysts can ship AI tools while engineering focuses on KAICY.

Microsoft supports conversational and autonomous agent modes, but SEB enablement has to be verified before promising background or event-triggered behavior. If the feature is enabled, it needs separate control design because the agent can act without a user starting a chat.

Known Limitations — Intellectual Honesty

Power Platform is powerful for Tier 1–2 but has real constraints CLM must understand:

  • Agent triggers disabled — Copilot Studio agents respond to user messages only. No scheduled, webhook, or event-triggered agents. Use Power Automate flows for scheduled automation.
  • No native FenX or GCP connectors — all internal API access via HTTP with Entra ID (preauthorized). No drag-and-drop FenX integration.
  • No custom RAG pipelines — Copilot Studio uses Microsoft’s built-in retrieval. Cannot control chunking, embedding model, or reranking. For domain-specific retrieval quality, Vertex AI is required.

  • No model lifecycle management — no versioning, A/B testing, drift monitoring, or rollback. For regulatory model monitoring, GCP is required.
  • AACA mandatory — every Copilot Studio agent and AI Builder feature requires AACA classification before production deployment.
  • MCP connectors limited — Work IQ and Morningstar MCP available in Personal Dev and Dedicated only. Custom MCP requires Dedicated environment.

chapters.title: Portfolio & Applications
chapters.html:
Portfolio & Applications

This section maps AI capabilities to the CLM processes they serve — from quick wins that deliver value in weeks, to autonomous agents that require mature infrastructure. Each capability is classified by governance tier and maturity status. Nothing here is committed. This is the analytical foundation for portfolio decisions.

Start with the low-hanging fruit

The most common mistake in AI portfolios is starting with the hardest problem. Start with Tier 1 capabilities — meeting transcription, policy Q&A, document classification — that deliver measurable value within weeks, build organisational trust, and create the infrastructure that later capabilities depend on. Every Assist-level capability you ship reduces the risk profile of the next Augment-level capability. The portfolio reads left to right, and the sequencing matters.

Infrastructure determines agent capability

AI agents are only as capable as the systems they can reach. Think of connected systems as roads — without them, agents face the same bottlenecks humans do: switching between screens, copy-pasting between applications, waiting for email responses. An agent with access to FenX APIs, policy documents, and screening databases via MCP servers can complete a review in minutes. The same agent without those connections is as stuck as a car without roads. The prerequisite chain in the next tab is not bureaucracy — it is the infrastructure that makes agents possible.

Capabilities before agents

For every row below, the sharper question is not "which agent?" but "what reusable capability does this leave behind?" A transcript-to-KYC use case should leave behind a field schema, an extraction capability, an evidence/provenance model and an evaluation dataset — not just one working agent. See CLM Intelligence Model (Section 11).

KAICY — AI for KYC Data Collection

KAICY is an AI tool that helps KYC analysts collect, extract, and verify client data. It uses call transcription, document extraction, and gap analysis to reduce manual outreach. A working prototype exists and the governance path has been pre-mapped using the SensAIa NPA precedent.

31%Potential outreach effort reduction in the original SEB–Bain estimate; no measured outcome established

T1–T3Spans Assist to Orchestrate — a full-stack AI product
NPAApproval path pre-mapped via SensAIa precedent

KAICY is the most mature reference case in the CLM portfolio. Most capabilities in the matrix below are still idea-stage options for discussion and prioritisation, not active delivery work right now. See Section 6 for the full deep dive.

Planning status (important context)

This matrix should be read as a portfolio planning map. Most capabilities are ideas with defined rationale and architecture direction, but they are not in active implementation today. Where prior prototype or design work exists (for example around KAICY), it provides learning input — not a commitment that delivery is currently underway. Any initiative would still need explicit prioritisation and lifecycle governance in Section 4 before build starts.

Reading the matrix pragmatically

Left column = low risk, fast value. Assist capabilities (Tier 1–2) can often be deployed using existing approved tools with minimal governance overhead. Middle column = draft outputs for review. Augment capabilities produce work products that humans verify — the AI does the first pass, the analyst has final say. Right column = agent territory. Orchestrate capabilities require connected infrastructure, mature data, proven Assist/Augment capabilities, and full governance approval. From a risk and compliance perspective, the most pragmatic path is building left-to-right: each shipped capability creates the evidence base, infrastructure, and organisational trust that the next tier requires.

AI Use-Case Network & Synergies

Each node is an illustrative AI use case. Lines show data or capability synergies — shared models, data pipelines, or architectural patterns that create compounding value when built together.

Explore proposed capability relationships. A shared dependency is an opportunity to investigate; it does not establish readiness or measured benefit.

Prerequisites That Unlock Capability

AI capabilities don't exist in isolation. Each layer of sophistication depends on infrastructure, data access, and governance being in place. These are the gates.

⚙️ GCP Projects Provisioned Dev / Acc / Prod environments, Vertex AI access, Cloud Run hosting Available
→
📊 FenX API Access Structured KYC data, policy fields, event ingress. The data unlock. Pending
→
🔌 MCP Servers Shared data access layer for AI applications. Build once, use many times. Not Started
→
📜 NPA Approved NPAC approval via NAMIS. SensAIa precedent (NAMIS 018543) maps the path. Pre-Mapped
Reading the chain

Assist-level capabilities (Tier 1–2) need GCP + basic FenX access. Augment-level capabilities add MCP servers for structured data access. Orchestrate-level capabilities require the full chain including NPA approval for production use. Each prerequisite unlocked expands the set of viable use cases.

Decisions Needed

This section intentionally provides a framework, not a plan. Turning it into a plan requires decisions that belong to leadership. These are the questions on the table.

1

What is the path from KAICY prototype to production?

The prototype works. The NPA path is pre-mapped via SensAIa precedent. The savings model is an original estimate developed with Bain. The architecture exists. The decision is what sequence of approvals, infrastructure, and staffing converts this prototype and its estimated opportunity into a production capability.

2

Should we invest in MCP servers as shared infrastructure?

Building FenX, BigQuery, and CRM data servers once means every future AI application gets immediate data access. This is the difference between building one integration and building a platform. The alternative is rebuilding data access for each new initiative.

3

What is the FenX AI integration priority?

The AI API work stream (ICBS-10787) directly enables KAICY integration. Where does this sit in the FenX backlog relative to other work streams? Every month of delay proportionally delays AI capability.

4

How do we position for the NPA reform?

The new 1st-line Change Risk Management framework (autumn 2026) explicitly reduces time-to-market while maintaining risk quality. Being an early adopter means faster approval paths for Tier 2–3 capabilities.

chapters.html:
Industry Synthesis

What the leading strategy firms are saying about AI in banking and client lifecycle management — plus the non-obvious considerations that determine whether initiatives compound or collapse. External validation and contrarian thinking, filtered for CLM relevance.

Reading scope

Contextual industry analysis from the supplied Hub. Reported dates, examples and estimates retain their original scope; they are not measured CLM results or current delivery commitments.

Industry Synthesis — External Signals Relevant to CLM

A synthesis of what the leading strategy firms, technology companies, and CLM vendors are signaling — distilled to what matters for CLM AI strategy at SEB. Latest refresh: August 2026. This section is maintained as a living synthesis; where specific reports are dated earlier, they remain because they are still the latest available source for that topic.

Last checked: 12 Aug 2026 (link validation in this runtime is network-constrained; verify external URLs from SEB network before stakeholder circulation).

The One-Line Summary

Agentic AI is no longer a research topic — it is shipping in production at leading institutions. 52% of enterprises with generative AI now have agents in production (Google Cloud, n=3,466). 88% of early adopters report positive ROI. The gap between AI leaders and laggards is widening. The differentiator is not technology (everyone has access to the same models) but operating model change, governance maturity, and the quality of domain knowledge encoded into systems.

Key Stats (latest available, refreshed Aug 2026)

52%

of executives in gen AI-using organizations already have AI agents in production. Not pilots — production.

Google Cloud ROI of AI 2025, n=3,466

$4.4 Trillion

McKinsey’s estimated annual economic potential from AI — yet only 1% of organizations are mature. 47% of executives say their organizations are moving too slowly.

McKinsey “Superagency in the Workplace” Jan 2025

60% Use, 0–20% Delegate

Developers use AI 60% of the time but fully delegate only 0–20%. 27% of AI-assisted work is net-new work that wouldn’t have been done otherwise — AI creates new capacity, not just speed.

Anthropic “Agentic Coding Trends 2026”

ADK 2.0 GA

Google’s Agent Development Kit went generally available 19 May 2026. First-class support for all 7 Anthropic composable agent patterns. SEB’s approved platform now has production-ready agent infrastructure.

Google Cloud, 19 May 2026

Seven Cross-Industry Consensus Points

#ConsensusWho Says ItCLM Translation
1Operating model > technologyMcKinsey, BCG, Bain, AccentureGovernance design, role clarity, and cultural readiness matter more than which model you pick
2You can’t scale what you can’t governBain, Anthropic, Google, MicrosoftPre-approved building blocks, tiered governance, and audit infrastructure must precede ambitious deployments
3Specialized narrow agents > monolithic AIFenergo, Amazon, OpenAI, Google ADKBuild small, purpose-built agents that collaborate — not one system that tries to do everything
4Persistent agents create institutional memoryBain, Google (Memory Bank), Microsoft (Copilot Cowork)KYC relationships are long-running — agents that retain context across reviews are fundamentally more valuable
5Safety is a system property, not a model propertyAnthropic (4-layer model), Google (Agent Platform), Microsoft (Agent 365)Model + harness + tools + environment must ALL be governed — KAICY governance addresses all four
6Open standards are winningAnthropic (MCP → Linux Foundation), Google (A2A, 50+ MCP servers), AWS (MCP in DevOps Agent)Build to MCP, not vendor-specific APIs. Integration investments become portable.
7Peer-to-peer adoption beats top-down mandatesBCG, BainKAICY adoption should focus on champion users and demonstrated value, not management directives

Platform Landscape — Where Each Fits

PlatformRole in SEB’s StackLatest Signal (as of Aug 2026 refresh)
M365 CopilotTier 1 productivity — meeting summaries, document drafting, KPI analysisAgentic capabilities GA in Word/Excel/PPT. Copilot Cowork for long-running tasks (Frontier).
Copilot StudioTier 2 automation — declarative agents, workflow orchestrationMulti-agent orchestration GA. Business apps integrated into Copilot flow.
GCP / Vertex AITier 3–4 engineering — custom RAG, data sovereignty, full lifecycle controlADK 2.0 GA (19 May 2026). Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. 50+ managed MCP servers. A2A protocol. Agent Identity + Gateway + Registry for governance.
GitHub CopilotBuilder productivity — agent mode, cloud agent, code reviewCloud Agent builds from issues autonomously. Multi-model selection (Opus 4.7, GPT-5, Gemini).
Fenergo (FenX)CLM platform — 6 production AI agents, periodic review automationDocument Agent, Screening Agent, Significance Agent shipping. 50% document processing reduction.

Four Contrarian Signals Worth Noting

⚠️ AI-Specific Reorgs Underperform

Bain finding: organizational changes specifically labeled “for AI” underperform general transformations. Implication: Embed AI into existing CLM workflows rather than creating a separate AI organization.

⚠️ The Value Gap Persists

Across ALL sources: most organizations are still failing to scale AI value beyond pilots. “Many pilot AI. Few have scaled value.” (Accenture). Only 1% of organizations are mature (McKinsey). SEB’s governance-first approach may actually be an advantage — building foundations before scaling.

⚠️ Employees Are 3× More Ready Than Leaders Think

McKinsey “Superagency”: employees are 3× more prepared for AI than their managers believe. The blockers are organisational — unclear mandates, missing tooling, cultural permission — not workforce resistance. Implication: CLM analysts are likely ahead of where leadership assumes.

⚠️ Survivorship Bias in Case Studies

The 67% review time reduction and 65% onboarding compression come from leading institutions with mature data and favorable conditions. They are real but not automatic. Plan for the median outcome, not the best case.

Implications for CLM

Near-term
Ship Tier 1–2 tools (Copilot agents, meeting summaries, document drafting). Earn credibility through demonstrated value. Codify tribal knowledge into structured formats AI can consume.
Build-out
Complete KAICY NPAC submission. Build MCP integrations to FenX. Establish evaluation and monitoring infrastructure on GCP. Get Tier 2 model validation done.
Longer-range
Multi-agent orchestration (CDD + SoW + Screening). Persistent agent memory across client reviews. Cross-border jurisdiction handling. Portfolio of 5+ coordinated AI tools.

Sources: McKinsey (Rewired 2.0, Factory CEO, Sovereign AI, Superagency in the Workplace), BCG (Enterprise as Code, Organizational Metabolism), Bain (AI’s Next Operating Model, Governance & Trust, Phasing Agentic AI), Deloitte (Agentic AI in CLM at SEB, Human Capital Trends 2026), Accenture (Top Banking Trends 2026, Intelligent Superhighway), Fenergo (FinCrime OS, AI Agents), Anthropic (Trustworthy Agents, Constitutional Classifiers, Agentic Coding Trends 2026, Building Effective Agents), Google (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, ADK 2.0 GA, AI Agent Trends 2026, Next ’26), Microsoft (Wave 3, Copilot Cowork, Agent 365, Multi-Agent GA). McKinsey — Paving the Road for AI Agents

Source: Interview with Factory CEO Matan Grinberg (April 2026) + Rewired 2.0 + Sovereign AI research

Last checked: 12 Aug 2026

Core Thesis

"Software development agents are like Ferraris. But if you drop a Ferrari into San Francisco in 1850 with dirt roads and horses, it's not going to perform well. Before organizations can benefit from agents, they need to pave the roads." — Matan Grinberg, Factory CEO

Key Insights for CLM

🛣️ Infrastructure Before Intelligence

"Paving the roads" means documentation, test coverage, CI/CD, observability, linters, integrations with internal tools, and access to tacit knowledge. If these aren't in place, agents struggle. Implication for SEB: FenX go-live is precisely this road-paving — structured, auditable KYC data as clean AI input.

🧠 Tacit Knowledge Is the Enemy

"The enemy of AI agents is tacit knowledge — things discussed but not written down." Factory records every meeting and stores notes in repositories that agents can query. Implication: CLM must codify tribal knowledge — policies, exception handling, decision rationale — to make it agent-accessible.

🔄 Delegation, Not Coding

"The new directive isn't to write a line of code — it's to delegate to an agent." Engineers think about what they can offload before meetings or before going to bed, then review results in the morning. This reframes the builder role from producer to supervisor.

📊 Phased Measurement

Phase 1: Adoption percentage and daily usage. Phase 2: Efficiency and business-aligned metrics. "Measuring success purely by engineering output might not make sense." Implication: KAICY's success should be measured by analyst workflow improvement, not lines of code.

Sovereign AI

McKinsey's research on sovereign AI tracks how nations are building independent AI capabilities to reduce dependency on foreign providers. For a Swedish bank operating under Finansinspektionen and EU AI Act, this has direct implications: data residency requirements, model hosting constraints, and the strategic importance of SEB's GCP-only (Google first-party) model policy all reflect sovereign AI considerations at the institutional level.

Rewired 2.0

McKinsey's follow-up research on companies winning with AI reinforces a finding consistent across all firms: the gap between AI leaders and laggards is widening. Leaders invest in operating model change, not just technology deployment. The firms generating real returns from AI have changed how teams are structured, how decisions are made, and how technology and business interact — which is precisely the design challenge for CLM AI governance.

McKinsey — Paving the Road for AI Agents ↗ · Sovereign AI ↗ · Rewired 2.0 ↗

BCG — Enterprise as Code

Source: "Enterprise as Code: An Operating Model for the AI Era" (December 2025) + "Design Your Company for AI" (2026)

Last checked: 12 Aug 2026

Core Thesis

"Automation doesn't create order; it depends on it. The enterprises that move fastest know where definition ends and discretion begins — clear at the edges, creative within." — Scognamiglio & Lenhard, BCG

Enterprise as Code — The Operating Model Shift

BCG argues that the next productivity frontier is not about migrating workloads to the cloud — that was last decade. It is about codifying operations: capturing the implicit operating model and expressing it as structured logic that both people and AI systems can understand, test, and improve.

📐 From Intuition to Specification

Most companies can define more of their work than they realise, but vital knowledge hides in binders, spreadsheets, side conversations, or people's heads. When operations are expressed as structured logic, everything changes: organisations can test, refine, and automate how work gets done.

🏗️ Readiness Determines Results

"When processes live only in people's heads, it is difficult to apply intelligence effectively. But when workflows and decision rules are written down, AI can amplify what already works." Enterprises that are legible to machines today are moving faster.

⚙️ The Platform Imperative

AI performs best on shared, hyperscale platforms. Multitenant systems are more efficient because they scale with demand. The question is no longer whether to use shared platforms, but how to optimise design with them in mind — balancing resilience, flexibility, and control.

🎯 Practical Starting Points

Identify high-volume, high-value processes. Capture their operating logic clearly. Build governance and controls into that logic from the start. Design work for continuous measurement. CLM parallel: KYC review, CDD evaluation, and onboarding are exactly these processes.

Design Your Company for AI, Not AI for Your Company

BCG's 2026 research extends this further: organisations should not bolt AI onto existing structures but redesign the organisation to be AI-native. This means rethinking team composition, decision rights, information flows, and performance measurement around AI capabilities rather than retrofitting AI into legacy operating models.

BCG — Enterprise as Code ↗ · Design Company for AI ↗ · AI-First Payments ↗

Bain — AI's Next Operating Model

Source: "AI's Next Operating Model" by Eric Sheng & Xun Yang (April 2026) + Agentic AI Governance + Phasing Agentic AI

Last checked: 12 Aug 2026

Core Thesis

"Most AI agents today are useful but forgetful. They arrive when prompted, perform the task, and disappear. They do not carry the work forward. In organizational terms, most AI agents still resemble highly capable temporary workers." — Bain & Company

Episodic vs. Long-Running Agents

Bain identifies a fundamental shift from episodic agents (bounded tasks, lose context between sessions) to long-running agents that maintain goals, preserve decisions, and accumulate domain knowledge across extended workflows.

🔁 Rediscovery Is Not Continuity

"A system that has to reconstruct the state of work each time must still decide what matters, infer what changed, resolve contradictions, recover priorities, and reconstruct rationale behind past decisions." Rebuilding context is not the same as carrying it forward. CLM implication: KYC reviews are exactly the kind of path-dependent, exception-rich work where persistent agents add most value.

📈 Economic Logic Changes

Episodic agents are measured transactionally: cost per task, speed, time saved. Long-running agents should be measured developmentally: context retained, rework eliminated, institutional knowledge built. "The prize is not only millions in labour savings; it is better decisions in functions that shape margin, resilience, and growth."

🏛️ Institutional Memory at Stake

"Who owns the institutional knowledge these agents accumulate? If the memory layer is locked inside a vendor's platform, the organization has outsourced its institutional memory." Build vs. buy becomes a critical strategic consideration — organisations that design knowledge portability from the start build competitive advantage.

⚠️ Governance Stakes Rise with Persistence

Long-running agents accumulate stale or conflicting memory, create larger permissioning surface area, and increase data leakage exposure. Operating them requires strong controls for memory hygiene, permissions, observability, rollback, human override, and cost management.

Where This Matters First

Bain identifies financial services explicitly: "They could persist across underwriting, claims, compliance reviews, or client servicing, maintaining the state of a case as conditions change." CLM — with its long-running customer relationships, periodic reviews, and accumulated context — is a textbook use case for persistent agents.

What Leaders Should Do Now

"Start with workflows that break because context gets lost over time. Redesign the workflow around continuity rather than simply inserting an agent into the current process. Build the control plane early. Evaluate these systems not just as tools but as developing operators: Do they retain context? Do they exercise sound judgment? Do they follow through reliably?"

Bain — AI's Next Operating Model ↗ · Governance & Trust ↗ · Phasing Agentic AI ↗

Deloitte — Agentic AI in Client Lifecycle Management

Source: "Unlocking Benefits with Agentic AI in the KYC Process" — SEB engagement (March 2026)

Last checked: 12 Aug 2026

Core Thesis

Leading institutions deploying agentic AI in KYC are achieving step-change operational improvements — not incremental gains. US banks and global wealth managers are ahead of Nordic institutions, but the benchmarks are now clearly established.

Industry North Stars

MetricIndustry AverageNew North StarImprovement
Average periodic KYC review time90 min<30 min−67%
End-to-end onboarding time14 days<5 days−65%
File revisit rate on onboarding49%<5%−90%

Agent Architecture — Four Layers

🎯 Orchestration Agents

Coordinate and engage functional agents to execute end-to-end processes. Goal-oriented or utility-driven. Decide what must be done.

⚙️ Functional Agents

Execute specific business process steps (e.g., name screening, SoW corroboration, CDD evaluation). Limited reusability — domain-specific.

🤖 Helper Agents

Bite-size tasks powered by LLM/AI (e.g., summarisation, extraction, discrepancy analysis). Higher reusability across processes.

🔧 Utility Agents

Plumbing-like tasks — API calls, data fetching, logging. Simple services with no AI intelligence. Highest reusability.

Key Trends in KYC

  • Vendor landscape consolidation: Move from "monolithic vs. best of breed" to "suite with composable modules"
  • Build the judgement, buy the capability: Focus on building orchestration, risk logic, and decision layers; buy detection capabilities as vendors innovate faster on adversarial tech
  • Continuous and integrated KYC: Shift from stand-alone periodic reviews to continuous, enterprise-wide KYC assessment
  • Nordic banks lag maturity: Despite strong national identity systems and corporate registries, Nordic banks trail in KYC process maturity
  • Human stays in the loop: Given high risk of KYC/AML processes, removing humans is "unlikely and unwise" in the foreseeable future

Source: Deloitte AB, internal engagement material — SEB SharePoint access required

Accenture — Top Banking Trends 2026: Unconstrained Banking

Source: "Top Banking Trends 2026" — comprehensive mixed-methods research across banking executives, commercial clients, and retail customers

Last checked: 12 Aug 2026

Core Thesis

"Banking is entering an era defined by the removal of long-standing constraints. The convergence of gen AI and agentic AI, digital assets and new business models is not only challenging those limits, but shattering them."

Six Megatrends

💰 Future of Money

Digital currencies (stablecoins, CBDCs, tokenised deposits) could shift $13 trillion in transaction value to alternative methods by 2030. Agentic payments — AI agents managing, optimising, and moving funds autonomously — represent the next frontier.

🎯 Future of Experience

Agentic technologies compressing the vertically integrated stack. Conversational, context-aware interactions replacing form-based processes. 35% of consumers willing to let AI handle final purchase decisions.

👥 Future of Work & Talent

The consensus narrative is "AI transforms everything." The following findings challenge common assumptions and have direct implications for how CLM approaches AI adoption:

"AI-focused organizational changes UNDERPERFORM other reorganizations" Bain, April 2026 Do not create a separate "AI team." Embed AI capability into existing CLM workflows and teams. The instinct to reorganize around AI is common — and counterproductive. KAICY succeeds by making existing analysts more effective, not by creating a parallel structure.
"AI adoption spreads peer to peer, not top-down" BCG, April 2026 Management mandates drive compliance, not adoption. Champion users — analysts who see KAICY save them 30 minutes per case — drive real usage. Invest in enablers (training, support, quick wins) rather than governance mandates for adoption.
"Many pilot AI. Few have scaled value." Accenture, 2026 The persistent AI value gap validates SEB's governance-first, infrastructure-first approach. Organizations that skip governance for speed end up slower — they hit scaling walls that governance-ready organizations sail through.
"AI won't fix your system. Redesigning it will." BCG, April 2026 AI amplifies process quality — it doesn't fix broken processes. If the KYC workflow has fundamental design flaws, KAICY will automate the flaws faster. Process clarity is a prerequisite, not a nice-to-have.
"Your product has a new user. It's not human." TLDR Tech, April 2026 FenX APIs must now be designed for AI agent consumers, not just human UI users. API response formats, error handling, rate limits — all need to work for autonomous agents that process thousands of requests. This shapes FenX integration architecture (Section 6).
"Organizational Metabolism Will Define AI Leaders" BCG, April 2026 Not just adopting AI — continuously absorbing new capabilities and translating them into value. The team that builds, learns, iterates, and ships fastest wins. Speed of learning > quality of first attempt.
The Contrarian Synthesis

Three signals that collectively challenge the "move fast" narrative: (1) AI-specific reorgs underperform, (2) top-down mandates fail, (3) most pilots don't scale. The consistent implication: success comes from embedding AI into existing work patterns, earning adoption through demonstrated value, and building governance infrastructure before scaling. SEB's measured approach may look slow from the outside — but the evidence suggests it is the approach that actually scales.

The Efficiency Paradox
The Efficiency Paradox

The obvious argument: AI makes reviews faster. First-order expectation: same team handles more volume.

The second-order effects are more important. Freed capacity can be redirected toward systematically under-invested activities: deeper relationship understanding, proactive risk identification, more thoughtful EDD, better onboarding experience.

The real prize is not doing the same work faster — it is doing different, higher-value work previously impossible.

Reframing: If measured only by headcount efficiency, AI is perceived as cost-cutting and resisted. If measured by quality improvement and capability expansion, it becomes an investment in professional development — aligning practitioner and organisational interests.

Governance as Competitive Signal
Governance as Competitive Signal

Counterintuitive insight: the quality of your governance framework is itself a competitive signal.

In a market where regulators are increasing AI scrutiny, an organisation demonstrating robust governance earns regulatory trust. That trust translates to: smoother interactions, faster approvals, and — in the event of an incident — a presumption of good faith.

Well-designed governance is an asset, not a tax. It is the reason regulators allow you to do things less-prepared organisations cannot.

The "10× Bank" Implication for CLM
The "10× Bank" Implication for CLM

Accenture's "10× bank" concept: one person + AI team = materially greater potential impact. Applied to CLM, AI support may increase analyst span over time; realized gains still depend on data quality, control design, and workflow fit.[1]

This is directional, not immediate. But implications for workforce planning, skills, and org design are significant.

Appropriate response: Not headcount reduction (creates resistance, loses knowledge) but capability expansion — same team doing fundamentally more valuable work. JPMorganChase's framing: "10,000 more people at zero cost."[1]

The Speed-Credibility Sequence
The Speed-Credibility Sequence

Tension: move quickly (capture opportunity) vs. move carefully (build credibility). First-level framing: binary choice.

Second-level recognition: credibility and speed are sequenced, not opposed.

Starting with Tier 1-2 is not "slow" — it is strategically fast. It builds the trust, patterns, and muscle memory that make Tier 3-4 possible. An organisation that ships five Tier 2 tools has earned the credibility to pursue a Tier 3 agent. An organisation that starts with Tier 3 ambition and gets stuck in approvals has earned nothing but frustration.

The sequence: earn the right to do the hard things by demonstrating competence at the simpler things.

The Leverage Asymmetry
The Leverage Asymmetry

There are two kinds of leverage: permissioned (capital and people — someone has to give them to you) and permissionless (code and media — you can create them while others sleep).

AI agents are the most powerful form of permissionless leverage ever available to a banking division. A two-person team with well-designed agents can produce output that previously required a department. But leverage is a force multiplier for judgment — good and bad. An agent that encodes poor risk logic scales poor decisions. An agent that encodes excellent domain expertise scales excellence.

This is the asymmetry most organisations miss: the constraint on AI value is not compute or budget — it is the quality of judgment encoded into the system. CLM's advantage is that it possesses deep, specific knowledge about KYC workflows, regulatory interpretation, and client risk. That knowledge is the real leverage. Gemini is a commodity; CLM domain expertise is not.

Implication: Invest in capturing and codifying judgment before investing in scaling infrastructure. The team that understands the problem most deeply will build the most valuable tools — regardless of team size.

Specific Knowledge as Moat
Specific Knowledge as Moat

The technology itself is not a differentiator. Every bank can access Gemini. Every vendor can wrap an LLM. The defensible advantage sits at the intersection of domain knowledge and building capability — and this intersection is exceedingly rare.

Specific knowledge is knowledge that cannot be trained for in a classroom. It is acquired through years of doing the work — understanding which KYC exceptions matter, knowing why a particular SoW structure signals risk, recognising the difference between a regulatory technicality and a genuine compliance gap. This knowledge lives in the heads of experienced CLM practitioners.

When that specific knowledge is encoded into AI systems by the people who possess it, you get something no external consultant, vendor, or generic platform can replicate. The practitioner who builds with AI has a compounding advantage: they understand both the problem and the tool. To everyone else, this looks like work. To the person doing it, it feels closer to play.

The moat is not technology. The moat is specific knowledge, compounded over time, encoded into systems that work while you focus on the next problem.

The Inversion Principle
The Inversion Principle

The natural question is: "How do we make AI succeed in CLM?" A more productive question: "How would AI in CLM certainly fail?" Then systematically avoid those paths.

AI in CLM fails when:

  • No one owns the outcome — the tool exists but no individual's reputation depends on it working
  • Compliance is consulted after the fact — rework is always slower and more expensive than right-work
  • Tools are built for imagined rather than observed problems — "wouldn't it be cool if…" instead of "I watched an analyst spend 40 minutes on this yesterday"
  • Data quality is assumed rather than verified — garbage in, confident garbage out
  • Adoption is mandated rather than earned — people use tools that make their day better; they resist tools imposed from above
  • Success is measured by what was built rather than what changed — output is vanity; outcome is sanity
  • The organisation optimises for avoiding mistakes rather than enabling learning — an environment where failure is punished produces an environment where nothing is tried

The path to success is the disciplined avoidance of the paths to failure. This is less glamorous than a bold vision, but considerably more reliable. Solve for not failing, and success has room to emerge.

Compound Interest in Capability
Compound Interest in Capability

All the returns — in wealth, in relationships, in knowledge, in organisational capability — come from compound interest. This is the most important mental model for AI strategy and the most frequently ignored.

The first AI tool an organisation builds is the hardest. It requires establishing patterns, navigating governance for the first time, earning trust, debugging the collaboration model between builders and business. The return on this first investment, measured in isolation, often looks poor.

The second tool is easier. Governance is faster because the pathway is known. Trust exists because the first tool shipped. Architecture is reusable. By the fifth tool, the organisation has compounding advantages: proven patterns, calibrated expectations, trained people, reusable components, and — critically — an institutional belief that this works.

Organisations that evaluate AI by the ROI of the first pilot miss the entire return curve. They are measuring a single deposit and concluding that compound interest doesn't work. The patience to keep compounding — through the inevitable slow early phase — is the strategy.

Play long-term games. The returns are back-loaded, and they are enormous.

The Systems View: Nodes and Connections
The Systems View: Nodes and Connections

Every AI use case in isolation looks like a point solution. Viewed as a system, each one becomes infrastructure for the next.

Document classification feeds onboarding. Entity extraction feeds risk scoring. Risk scoring feeds review prioritisation. Policy Q&A trains the knowledge base that the regulatory tracker monitors. The SoW corroboration agent and the CDD evaluation agent share entity data, external source connections, and risk logic.

This is not accidental — it is the natural structure of CLM work. The processes are already interconnected; the AI portfolio should mirror that interconnection. Organisations that plan atomistically build disconnected tools. Organisations that think in systems build platforms where each new capability amplifies every existing one.

The practical consequence: architectural decisions made for the first tool — data models, API patterns, logging standards, governance templates — should be made with the tenth tool in mind. Not because you're building ten tools now, but because the cost of good foundations is paid once and the return compounds forever.

The value of a network grows with the square of its nodes. This applies to AI portfolios as much as it applies to telecommunications.

The Accountability Paradox
The Accountability Paradox

Accountability is a double-edged instrument. It allows you to take credit when things go well and to bear the brunt when things go badly. Most organisations are structured to diffuse accountability — committees, working groups, shared ownership — precisely to avoid the downside.

But diffused accountability is where AI initiatives go to die. When everyone owns the outcome, no one owns the outcome. The committee meets, discusses, defers. The prototype stalls. The momentum dissipates.

The organisations that ship AI fastest have a clear structure: a named individual owns each initiative, under their own reputation. They have the authority to make decisions, the resources to execute, and the visibility that comes with both success and failure. This is uncomfortable. It is also the only model that produces results.

The paradox: the people willing to take on personal accountability for AI outcomes are the people most likely to succeed — because accountability creates the incentive structure that drives careful execution. The person whose name is on the outcome checks the data quality, validates the model, tests with users, and iterates until it works.

Society rewards those who take risks under their own name. Organisations should do the same.

The Survivorship Bias in AI Case Studies
The Survivorship Bias in AI Case Studies

Every conference presentation, every consulting report, every vendor pitch deck tells the same story: AI was deployed, results were impressive, the future is bright. What you never see: the projects that failed, the pilots that were quietly shelved, the implementations that produced technically correct but operationally useless outputs.

This is survivorship bias at industrial scale. We study the successes and derive "best practices" from a non-representative sample. The 67% review time reduction and 65% onboarding compression cited in this document come from leading institutions with mature data, strong governance, and favourable conditions. They are real — but they are not automatic.

The antidote is probabilistic thinking. Instead of asking "what is the expected outcome?", ask "what is the range of possible outcomes, and what are the conditions that determine where in that range we land?" The conditions that matter most: data quality, process clarity, governance maturity, practitioner engagement, and realistic expectations.

A team that plans for the median outcome and prepares for the downside will outperform a team that plans for the best case and is paralysed by the first setback.

Be sceptical of certainty. Plan for variance. The world is more random than the case studies suggest.

Outstanding Questions

Intellectual honesty requires acknowledging what is not yet resolved. These questions are genuinely open — surfacing them explicitly is itself progress.

Open Question

FenX platform readiness & fallback: KAICY’s next step depends on FenX AI API availability (work stream ICBS-10787). What is the realistic timeline for API readiness across the 5-country rollout? If delayed beyond H2 2026, what interim architecture delivers value without the integration dependency?

Open Question

Dedicated vs. shared GCP project: Should CLM AI workloads run in a dedicated GCP project (clearer cost attribution, capacity guarantees, isolation) or within the broader PWM&FO environment (reduced overhead, existing configurations)? Shared risks noisy-neighbour effects; dedicated risks under-utilisation.

Open Question

Client data scope & residency: Which client data fields are permissible as AI model inputs, under what lawful basis conditions, and with what data residency requirements? AML/KYC provides legal basis, but specific field-level scope (e.g., transaction narratives, beneficial ownership chains) requires DPOR sign-off and DPIA completion.

Open Question

Human oversight at scale: When agentic workflows process hundreds of CDD cases daily, how do we design human-in-the-loop that is genuinely meaningful — not just rubber-stamping? What cognitive load limits apply? What exception-rate triggers escalation redesign?

Open Question

Cross-border regulatory variance: CLM operates across 5 jurisdictions (SE, NO, DK, FI, LU). Swedish-tuned AI prompts and policy references may not transfer. How do we ensure jurisdiction-specific compliance grounding without maintaining 5 separate model configurations?

Open Question

NPA reform impact on AI submissions: The April 2026 NPA reform introduces NAMIS-based workflows and revised committee structures. How does this change the approval path for AI use cases already in pipeline? Do existing NPAC conditions (e.g., SensAIa’s 8 conditions) carry forward or require re-submission?

Open Question

Builder team composition & capacity: What’s the right size and skill mix for an internal CLM AI builder team? The proposed skill mix combines engineering and domain expertise; scope and ownership need to be established. Requires validation against portfolio ambition, Data & Analytics capacity, and Deloitte engagement scope.

Open Question

Model drift & revalidation triggers: For production AI models in regulated workflows, what triggers revalidation — time-based (quarterly?), performance-based (accuracy drift threshold?), or event-based (regulatory change, policy update, new sanctions list)? The EU AI Act requires “continuous monitoring” but does not prescribe cadence.

Open Question

External data sources for AI agents: For SoW corroboration, adverse media screening, and beneficial ownership verification — which external sources can AI agents access? Contractual terms, API reliability, data quality SLAs, and regulatory permissibility each need mapping per source.

Open Question

Cost model & funding structure: Central investment, CLM operational budget, or shared-services charge-back? Central funding encourages experimentation; local funding enforces ROI discipline. GCP model costs, Deloitte advisory fees, and internal FTE allocation each follow different governance paths.

The One-Line Summary

Agentic AI is no longer a research topic — it is shipping in production at leading institutions. 52% of enterprises with generative AI now have agents in production (Google Cloud, n=3,466). 88% of early adopters report positive ROI. The gap between AI leaders and laggards is widening. ⚠️ AI-Specific Reorgs Underperform

⚠️ The Value Gap Persists

McKinsey — Paving the Road for AI Agents

Source: Interview with Factory CEO Matan Grinberg (April 2026) + Rewired 2.0 + Sovereign AI research

Last checked: 12 Aug 2026

Core Thesis

"Software development agents are like Ferraris. But if you drop a Ferrari into San Francisco in 1850 with dirt roads and horses, it's not going to perform well. Before organizations can benefit from agents, they need to pave the roads." — Matan Grinberg, Factory CEO

Key Insights for CLM

🛣️ Infrastructure Before Intelligence

"Paving the roads" means documentation, test coverage, CI/CD, observability, linters, integrations with internal tools, and access to tacit knowledge. If these aren't in place, agents struggle. Implication for SEB: FenX go-live is precisely this road-paving — structured, auditable KYC data as clean AI input.

🧠 Tacit Knowledge Is the Enemy

"The enemy of AI agents is tacit knowledge — things discussed but not written down." Factory records every meeting and stores notes in repositories that agents can query. Implication: CLM must codify tribal knowledge — policies, exception handling, decision rationale — to make it agent-accessible.

🔄 Delegation, Not Coding

"The new directive isn't to write a line of code — it's to delegate to an agent." Engineers think about what they can offload before meetings or before going to bed, then review results in the morning. This reframes the builder role from producer to supervisor.

📊 Phased Measurement

Phase 1: Adoption percentage and daily usage. Phase 2: Efficiency and business-aligned metrics. "Measuring success purely by engineering output might not make sense." Implication: KAICY's success should be measured by analyst workflow improvement, not lines of code.

Sovereign AI

McKinsey's research on sovereign AI tracks how nations are building independent AI capabilities to reduce dependency on foreign providers. For a Swedish bank operating under Finansinspektionen and EU AI Act, this has direct implications: data residency requirements, model hosting constraints, and the strategic importance of SEB's GCP-only (Google first-party) model policy all reflect sovereign AI considerations at the institutional level.

Rewired 2.0

McKinsey's follow-up research on companies winning with AI reinforces a finding consistent across all firms: the gap between AI leaders and laggards is widening. Leaders invest in operating model change, not just technology deployment. The firms generating real returns from AI have changed how teams are structured, how decisions are made, and how technology and business interact — which is precisely the design challenge for CLM AI governance.

BCG — Enterprise as Code

Source: "Enterprise as Code: An Operating Model for the AI Era" (December 2025) + "Design Your Company for AI" (2026)

Last checked: 12 Aug 2026

Core Thesis

"Automation doesn't create order; it depends on it. The enterprises that move fastest know where definition ends and discretion begins — clear at the edges, creative within." — Scognamiglio & Lenhard, BCG

Enterprise as Code — The Operating Model Shift

BCG argues that the next productivity frontier is not about migrating workloads to the cloud — that was last decade. It is about codifying operations: capturing the implicit operating model and expressing it as structured logic that both people and AI systems can understand, test, and improve.

📐 From Intuition to Specification

Most companies can define more of their work than they realise, but vital knowledge hides in binders, spreadsheets, side conversations, or people's heads. When operations are expressed as structured logic, everything changes: organisations can test, refine, and automate how work gets done.

🏗️ Readiness Determines Results

"When processes live only in people's heads, it is difficult to apply intelligence effectively. But when workflows and decision rules are written down, AI can amplify what already works." Enterprises that are legible to machines today are moving faster.

⚙️ The Platform Imperative

Bain — AI's Next Operating Model

Source: "AI's Next Operating Model" by Eric Sheng & Xun Yang (April 2026) + Agentic AI Governance + Phasing Agentic AI

Last checked: 12 Aug 2026

Core Thesis

"Most AI agents today are useful but forgetful. They arrive when prompted, perform the task, and disappear. They do not carry the work forward. In organizational terms, most AI agents still resemble highly capable temporary workers." — Bain & Company

Episodic vs. Long-Running Agents

Bain identifies a fundamental shift from episodic agents (bounded tasks, lose context between sessions) to long-running agents that maintain goals, preserve decisions, and accumulate domain knowledge across extended workflows.

🔁 Rediscovery Is Not Continuity

"A system that has to reconstruct the state of work each time must still decide what matters, infer what changed, resolve contradictions, recover priorities, and reconstruct rationale behind past decisions." Rebuilding context is not the same as carrying it forward. CLM implication: KYC reviews are exactly the kind of path-dependent, exception-rich work where persistent agents add most value.

📈 Economic Logic Changes

Episodic agents are measured transactionally: cost per task, speed, time saved. Long-running agents should be measured developmentally: context retained, rework eliminated, institutional knowledge built. "The prize is not only millions in labour savings; it is better decisions in functions that shape margin, resilience, and growth."

🏛️ Institutional Memory at Stake

"Who owns the institutional knowledge these agents accumulate? If the memory layer is locked inside a vendor's platform, the organization has outsourced its institutional memory." Build vs. buy becomes a critical strategic consideration — organisations that design knowledge portability from the start build competitive advantage.

⚠️ Governance Stakes Rise with Persistence

Long-running agents accumulate stale or conflicting memory, create larger permissioning surface area, and increase data leakage exposure. Operating them requires strong controls for memory hygiene, permissions, observability, rollback, human override, and cost management.

Where This Matters First

Bain identifies financial services explicitly: "They could persist across underwriting, claims, compliance reviews, or client servicing, maintaining the state of a case as conditions change." CLM — with its long-running customer relationships, periodic reviews, and accumulated context — is a textbook use case for persistent agents.

What Leaders Should Do Now

"Start with workflows that break because context gets lost over time. Redesign the workflow around continuity rather than simply inserting an agent into the current process. Build the control plane early. Evaluate these systems not just as tools but as developing operators: Do they retain context? Do they exercise sound judgment? Do they follow through reliably?"

The Four-Layer Agent Model

Anthropic defines agents as four interdependent components — each a source of capability AND a potential point of failure:

LayerWhat It IsSafety ImplicationCLM Relevance
ModelThe intelligence — trained capabilities and reasoningWhere core capabilities and risks originateGemini model selection (approved list), tiering determines which model is appropriate
HarnessInstructions and guardrails the model operates underPoorly configured harness = exploitation riskSystem prompts, KYC policy grounding, role definitions, output constraints
ToolsServices and applications the model can invokeEach tool extends the attack surfaceFenX API, sanctions screening, CRM, document stores — scope carefully
EnvironmentWhere the agent runs and what data it can accessSame agent in different environments = different risk profilesGCP project isolation, IAM controls, data classification (C1-C4)

Key Developments (April 2026)

🛡️ Project Glasswing

Multi-company initiative (AWS, Apple, Broadcom, Cisco, CrowdStrike, Google, JPMorganChase, Linux Foundation, Microsoft, NVIDIA, Palo Alto Networks) to secure the world’s most critical software. Signal: AI security is now a collaborative industry problem, not a competitive one.

🔬 Constitutional Classifiers

Input/output classifiers trained to block harmful requests. Reduced jailbreak success 86% → 4.4% with only 0.38% increase in false positives. 3,000+ hours of red-teaming. Pattern for building guardrails around regulated AI agents.

🌐 MCP → Linux Foundation

Anthropic donated the Model Context Protocol to the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation. Open standard means security properties can be designed into infrastructure once rather than patched per deployment. MCP is the integration standard for KAICY-to-FenX.

📊 Economic Index

81,000-person survey on AI usage patterns. Research shows Claude’s own rate of checking in with users roughly doubles on complex tasks — demonstrating calibrated human-in-the-loop behavior. Validates that AI assistive patterns work at scale.

What This Means for CLM

Agent safety = system design
Safety is not a model property alone — it emerges from model + harness + tools + environment. KAICY governance must address all four layers, not just model selection.
Prompt injection is real
Anthropic explicitly states “no single line of defense is enough to guarantee protection.” For KAICY processing external documents, defense-in-depth: input validation + output classification + tool scoping + environment isolation.
Human control ≠ constant approval
Anthropic’s research shows Plan Mode works better than step-by-step approval. For CLM: let the agent present its full review plan, get human approval on strategy, then execute with intervention only on flagged items.
Open standards reduce vendor lock-in
MCP as Linux Foundation open standard means CLM’s tool integrations work regardless of which model provider is used. Build to MCP, not to vendor-specific APIs.

Web-based AI chat for all M365 users. No Graph grounding — cannot see your files/emails/calendar. Web search only. Enterprise data protection (not used to train models). Good for general brainstorming, not for work requiring organizational context.

⚡ M365 Copilot (Licensed)

Full enterprise Copilot with Microsoft Graph. Accesses user’s emails, files, chats, meetings — scoped to existing permissions (RBAC). Semantic Index for rich retrieval. Full app capabilities: Word drafts, Excel analysis, Teams meeting summaries, PowerPoint creation. GPT-5.2 backbone.

🏗️ Copilot Studio + Agents

Build custom agents with low-code tools. Declarative agents (JSON + instructions), custom engine agents (external LLMs), plugins and connectors. Multi-agent orchestration now GA. M365 Agents Toolkit for VS Code development.

🧑‍💻 GitHub Copilot

AI coding assistant for builders. Agent mode (autonomous multi-step coding), Cloud Agent (background coding from issues), code review, multi-model selection. Enterprise plan with SAML SSO, policy controls, audit logs, IP indemnity. Used at SEB via github.sebank.se.

SEB Operating Model Alignment

Start in M365 Copilot
Tier 1 productivity. Licensed Copilot for meeting summaries, document drafting, KPI analysis, email management. Immediate value, minimal governance overhead.
Scale in Power Platform
Tier 1–2 solutions. Copilot Studio agents grounded in SharePoint knowledge. AI Builder for document processing. Power Automate for workflow automation and FenX integration. Dedicated environments for C4 data.
Orchestrate in Copilot Studio
Tier 2 agent orchestration. Multi-agent workflows, custom agents with enterprise data grounding, Power Automate integration for action execution. Where Copilot Studio cannot deliver the requirements — move to GCP.
Engineer in Vertex AI
Tier 3–4 engineering. KAICY, custom RAG, multi-model orchestration, data sovereignty for client PII, EU AI Act audit infrastructure. Where Power Platform cannot deliver the requirements.
Key Insight

Microsoft is converging on the SAME architecture Anthropic describes: model + harness + tools + environment. Copilot Studio provides the harness (instructions, guardrails), connectors provide tools, the Microsoft tenant is the environment, and GPT-5.2/Claude Opus are the models. The difference for Tier 3+ is that you need to OWN all four layers — which means GCP.

Agent 365 — The Cross-Platform Control Plane

Source: microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-agent-365 (GA, $15/user/month or included in M365 E7 at $99/user/month)

Agent 365 is not an agent builder — it is a governance and observability control plane for IT and security teams. It governs agents regardless of where they were built — including agents on GCP/Vertex AI that surface through Teams or M365.

CapabilityWhat It ProvidesCLM Relevance
Agent RegistryUnified inventory of ALL agents across the organization, regardless of framework or platformSingle view: KAICY (GCP), Copilot agents (M365), Declarative agents — all visible in one registry

Two-Platform Governance

SEB's AI agent governance will span two platforms: Google Agent Platform (build, deploy, runtime governance) and Microsoft Agent 365 (enterprise visibility, security, compliance). This is not duplication — it is layered governance. GCP governs the agent's technical behavior; Agent 365 governs its organizational context. Both are needed for enterprise-scale agent deployment.
