Regulatory EngineCompliance / KYC policy owners + relevant legal/regulatory owners
Knowledge productsKnowledge owner / business domain owner
Data productsData owner / domain owner
CLM Context Graph semanticsCLM product + data/architecture owners
RequirementsCLM Product / BA, validated by the relevant domain owner
Operating PlaneProcess/control owners + CLM Product
Agent/service purposeBusiness/Product Owner
Runtime / deploymentTechnical Service / IT Delivery Owner
Model/harness/platformTechnology / D&A as applicable
EvaluationProduct + Risk/Compliance + Technical Owner
Incident / rollbackNamed technical/operational owner

Change Governance by Object, Not by Monolith

A scalable operating model asks what changed, rather than automatically re-reviewing the whole product. This enables faster governance without lowering the control standard.

ChangeRequired response
Knowledge wording or meaning changeKnowledge validation and downstream impact assessment
Regulatory interpretation changeDownstream revalidation
Data schema changeData-contract + consumer regression
Tool permission changeSecurity/control reassessment
Model changeEvaluation regression
Prompt/skill changeBehavioural regression tests
New customer-impacting actionRisk-tier reassessment (Section 2)
FenX capability changeRequirement/control/test traceability check
panels.intel-antipatterns:
Nine Ways This Model Fails in Practice

Two anti-patterns are already called out elsewhere in this Hub — over/under-classifying AI risk tiers (Section 2) and the "AI-specific reorg" anti-pattern (Section 3). The nine below are specific to how CLM intelligence itself can quietly stop compounding.

❌ Agent-first portfolio

Symptom: agent count rises while shared knowledge/data/eval maturity does not. Consequence: duplicated prompts, integrations, controls and inconsistent answers.

❌ SharePoint as runtime architecture

Symptom: knowledge files are assumed to behave like executable skills. Consequence: false expectations about orchestration and tool behaviour.

❌ FenX duplication

Symptom: an AI platform creates a second KYC state store. Consequence: competing truths and increased audit complexity.

❌ Graph theatre

Symptom: building a graph database/visualisation before stable IDs, source authority or semantic relationships exist. Consequence: a beautiful graph of unreliable assumptions.

❌ Regulatory RAG as Regulatory Engine

Symptom: search over PDFs is described as computable compliance. Consequence: repeated runtime interpretation and poor traceability.

❌ Requirement prose trap

Symptom: critical semantics live only in Jira narrative. Consequence: AI cannot reliably reuse intent, source lineage or acceptance logic.

❌ AI inference becomes truth

Symptom: a plausible AI mapping is reused without validation. Consequence: errors compound across downstream agents and requirements.

❌ Usage as value

Symptom: token consumption, active users or generated code are presented as ROI. Consequence: high activity may hide rework and review cost.

❌ Verification starvation

Symptom: AI increases generation volume but review capacity stays fixed. Consequence: the bottleneck shifts to expert validation and defect triage.
panels.intel-checklist:
15 Questions Before Starting (or Continuing) an AI Initiative

  1. What business problem or regulatory outcome are we solving?
  2. Which layer does it primarily belong to — Regulatory Engine, CLM Context Graph, Operating Plane, or Agentic Execution?
  3. Which enablers are required?
  4. Do required data products exist and have owners?
  5. Do required knowledge products exist and have authority metadata?
  6. Can the work be solved deterministically, more safely and cheaply?
  7. What reusable capability will this initiative leave behind?
  8. What is the human definition of good?
  9. What can AI execute and what must a human verify?
  10. What evidence proves success?
  11. Who owns this when it fails on Monday morning?
  12. What is the customer/regulatory impact if it is wrong?
  13. Can we observe the AI before granting write authority?
  14. What changes would trigger revalidation?
  15. How does this integrate into normal CLM portfolio governance rather than becoming an isolated AI backlog?

Inversion Check — What Would Make This Strategy Fail?

Warning signs
  • CLM has many agents but no common semantic model.
  • Each AI project builds its own pipeline to FenX/MDM.
  • Requirements remain prose and cannot be traced to source or tests.
  • AI-generated regulatory interpretations become de facto policy.
  • The graph becomes a second source of customer truth.
  • AI cost rises but cycle time, quality and delivered outcomes do not improve.
  • Human verification becomes the bottleneck but is not measured.
  • Governance review stays monolithic instead of risk/change-specific.
End state

The intended CLM end state is not "many AI agents." It is a CLM organisation where regulatory knowledge is computable and traceable, customer/process context is reusable and current, implementation/control state is observable, development artefacts become reusable institutional knowledge, data and knowledge products are owned, AI services share harnesses and evaluations, humans concentrate on context, judgement and verification, and every new delivery improves the foundations for the next one.

chapters.title: AI Use Case Classifier
chapters.html:
AI Use Case Classifier

A proof-of-concept classification aid that applies the governance framework consistently. Describe your use case, provide context, and get an auditable tier recommendation with reasoning — useful for discussion, but not a substitute for ACAA, MRM, or NPAC approval.

Blocked by design

This POC should stop work early on use cases that rely on prohibited profiling, autonomous decisions without human review, or event-triggered Power Platform agents in SEB environments unless platform enablement is explicitly confirmed. If the answer is unclear, the use case belongs in the review queue, not the build queue.

The advisory scoping tool keeps unknown inputs unresolved, retains your inputs and exports the same result you see. History is local to your browser.

Scope a task

The advisory scoping tool keeps unknown inputs unresolved, retains your inputs and exports the same result you see. History is local to your browser.

Scope a task
Reading scope

Original classifier design documentation, retained for its scoping questions and provenance. Its legal/tier rules and prior implementation description are not the current advisory engine. The integrated tool uses unresolved inputs and working patterns only; current formal governance requires the applicable primary authority.

What Is the AI Use Case Classifier?

The classifier supports the scoping step of the “From Idea to Production” lifecycle (Section 4). In this v0.5 POC, it provides a structured recommendation for governance tiering by applying the 4-question decision tree, ACAA mapping, 6-pillar AI Risk Instruction, GDPR triggers, NPA significance thresholds, and worked examples.

Core Principle

The classifier is advisory, not authoritative. It accelerates and objectifies the scoping conversation — it does not replace human judgment or formal NPAC/Risk approval. Every classification can be overridden, but overrides require a documented reason. This design makes the tool defensible under audit.

Why Build This?

⚡ Speed

Reduce initial scoping effort from unstructured discussions to a structured first recommendation in minutes, giving teams a better starting point for governance conversations.

🎯 Objectivity

Reduce subjective variance in early classification. For similar inputs, the classifier is designed to produce stable recommendations, while borderline cases still require Risk & Compliance judgment.

📋 Audit Trail

Each classification creates a local audit record in this POC: what was submitted, what reasoning was returned, what tier was suggested, and whether it was overridden. Target production state: immutable centralized audit storage.

🔄 Consistency

As the team grows and more people submit use cases, classification logic stays consistent. The knowledge base is the single source of truth, not individual interpretation.

⛔ Prohibited Practice Screening

Art. 5 EU AI Act compliance built in. Social scoring, emotion inference at work, subliminal manipulation, and biometric categorisation are blocked before classification — not just flagged.

📄 Model Card Generation

One-click export of a 12-section model card pre-filled from classification data. Matches SEB’s model card repository template. Includes monitoring plan, legal basis, and governance requirements.

Architecture — Software 3.0 Approach

The Software 3.0 principle: “Forget the code exists, never forget the product exists.” The code is the least interesting part. The interesting parts are:

  1. The dataset — What structured knowledge does the model reason over? How is it maintained?
  2. The eval — How do you know the classifier is correct? What does the test suite look like?
  3. The UX — The user experience of providing input and understanding output matters more than the model.

In this v0.5 prototype, classification is executed by a deterministic browser-side rules engine using structured user input. Target production options may include governed model-assisted classification, but that is not implemented in this HTML.

Target-state architecture (proposed, not implemented in this HTML prototype)

Frontend
Knowledge Hub SPA with structured input form and result renderer. Current state: browser-only prototype. Target state: frontend submits to governed backend service.
Backend
Target state: GCP Cloud Run service (Python/Node.js) receiving form data, constructing prompt chain, calling Vertex AI, and returning structured output.
Model
Target default: approved Gemini variant selected from the current governance register. No fine-tuning. Classification logic lives in the prompt/rule design, not model weights.
Knowledge Base
Compiled from curated knowledge files: decision tree, tier definitions, ACAA mapping, 6-pillar checklist, worked examples, GDPR/NPA triggers. Versioned in Git.
Audit Log
Current state: local browser session log. Target state: immutable centralized store (for example BigQuery) with input, prompt/model version, output, reasoning, acceptance/override, and retention per SEB policy.
Eval Suite
25–30 worked examples with known-correct classifications. Automated regression on every prompt change. <90% accuracy on clear cases = change rejected.

The Classification Chain

Classification is a structured reasoning chain that walks through multiple assessment dimensions sequentially. Each step produces a discrete output that feeds the next.

Step 0
Art. 5 Prohibited Practice Screening — BLOCKING check. Screens for social scoring, emotion inference at work, subliminal manipulation, and biometric categorisation. If triggered, classification is blocked entirely — not escalated to a higher tier. Output: { prohibited: true, practice: "Social scoring" } or proceed.
Step 1
Decision Tree Walk — The 4-question tree (Q4→Q1, highest risk first). Walks through each question with the user’s input, applying upgrade rules for boundary cases (output type + sensitive data, continuous + client data). Output: { tier: 3, reasoning: "Output directly informs client risk decisions (Q3=Yes)" }
Step 2
ACAA Category Mapping — Cross-reference tier against ACAA categories and EU AI Act risk levels (Minimal, Limited, High, Unacceptable). Output: { acaa_category: 3, eu_ai_act: "high-risk" }
Step 3
6-Pillar Risk Assessment — Score each pillar (Valid & Reliable, Fair, Explainable, Transparent, Third-Party & Data, Resilient & Secure) as Low/Medium/High concern. Output type and frequency feed into explainability and resilience scoring. Output: pillar heatmap.
Step 4
GDPR Impact Screening — Based on data types selected: DPIA required? DPOR consultation needed? Personal data in processing scope? Output: GDPR requirements list.
Step 5
NPA Significance Assessment — Does this constitute a “significant change”? Triggers: Tier 3+, client-facing, FenX integration, third-party AI, new AI capability at Tier 2+. Change type (new vs modification) affects significance.
Step 6
Governance Requirements Summary — Compile full requirements: approvals needed, documentation level, governance bodies to engage, estimated timeline, specific next steps.
Step 7
Confidence Assessment — Evaluates boundary factors (indirect influence, sensitive data + full review, inconsistencies, ambiguous output type). Assigns High/Medium/Low confidence. Low confidence triggers “discuss with Risk & Compliance” recommendation.
Step 8
Monitoring Plan — Generates tier-appropriate monitoring requirements: what to monitor (accuracy drift, fairness, latency), cadence, alerting thresholds, and responsible owner. Frequency and data types determine monitoring intensity.
Step 9
GDPR Legal Basis — Auto-suggests the most likely lawful basis under Art. 6: Legal Obligation (AML/sanctions), Contract Performance (KYC onboarding), or Legitimate Interest (internal productivity). Owner must validate with DPOR.

Consistency Design

For similar inputs, the classifier is designed to produce stable recommendations because:

  • Classification logic is versioned in this file/repository
  • The current engine is deterministic rule logic (no runtime LLM call in this prototype)
  • Each classification records classification ID and timestamp for traceability
  • When the knowledge base updates, the prompt version increments and the eval suite re-runs

Adversarial Input Handling

The classifier does not naively accept user assertions. If a user states “this does not influence client decisions” but describes a system that processes CDD data and generates risk scores, the logic is designed to flag inconsistencies:

⚠️ Inconsistency Detected

“You stated this does not influence client decisions, but the system processes CDD data and generates risk scores. This appears inconsistent — the classification assumes client-decision influence is present. Override available with documented justification.”

Reading scope

Original classifier design documentation, retained for its scoping questions and provenance. Its legal/tier rules and prior implementation description are not the current advisory engine. The integrated tool uses unresolved inputs and working patterns only; current formal governance requires the applicable primary authority.

Model Documentation & Model Card

Every AI system at SEB requires documentation proportional to its risk tier. The classifier generates this documentation automatically from classification results. This aligns with EU AI Act Art. 11 (technical documentation) and SEB’s Model Risk Management Instruction.

How To Use

After classifying a use case in the “Classify Now” tab, click “📄 Generate Model Card” in the result panel. This produces a structured document pre-filled with classification data, governance requirements, and monitoring obligations. Export as JSON for NAMIS attachment or copy into SEB’s model card repository.

What Gets Generated

The Model Card follows SEB’s template (Model-cards repo ↗) enriched with governance data from the classification.

SectionSourceContent
1. IdentityFormUse case name, owner, sponsoring team, classification ID, date, prompt version used.
2. Intended UseFormDescription, output type, audience, scope. What the system is designed to do — and what it must NOT be used for (out-of-scope uses).
3. Risk ClassificationEngineTier assignment, ACAA category, EU AI Act risk level, confidence score, decision tree reasoning, any boundary warnings.
4. Data & PrivacyEngineData types processed, GDPR legal basis, DPIA requirement, DPOR consultation status, data retention policy, data minimisation approach.
5. Fairness & BiasEngineBias risk level (from 6-pillar “Fair” assessment), protected attributes at risk, recommended fairness metrics, 80% rule applicability.
6. ExplainabilityEngineExplainability requirement level, recommended approach (SHAP, Vertex Explainable AI, inherent interpretability), Art. 13 obligations.
7. Human OversightFormOversight model (full/spot/exception/minimal), Art. 14 mapping, escalation path, who reviews and how often.
8. Monitoring PlanEngineWhat to monitor (accuracy drift, fairness drift, latency, usage volume), review cadence, alerting thresholds, who is responsible.
9. Technical ArchitectureFormSystems involved, integration points, deployment platform, model/service used, frequency of execution.
10. Governance & ApprovalEngineRequired approvals, bodies to engage, NPA requirement, timeline estimate, regulatory deadlines.
11. Limitations & RisksEngineKnown limitations, failure modes, inconsistency warnings, what the system cannot do, degradation scenarios.
12. Version HistoryAutoClassification version, any overrides with justification, re-classification history from audit log.

Documentation Requirements by Tier

Tier 1 — Minimal

  • Usage guidelines document
  • Acceptable use boundaries
  • Line manager sign-off

Generated automatically from classification. No additional documentation required.

Tier 2 — Standard Model Card

  • Full model card (all 12 sections)
  • Data processing agreement
  • ACAA Portal submission
  • Quarterly review schedule

Model card auto-generated. Owner validates and submits to repo ↗.

Tier 3 — Full Technical Documentation

  • Everything in Tier 2, plus:
  • Bias assessment with fairness metrics
  • Explainability approach (SHAP/LIME)
  • DPIA documentation
  • NPA proposal for NAMIS
  • Monthly drift monitoring spec

Model card is the starting point. Owner must expand with bias assessment and XAI approach before Group NFR review.

Tier 4 — Comprehensive + Continuous

  • Everything in Tier 3, plus:
  • Red-team testing results
  • Kill-switch mechanism spec
  • Real-time monitoring dashboard
  • Incident response runbook
  • Board Risk Committee briefing

Auto-generated model card is a draft only. Executive sponsor and external reviewer must validate before production.

Input Requirements

The classification form captures the minimum information needed for accurate tier determination and model card generation. Every field maps to a specific compliance obligation:

FieldRequiredMaps ToWhy Risk Cares
Use Case NameYesIdentityTraceability in audit log and model inventory. Must match STEP/NAMIS naming.
Owner & TeamYesAccountabilityNamed human owner is mandatory per AI Risk Instruction. No ownerless AI.
DescriptionYesDecision TreeCore input for the 4-question tree. Quality determines classification accuracy.
Output TypeYesExplainabilityScores/recommendations require XAI. Text/extraction may not. Art. 13 mapping.
Data TypesYesGDPR + FairnessTriggers DPIA, identifies protected attributes, determines data classification level.
AudienceYesTransparencyClient-facing triggers Art. 52 obligations. Regulatory triggers audit trail requirements.
Client InfluenceYesTier BoundaryTHE critical Tier 2 vs 3 question. Subject to inconsistency detection.
Human OversightYesArt. 14Full vs minimal determines if AI Act human oversight requirements are met.
FrequencyYesMonitoringContinuous systems need drift detection. Ad-hoc may only need periodic review.
New vs ChangeYesNPANew Tier 2+ capabilities require NPA. Modifications need Change Risk Assessment.
SystemsNoThird-Party RiskExternal APIs = supply chain risk. FenX = NPA consideration. STEP registration required.
Users & ScopeNoProportionalityBank-wide deployment at Tier 3 gets more scrutiny than team-level.
ContextNoNuanceCatches regulatory constraints, precedents, and timeline pressures the fields miss.
DocumentsNoEvidenceProcessed in memory only. Supports richer classification. Never persisted.

Prohibited Practice Screening (Art. 5)

Before any tier classification, the engine screens for prohibited AI practices under EU AI Act Art. 5. If triggered, the classification is BLOCKED — not merely escalated to a higher tier.

Prohibited PracticeHow the Classifier Detects It
Social scoringDescription mentions scoring individuals based on social behaviour, personality traits, or trustworthiness metrics unrelated to a specific, lawful purpose.
Subliminal manipulationOutput type is “automated actions” + audience is “client-facing” + no human oversight + description suggests behaviour modification without awareness.
Emotion inference at workData includes call transcripts/video + description mentions sentiment scoring of employees or measuring emotional states in workplace context.
Biometric categorisation (sensitive attributes)Data includes biometric identifiers + description mentions inferring race, religion, sexual orientation, or political opinions.
Untargeted facial recognitionSystems include CCTV/camera feeds + description mentions building or querying face databases.
⚠️ Blocked Classification Example

“This use case appears to involve [prohibited practice]. Under EU AI Act Art. 5, this is prohibited regardless of risk tier. Penalties: up to €35M or 7% of global annual turnover. This classification cannot proceed. Contact: Legal (AI Act compliance) or AI Governance Forum.”

GDPR Legal Basis Requirements

When personal data is processed, GDPR Art. 6 requires a lawful basis. The classifier identifies which applies:

Legal BasisWhen It Applies in CLM Context
Legitimate Interest (Art. 6(1)(f))Internal efficiency improvements, colleague productivity tools, operational analytics where no client-decision influence exists.
Contract Performance (Art. 6(1)(b))KYC processes that are necessary to fulfil the client contract (onboarding, periodic review).
Legal Obligation (Art. 6(1)(c))AML screening, regulatory reporting, sanctions compliance — mandatory by law.
Consent (Art. 6(1)(a))Rarely appropriate for AI in banking. Cannot be freely given where power imbalance exists.

Contacts & Resources

NeedContact
Model cards & model inventorydaaa@seb.se (Team 42, Charlie Jeansson)
GDPR / DPOR consultationLocal DPOR (Data Protection Operative Responsible)
AI Risk Instruction questionsGroup Non-Financial Risk
GCP / Vertex AI platformcloudcoreteam@seb.se
NPA / NAMIS process1st line risk team + NPAC secretariat
Explainability (SHAP/XAI)DNA Advanced Analytics (Team 42)

What You Get Back

The classification result is rendered immediately on the page and simultaneously written to the immutable audit log.

Classification Output

Tier Badge

Visual tier assignment (1–4) with colour coding matching the Knowledge Hub design system.

Decision Tree Walkthrough

Shows which question triggered the classification, with the model’s reasoning at each step.

6-Pillar Heatmap

Visual indicator for each risk pillar (green/amber/red) showing where attention is needed.

Governance Checklist

Specific requirements for this tier: approvals, documentation, bodies to engage, estimated timeline.

GDPR & NPA Assessment

DPIA required? DPOR consultation? NPA significance triggers? Clear yes/no with rationale.

Recommended Next Steps

Who to contact, what to prepare, links to relevant Knowledge Hub sections and SEB portals.

The Audit Log — Non-Negotiable

Every classification writes an immutable record to BigQuery (SEB’s standard for AI logging, same pattern as KAICY). The record is never editable after creation.

FieldContent
classification_idUUID — unique identifier for this classification event
timestampISO-8601 — when the classification was performed
user_idAuthenticated SEB user who submitted the classification
input_structuredAll form fields as submitted (use case name, description, data types, systems, etc.)
model_usede.g., gemini-2.5-flash-001
prompt_versione.g., v1.3 — versioned prompt template from Git
classification_outputFull structured result: tier, ACAA category, pillar scores, GDPR/NPA assessment, governance requirements
full_reasoningComplete chain-of-thought from the model — raw audit trail of the reasoning process
user_acceptedBoolean — did the user accept the classification?
user_override_tierIf overridden, to which tier? (null if accepted)
user_override_reasonMandatory free-text justification if overridden
Auditor Access

Auditors receive read-only BigQuery access to the classification log. They can query: all classifications for a given use case, all overrides, all Tier 3+ classifications, all classifications by a specific user, and the exact reasoning chain for any individual classification. The log answers: “Why was case X classified as Tier Y?” with full traceability.

Override Workflow

The classifier is advisory. If a user disagrees with the classification:

  1. Click “Override Classification”
  2. Select the tier they believe is correct
  3. Provide a mandatory written justification explaining why
  4. Both the original classification and the override are logged — nothing is erased

Overrides are visible in the audit log and can be reviewed by Risk & Compliance. A pattern of overrides in one direction may indicate the prompt needs updating.

Reading scope

Original classifier design documentation, retained for its scoping questions and provenance. Its legal/tier rules and prior implementation description are not the current advisory engine. The integrated tool uses unresolved inputs and working patterns only; current formal governance requires the applicable primary authority.

Build Strategy — Phased Delivery

Following the Software 3.0 principle: ship the simplest thing that produces correct classifications, then add features when evidence demands them.

Phase 1 — Core Classification (MVP)

ComponentImplementationComplexity
Input formHTML/JS in Knowledge Hub SPA. Structured fields as defined in Documentation & Output tab.Low
BackendGCP Cloud Run (Python). Receives POST, constructs prompt, calls Vertex AI, returns JSON.Medium
Prompt chainSystem prompt with full classification logic. 6-step reasoning chain. Temperature 0.Medium-High
Audit logBigQuery table. Write on every classification. Immutable.Low
Result rendererClient-side JS renders tier badge, reasoning, requirements.Low
Eval suite25–30 worked examples. Automated test on prompt changes.Medium

Phase 2 — Enhancement

  • Document upload — Gemini multimodal input for PDF/image context extraction (processed in memory, not persisted)
  • PDF export — “Download as PDF” for attaching to NAMIS proposals
  • Override analytics — Dashboard showing override patterns to inform prompt improvement
  • Feedback loop — When NPAC assigns a different tier than the classifier predicted, capture as training data for the eval set

Phase 3 — Integration & Compliance Documentation

  • NAMIS pre-population — Export classification directly to NAMIS proposal fields
  • Backlog linkage — Classification triggers portfolio item creation with pre-filled governance requirements
  • Trend analysis — Dashboard showing classification distribution over time, emerging patterns, governance bottlenecks
  • R&C documentation generator — Based on the classification result, automatically produce a draft compliance package containing:
    • NPAC submission narrative (purpose, scope, risk justification, tier rationale)
    • Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) template pre-filled with data types, lawful basis, retention, and processing scope from the classifier inputs
    • Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) where Art. 6(1)(f) is the claimed basis
    • Model Risk Management checklist (validation cadence, drift triggers, human oversight design)
    • EU AI Act conformity self-assessment (Annex III mapping, risk category justification, Article 9 obligations)
    • Art. 5 prohibited practices exclusion statement
    • STEP/DSD integration requirements summary (which systems, which data flows, what approvals needed)
    • Human oversight specification (who reviews, escalation path, override authority, cognitive load limits)
  • Committee-ready output — One-click export of the full documentation package as structured PDF, formatted for NPAC/governance committee review. Includes classification rationale, all supporting assessments, and a “conditions to satisfy before production” section modelled on SensAIa’s 8-condition approval pattern.
Design Principle

The classifier does not approve anything — it produces a first draft that saves 60–80% of the documentation effort. Every output is explicitly marked “DRAFT — requires human review and sign-off by designated Risk & Compliance function.” The goal: reduce time from idea to committee submission, not bypass the committee.

The Knowledge Base as Moat

The LLM is commodity (Gemini). The value is in the structured knowledge it reasons over:

  • The 4-question decision tree (Section 2)
  • The ACAA mapping table (Section 2)
  • The 6-pillar AI Risk Instruction (Section 5)
  • GDPR 7 principles with CLM implications (Section 5)
  • NPA significance triggers (Section 5)
  • The worked examples from Section 2
  • Governance requirements per tier (Section 2)

This knowledge comes from the Knowledge Agent canonical files. The prompt template is a compiled derivative — when the source knowledge updates, the prompt is regenerated and re-evaluated. Single source of truth, no drift.

Self-Classification

First Test Case

The classifier itself must pass through its own classification. Expected result: Tier 1 — internal productivity tool, no client data, no client-decision influence, human reviews every output. If it classifies itself as anything higher, the logic has a bug.

What Could Go Wrong — And How We Prevent It

Applying inversion thinking: before celebrating the upside, map the failure modes and design them out.

RiskFailure ModeMitigation
False precision Model outputs “Tier 2” with apparent confidence on an ambiguous case. Users treat it as authoritative. Explicit uncertainty surfacing: “This could be Tier 2 or 3 depending on [specific factor]. Discuss with Risk.” The tool is framed as advisory everywhere.
Gaming Users learn to phrase descriptions to get a lower tier. Inconsistency detection in the prompt chain. Cross-reference data types against claimed decision-influence. Flag contradictions.
Staleness Knowledge base drifts as regulations change (EU AI Act enforcement, NPA reform). Prompt versioning. Knowledge Agent maintains canonical source. Eval suite re-runs on every change. Staleness scan on policy dates.
Scope creep to authoritative People start treating classifier output as “approved” rather than “recommended.” Design constraint: output always states “This is an advisory classification. Formal approval requires [specific body].” Override button always visible.
Hallucination Model invents governance requirements or misapplies the decision tree. Temperature 0. Structured output format (JSON schema). Eval suite catches regression. Chain-of-thought logged for audit review.
Data leakage Uploaded documents containing client PII processed and stored. Documents processed in memory only. No persistence. Use case descriptions should never contain client-identifiable data (enforced via input guidelines).
The tool classifying itself wrong If the classifier is deemed Tier 2+ it requires its own governance overhead before shipping. Self-classification as first eval case. Expected: Tier 1 (no client data, no decision influence, human reviews output). Design ensures this remains true.

Build Priorities

1. Eval Set First

Before writing any UI code, build 25+ worked examples with expert-verified classifications. If the prompt can’t get these right, nothing else matters. The eval set is the product.

2. Prompt > Architecture

Spend 80% of effort on prompt engineering, 20% on infrastructure. A perfect Cloud Run setup with a mediocre prompt produces mediocre classifications. A brilliant prompt on a minimal backend produces excellent ones.

3. Log Everything

Every single classification, every input, every output, every override. This is your training data for improvement. This is your audit defence. This is your product analytics.

4. Ship, Then Improve

v1 is a textarea, structured fields, a “Classify” button, and a result display. No file upload, no PDF export, no NAMIS integration. Get the core classification right. Add features when you have evidence they’re needed.

Build vs. Buy

This is firmly build. No vendor sells a “classify your AI use case against your internal governance model” tool. The classification logic is entirely SEB-specific — the tier definitions, ACAA mapping, 6-pillar instruction, NPA triggers. This is the “specific knowledge inside SEB that creates AI advantages no external consultant can replicate.”

Technical Stack (All SEB-Approved)

ComponentTechnologyPrecedent
FrontendHTML/JS (extends Knowledge Hub SPA)Existing page architecture
BackendGCP Cloud Run (Python or Node.js)KAICY uses same pattern
ModelGemini 2.5 Flash via Vertex AIApproved model list
Audit logBigQueryKAICY logging pattern
AuthSEB SSO (same as NAMIS)Standard SEB auth
Prompt storageSEB GitHub Enterprise (versioned)Builder Council patterns repo
The Honest Assessment

This is a high-leverage, low-risk build if scoped correctly. The ingredients exist: classification logic already written (decision tree, ACAA mapping, tier requirements), knowledge base curated, infrastructure approved (GCP, Gemini, BigQuery, Cloud Run), audit pattern exists (KAICY). The highest-risk component is the prompt chain — getting classification right for boundary cases. Everything else is plumbing.

🎫
Jira Integration
In the current v0.5 browser POC, no Jira ticket is created automatically. Teams export the result and create a CLM AI Jira board item manually.
🏛️
CLM AI Portfolio
Once the agent or application goes live, it joins the CLM AI Portfolio — a governed registry of all production AI systems with ongoing monitoring and review.

panels.clf-tool:
Classify a Use Case

Advisory Tool — Not Formal Approval

Describe your AI use case below. This POC applies the 4-question decision tree, ACAA mapping, 6-pillar risk assessment, GDPR screening, and NPA significance test to produce a governance tier recommendation with full reasoning.

Form completion0%
1
Identity
Name, owner, and system type
Required
A clear, specific name for audit trail and model inventory. Avoid generic names like "AI tool" — be precise about what it does.
The named person accountable in production. Per SEB AI Risk Instruction: every AI system must have a human owner — this person is the GDPR Controller and model risk owner.
The team that will operate and maintain this in production. Maps to STEP application ownership.
POC status does not reduce the tier. It only tells the reviewer how mature the use case is today: proof of concept, prototype, or live production.

Original choices · historical
— Select — / POC — proof of concept / idea validation / Prototype — working build with limited users / Live — production or production-like operation

Applications produce output from input. Agents go further — they use tools, hold memory, and take multi-step actions toward a goal. Pick the one that best describes your system.

panels.clf-how:
Reading scope

Original classifier design documentation, retained for its scoping questions and provenance. Its legal/tier rules and prior implementation description are not the current advisory engine. The integrated tool uses unresolved inputs and working patterns only; current formal governance requires the applicable primary authority.

What Is the AI Use Case Classifier?

The classifier supports the scoping step of the “From Idea to Production” lifecycle (Section 4). In this v0.5 POC, it provides a structured recommendation for governance tiering by applying the 4-question decision tree, ACAA mapping, 6-pillar AI Risk Instruction, GDPR triggers, NPA significance thresholds, and worked examples.

Core Principle

The classifier is advisory, not authoritative. It accelerates and objectifies the scoping conversation — it does not replace human judgment or formal NPAC/Risk approval. Every classification can be overridden, but overrides require a documented reason. This design makes the tool defensible under audit.

Why Build This?

⚡ Speed

Reduce initial scoping effort from unstructured discussions to a structured first recommendation in minutes, giving teams a better starting point for governance conversations.

🎯 Objectivity

Reduce subjective variance in early classification. For similar inputs, the classifier is designed to produce stable recommendations, while borderline cases still require Risk & Compliance judgment.

📋 Audit Trail

Each classification creates a local audit record in this POC: what was submitted, what reasoning was returned, what tier was suggested, and whether it was overridden. Target production state: immutable centralized audit storage.

🔄 Consistency

As the team grows and more people submit use cases, classification logic stays consistent. The knowledge base is the single source of truth, not individual interpretation.

⛔ Prohibited Practice Screening

Art. 5 EU AI Act compliance built in. Social scoring, emotion inference at work, subliminal manipulation, and biometric categorisation are blocked before classification — not just flagged.

📄 Model Card Generation

One-click export of a 12-section model card pre-filled from classification data. Matches SEB’s model card repository template. Includes monitoring plan, legal basis, and governance requirements.

Architecture — Software 3.0 Approach

The Software 3.0 principle: “Forget the code exists, never forget the product exists.” The code is the least interesting part. The interesting parts are:

  1. The dataset — What structured knowledge does the model reason over? How is it maintained?
  2. The eval — How do you know the classifier is correct? What does the test suite look like?
  3. The UX — The user experience of providing input and understanding output matters more than the model.

In this v0.5 prototype, classification is executed by a deterministic browser-side rules engine using structured user input. Target production options may include governed model-assisted classification, but that is not implemented in this HTML.

Target-state architecture (proposed, not implemented in this HTML prototype)

Frontend
Knowledge Hub SPA with structured input form and result renderer. Current state: browser-only prototype. Target state: frontend submits to governed backend service.
Backend
Target state: GCP Cloud Run service (Python/Node.js) receiving form data, constructing prompt chain, calling Vertex AI, and returning structured output.
Model
Target default: approved Gemini variant selected from the current governance register. No fine-tuning. Classification logic lives in the prompt/rule design, not model weights.
Knowledge Base
Compiled from curated knowledge files: decision tree, tier definitions, ACAA mapping, 6-pillar checklist, worked examples, GDPR/NPA triggers. Versioned in Git.
Audit Log
Current state: local browser session log. Target state: immutable centralized store (for example BigQuery) with input, prompt/model version, output, reasoning, acceptance/override, and retention per SEB policy.
Eval Suite
25–30 worked examples with known-correct classifications. Automated regression on every prompt change. <90% accuracy on clear cases = change rejected.

The Classification Chain

Classification is a structured reasoning chain that walks through multiple assessment dimensions sequentially. Each step produces a discrete output that feeds the next.

Step 0
Art. 5 Prohibited Practice Screening — BLOCKING check. Screens for social scoring, emotion inference at work, subliminal manipulation, and biometric categorisation. If triggered, classification is blocked entirely — not escalated to a higher tier. Output: { prohibited: true, practice: "Social scoring" } or proceed.
Step 1
Decision Tree Walk — The 4-question tree (Q4→Q1, highest risk first). Walks through each question with the user’s input, applying upgrade rules for boundary cases (output type + sensitive data, continuous + client data). Output: { tier: 3, reasoning: "Output directly informs client risk decisions (Q3=Yes)" }
Step 2
ACAA Category Mapping — Cross-reference tier against ACAA categories and EU AI Act risk levels (Minimal, Limited, High, Unacceptable). Output: { acaa_category: 3, eu_ai_act: "high-risk" }
Step 3
6-Pillar Risk Assessment — Score each pillar (Valid & Reliable, Fair, Explainable, Transparent, Third-Party & Data, Resilient & Secure) as Low/Medium/High concern. Output type and frequency feed into explainability and resilience scoring. Output: pillar heatmap.
Step 4
GDPR Impact Screening — Based on data types selected: DPIA required? DPOR consultation needed? Personal data in processing scope? Output: GDPR requirements list.
Step 5
NPA Significance Assessment — Does this constitute a “significant change”? Triggers: Tier 3+, client-facing, FenX integration, third-party AI, new AI capability at Tier 2+. Change type (new vs modification) affects significance.
Step 6
Governance Requirements Summary — Compile full requirements: approvals needed, documentation level, governance bodies to engage, estimated timeline, specific next steps.
Step 7
Confidence Assessment — Evaluates boundary factors (indirect influence, sensitive data + full review, inconsistencies, ambiguous output type). Assigns High/Medium/Low confidence. Low confidence triggers “discuss with Risk & Compliance” recommendation.
Step 8
Monitoring Plan — Generates tier-appropriate monitoring requirements: what to monitor (accuracy drift, fairness, latency), cadence, alerting thresholds, and responsible owner. Frequency and data types determine monitoring intensity.
Step 9
GDPR Legal Basis — Auto-suggests the most likely lawful basis under Art. 6: Legal Obligation (AML/sanctions), Contract Performance (KYC onboarding), or Legitimate Interest (internal productivity). Owner must validate with DPOR.

Consistency Design

For similar inputs, the classifier is designed to produce stable recommendations because:

  • Classification logic is versioned in this file/repository
  • The current engine is deterministic rule logic (no runtime LLM call in this prototype)
  • Each classification records classification ID and timestamp for traceability
  • When the knowledge base updates, the prompt version increments and the eval suite re-runs

Adversarial Input Handling

The classifier does not naively accept user assertions. If a user states “this does not influence client decisions” but describes a system that processes CDD data and generates risk scores, the logic is designed to flag inconsistencies:

⚠️ Inconsistency Detected

“You stated this does not influence client decisions, but the system processes CDD data and generates risk scores. This appears inconsistent — the classification assumes client-decision influence is present. Override available with documented justification.”

Reading scope

Original classifier design documentation, retained for its scoping questions and provenance. Its legal/tier rules and prior implementation description are not the current advisory engine. The integrated tool uses unresolved inputs and working patterns only; current formal governance requires the applicable primary authority.

Model Documentation & Model Card

Every AI system at SEB requires documentation proportional to its risk tier. The classifier generates this documentation automatically from classification results. This aligns with EU AI Act Art. 11 (technical documentation) and SEB’s Model Risk Management Instruction.

How To Use

After classifying a use case in the “Classify Now” tab, click “📄 Generate Model Card” in the result panel. This produces a structured document pre-filled with classification data, governance requirements, and monitoring obligations. Export as JSON for NAMIS attachment or copy into SEB’s model card repository.

What Gets Generated

The Model Card follows SEB’s template (Model-cards repo ↗) enriched with governance data from the classification.

SectionSourceContent
1. IdentityFormUse case name, owner, sponsoring team, classification ID, date, prompt version used.
2. Intended UseFormDescription, output type, audience, scope. What the system is designed to do — and what it must NOT be used for (out-of-scope uses).
3. Risk ClassificationEngineTier assignment, ACAA category, EU AI Act risk level, confidence score, decision tree reasoning, any boundary warnings.
4. Data & PrivacyEngineData types processed, GDPR legal basis, DPIA requirement, DPOR consultation status, data retention policy, data minimisation approach.
5. Fairness & BiasEngineBias risk level (from 6-pillar “Fair” assessment), protected attributes at risk, recommended fairness metrics, 80% rule applicability.
6. ExplainabilityEngineExplainability requirement level, recommended approach (SHAP, Vertex Explainable AI, inherent interpretability), Art. 13 obligations.
7. Human OversightFormOversight model (full/spot/exception/minimal), Art. 14 mapping, escalation path, who reviews and how often.
8. Monitoring PlanEngineWhat to monitor (accuracy drift, fairness drift, latency, usage volume), review cadence, alerting thresholds, who is responsible.
9. Technical ArchitectureFormSystems involved, integration points, deployment platform, model/service used, frequency of execution.
10. Governance & ApprovalEngineRequired approvals, bodies to engage, NPA requirement, timeline estimate, regulatory deadlines.
11. Limitations & RisksEngineKnown limitations, failure modes, inconsistency warnings, what the system cannot do, degradation scenarios.
12. Version HistoryAutoClassification version, any overrides with justification, re-classification history from audit log.

Documentation Requirements by Tier

Tier 1 — Minimal

  • Usage guidelines document
  • Acceptable use boundaries
  • Line manager sign-off

Generated automatically from classification. No additional documentation required.

Tier 2 — Standard Model Card

  • Full model card (all 12 sections)
  • Data processing agreement
  • ACAA Portal submission
  • Quarterly review schedule

Model card auto-generated. Owner validates and submits to repo ↗.

Tier 3 — Full Technical Documentation

  • Everything in Tier 2, plus:
  • Bias assessment with fairness metrics
  • Explainability approach (SHAP/LIME)
  • DPIA documentation
  • NPA proposal for NAMIS
  • Monthly drift monitoring spec

Model card is the starting point. Owner must expand with bias assessment and XAI approach before Group NFR review.

Tier 4 — Comprehensive + Continuous

  • Everything in Tier 3, plus:
  • Red-team testing results
  • Kill-switch mechanism spec
  • Real-time monitoring dashboard
  • Incident response runbook
  • Board Risk Committee briefing

Auto-generated model card is a draft only. Executive sponsor and external reviewer must validate before production.

Input Requirements

The classification form captures the minimum information needed for accurate tier determination and model card generation. Every field maps to a specific compliance obligation:

FieldRequiredMaps ToWhy Risk Cares
Use Case NameYesIdentityTraceability in audit log and model inventory. Must match STEP/NAMIS naming.
Owner & TeamYesAccountabilityNamed human owner is mandatory per AI Risk Instruction. No ownerless AI.
DescriptionYesDecision TreeCore input for the 4-question tree. Quality determines classification accuracy.
Output TypeYesExplainabilityScores/recommendations require XAI. Text/extraction may not. Art. 13 mapping.
Data TypesYesGDPR + FairnessTriggers DPIA, identifies protected attributes, determines data classification level.
AudienceYesTransparencyClient-facing triggers Art. 52 obligations. Regulatory triggers audit trail requirements.
Client InfluenceYesTier BoundaryTHE critical Tier 2 vs 3 question. Subject to inconsistency detection.
Human OversightYesArt. 14Full vs minimal determines if AI Act human oversight requirements are met.
FrequencyYesMonitoringContinuous systems need drift detection. Ad-hoc may only need periodic review.
New vs ChangeYesNPANew Tier 2+ capabilities require NPA. Modifications need Change Risk Assessment.
SystemsNoThird-Party RiskExternal APIs = supply chain risk. FenX = NPA consideration. STEP registration required.
Users & ScopeNoProportionalityBank-wide deployment at Tier 3 gets more scrutiny than team-level.
ContextNoNuanceCatches regulatory constraints, precedents, and timeline pressures the fields miss.
DocumentsNoEvidenceProcessed in memory only. Supports richer classification. Never persisted.

Prohibited Practice Screening (Art. 5)

Before any tier classification, the engine screens for prohibited AI practices under EU AI Act Art. 5. If triggered, the classification is BLOCKED — not merely escalated to a higher tier.

Prohibited PracticeHow the Classifier Detects It
Social scoringDescription mentions scoring individuals based on social behaviour, personality traits, or trustworthiness metrics unrelated to a specific, lawful purpose.
Subliminal manipulationOutput type is “automated actions” + audience is “client-facing” + no human oversight + description suggests behaviour modification without awareness.
Emotion inference at workData includes call transcripts/video + description mentions sentiment scoring of employees or measuring emotional states in workplace context.
Biometric categorisation (sensitive attributes)Data includes biometric identifiers + description mentions inferring race, religion, sexual orientation, or political opinions.
Untargeted facial recognitionSystems include CCTV/camera feeds + description mentions building or querying face databases.
⚠️ Blocked Classification Example

“This use case appears to involve [prohibited practice]. Under EU AI Act Art. 5, this is prohibited regardless of risk tier. Penalties: up to €35M or 7% of global annual turnover. This classification cannot proceed. Contact: Legal (AI Act compliance) or AI Governance Forum.”

GDPR Legal Basis Requirements

When personal data is processed, GDPR Art. 6 requires a lawful basis. The classifier identifies which applies:

Legal BasisWhen It Applies in CLM Context
Legitimate Interest (Art. 6(1)(f))Internal efficiency improvements, colleague productivity tools, operational analytics where no client-decision influence exists.
Contract Performance (Art. 6(1)(b))KYC processes that are necessary to fulfil the client contract (onboarding, periodic review).
Legal Obligation (Art. 6(1)(c))AML screening, regulatory reporting, sanctions compliance — mandatory by law.
Consent (Art. 6(1)(a))Rarely appropriate for AI in banking. Cannot be freely given where power imbalance exists.

Contacts & Resources

NeedContact
Model cards & model inventorydaaa@seb.se (Team 42, Charlie Jeansson)
GDPR / DPOR consultationLocal DPOR (Data Protection Operative Responsible)
AI Risk Instruction questionsGroup Non-Financial Risk
GCP / Vertex AI platformcloudcoreteam@seb.se
NPA / NAMIS process1st line risk team + NPAC secretariat
Explainability (SHAP/XAI)DNA Advanced Analytics (Team 42)

What You Get Back

The classification result is rendered immediately on the page and simultaneously written to the immutable audit log.

Classification Output

Tier Badge

Visual tier assignment (1–4) with colour coding matching the Knowledge Hub design system.

Decision Tree Walkthrough

Shows which question triggered the classification, with the model’s reasoning at each step.

6-Pillar Heatmap

Visual indicator for each risk pillar (green/amber/red) showing where attention is needed.

Governance Checklist

Specific requirements for this tier: approvals, documentation, bodies to engage, estimated timeline.

GDPR & NPA Assessment

DPIA required? DPOR consultation? NPA significance triggers? Clear yes/no with rationale.

Recommended Next Steps

Who to contact, what to prepare, links to relevant Knowledge Hub sections and SEB portals.

The Audit Log — Non-Negotiable

Every classification writes an immutable record to BigQuery (SEB’s standard for AI logging, same pattern as KAICY). The record is never editable after creation.

FieldContent
classification_idUUID — unique identifier for this classification event
timestampISO-8601 — when the classification was performed
user_idAuthenticated SEB user who submitted the classification
input_structuredAll form fields as submitted (use case name, description, data types, systems, etc.)
model_usede.g., gemini-2.5-flash-001
prompt_versione.g., v1.3 — versioned prompt template from Git
classification_outputFull structured result: tier, ACAA category, pillar scores, GDPR/NPA assessment, governance requirements
full_reasoningComplete chain-of-thought from the model — raw audit trail of the reasoning process
user_acceptedBoolean — did the user accept the classification?
user_override_tierIf overridden, to which tier? (null if accepted)
user_override_reasonMandatory free-text justification if overridden
Auditor Access

Auditors receive read-only BigQuery access to the classification log. They can query: all classifications for a given use case, all overrides, all Tier 3+ classifications, all classifications by a specific user, and the exact reasoning chain for any individual classification. The log answers: “Why was case X classified as Tier Y?” with full traceability.

Override Workflow

The classifier is advisory. If a user disagrees with the classification:

  1. Click “Override Classification”
  2. Select the tier they believe is correct
  3. Provide a mandatory written justification explaining why
  4. Both the original classification and the override are logged — nothing is erased

Overrides are visible in the audit log and can be reviewed by Risk & Compliance. A pattern of overrides in one direction may indicate the prompt needs updating.

Reading scope

Original classifier design documentation, retained for its scoping questions and provenance. Its legal/tier rules and prior implementation description are not the current advisory engine. The integrated tool uses unresolved inputs and working patterns only; current formal governance requires the applicable primary authority.

Build Strategy — Phased Delivery

Following the Software 3.0 principle: ship the simplest thing that produces correct classifications, then add features when evidence demands them.

Phase 1 — Core Classification (MVP)

ComponentImplementationComplexity
Input formHTML/JS in Knowledge Hub SPA. Structured fields as defined in Documentation & Output tab.Low
BackendGCP Cloud Run (Python). Receives POST, constructs prompt, calls Vertex AI, returns JSON.Medium
Prompt chainSystem prompt with full classification logic. 6-step reasoning chain. Temperature 0.Medium-High
Audit logBigQuery table. Write on every classification. Immutable.Low
Result rendererClient-side JS renders tier badge, reasoning, requirements.Low
Eval suite25–30 worked examples. Automated test on prompt changes.Medium

Phase 2 — Enhancement

  • Document upload — Gemini multimodal input for PDF/image context extraction (processed in memory, not persisted)
  • PDF export — “Download as PDF” for attaching to NAMIS proposals
  • Override analytics — Dashboard showing override patterns to inform prompt improvement
  • Feedback loop — When NPAC assigns a different tier than the classifier predicted, capture as training data for the eval set

Phase 3 — Integration & Compliance Documentation

  • NAMIS pre-population — Export classification directly to NAMIS proposal fields
  • Backlog linkage — Classification triggers portfolio item creation with pre-filled governance requirements
  • Trend analysis — Dashboard showing classification distribution over time, emerging patterns, governance bottlenecks
  • R&C documentation generator — Based on the classification result, automatically produce a draft compliance package containing:
    • NPAC submission narrative (purpose, scope, risk justification, tier rationale)
    • Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) template pre-filled with data types, lawful basis, retention, and processing scope from the classifier inputs
    • Legitimate Interest Assessment (LIA) where Art. 6(1)(f) is the claimed basis
    • Model Risk Management checklist (validation cadence, drift triggers, human oversight design)
    • EU AI Act conformity self-assessment (Annex III mapping, risk category justification, Article 9 obligations)
    • Art. 5 prohibited practices exclusion statement
    • STEP/DSD integration requirements summary (which systems, which data flows, what approvals needed)
    • Human oversight specification (who reviews, escalation path, override authority, cognitive load limits)
  • Committee-ready output — One-click export of the full documentation package as structured PDF, formatted for NPAC/governance committee review. Includes classification rationale, all supporting assessments, and a “conditions to satisfy before production” section modelled on SensAIa’s 8-condition approval pattern.
Design Principle

The classifier does not approve anything — it produces a first draft that saves 60–80% of the documentation effort. Every output is explicitly marked “DRAFT — requires human review and sign-off by designated Risk & Compliance function.” The goal: reduce time from idea to committee submission, not bypass the committee.

The Knowledge Base as Moat

The LLM is commodity (Gemini). The value is in the structured knowledge it reasons over:

  • The 4-question decision tree (Section 2)
  • The ACAA mapping table (Section 2)
  • The 6-pillar AI Risk Instruction (Section 5)
  • GDPR 7 principles with CLM implications (Section 5)
  • NPA significance triggers (Section 5)
  • The worked examples from Section 2
  • Governance requirements per tier (Section 2)

This knowledge comes from the Knowledge Agent canonical files. The prompt template is a compiled derivative — when the source knowledge updates, the prompt is regenerated and re-evaluated. Single source of truth, no drift.

Self-Classification

First Test Case

The classifier itself must pass through its own classification. Expected result: Tier 1 — internal productivity tool, no client data, no client-decision influence, human reviews every output. If it classifies itself as anything higher, the logic has a bug.

What Could Go Wrong — And How We Prevent It

Applying inversion thinking: before celebrating the upside, map the failure modes and design them out.

RiskFailure ModeMitigation
False precision Model outputs “Tier 2” with apparent confidence on an ambiguous case. Users treat it as authoritative. Explicit uncertainty surfacing: “This could be Tier 2 or 3 depending on [specific factor]. Discuss with Risk.” The tool is framed as advisory everywhere.
Gaming Users learn to phrase descriptions to get a lower tier. Inconsistency detection in the prompt chain. Cross-reference data types against claimed decision-influence. Flag contradictions.
Staleness Knowledge base drifts as regulations change (EU AI Act enforcement, NPA reform). Prompt versioning. Knowledge Agent maintains canonical source. Eval suite re-runs on every change. Staleness scan on policy dates.
Scope creep to authoritative People start treating classifier output as “approved” rather than “recommended.” Design constraint: output always states “This is an advisory classification. Formal approval requires [specific body].” Override button always visible.
Hallucination Model invents governance requirements or misapplies the decision tree. Temperature 0. Structured output format (JSON schema). Eval suite catches regression. Chain-of-thought logged for audit review.
Data leakage Uploaded documents containing client PII processed and stored. Documents processed in memory only. No persistence. Use case descriptions should never contain client-identifiable data (enforced via input guidelines).
The tool classifying itself wrong If the classifier is deemed Tier 2+ it requires its own governance overhead before shipping. Self-classification as first eval case. Expected: Tier 1 (no client data, no decision influence, human reviews output). Design ensures this remains true.

Build Priorities

1. Eval Set First

Before writing any UI code, build 25+ worked examples with expert-verified classifications. If the prompt can’t get these right, nothing else matters. The eval set is the product.

2. Prompt > Architecture

Spend 80% of effort on prompt engineering, 20% on infrastructure. A perfect Cloud Run setup with a mediocre prompt produces mediocre classifications. A brilliant prompt on a minimal backend produces excellent ones.

3. Log Everything

Every single classification, every input, every output, every override. This is your training data for improvement. This is your audit defence. This is your product analytics.

4. Ship, Then Improve

v1 is a textarea, structured fields, a “Classify” button, and a result display. No file upload, no PDF export, no NAMIS integration. Get the core classification right. Add features when you have evidence they’re needed.

Build vs. Buy

This is firmly build. No vendor sells a “classify your AI use case against your internal governance model” tool. The classification logic is entirely SEB-specific — the tier definitions, ACAA mapping, 6-pillar instruction, NPA triggers. This is the “specific knowledge inside SEB that creates AI advantages no external consultant can replicate.”

Technical Stack (All SEB-Approved)

ComponentTechnologyPrecedent
FrontendHTML/JS (extends Knowledge Hub SPA)Existing page architecture
BackendGCP Cloud Run (Python or Node.js)KAICY uses same pattern
ModelGemini 2.5 Flash via Vertex AIApproved model list
Audit logBigQueryKAICY logging pattern
AuthSEB SSO (same as NAMIS)Standard SEB auth
Prompt storageSEB GitHub Enterprise (versioned)Builder Council patterns repo
The Honest Assessment

This is a high-leverage, low-risk build if scoped correctly. The ingredients exist: classification logic already written (decision tree, ACAA mapping, tier requirements), knowledge base curated, infrastructure approved (GCP, Gemini, BigQuery, Cloud Run), audit pattern exists (KAICY). The highest-risk component is the prompt chain — getting classification right for boundary cases. Everything else is plumbing.

Comprehensive analysis of six banking megatrends: money, experience, work & talent, technology, risk & regulation, competition. Includes survey data from banking executives, corporate clients, and retail customers.		 Industry Report accenture.com ↗
2 Deloitte — Agentic AI in Client Lifecycle Management at SEB (March 2026)
KYC trends, benchmarks (90→30 min review, 14→5 day onboarding, 49%→<5% revisit rate), agent architecture (Orchestrator → Functional → Helper → Utility), SoW & CDD agent breakdowns, human-in-the-loop requirements.		 Consulting Engagement Internal — SEB SharePoint
3 EU AI Act — Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
Risk-based AI classification framework. General provisions Dec 2025, high-risk obligations now in force as of 2 Aug 2026. Relevant provisions: Articles 6-7 (classification), Article 9 (risk management), Article 14 (human oversight), Article 52 (transparency).		 Regulation EUR-Lex ↗
4 SEB AI Governance, Risk & Compliance
ACAA classification (mirrors EU AI Act risk tiers), Model Risk Management framework (tiered decision tree, approved by Group Non-Financial Risk), AI Ethics Policy (4 principles, 7 requirements), bias/fairness (80% rule), explainability (SHAP, Vertex Explainable AI), governance bodies (Group Risk Committee, NPAC, AI Governance Forum, DPOR, Data & Analytics).		 Internal Policy Internal — SEB Intranet / Policy Portal
5 SEB AI Projects and Tools
SensAIa (PWM&FO call transcription, Python/FastAPI/React, GCP Cloud Run, NPAC-approved), Axiom (email extraction), AI Showroom, TestPilotX/PerfPilotX, SEBx Agentic AI (NVIDIA, ADK, Global Market Outlook), Privacy-Preserving AI with KTH, AIDA chatbot.		 Internal Documentation Internal — SEB Developer Garden / SharePoint
6 SEB GCP Approved AI Models (governance register)
Google first-party only, according to the active internal governance register. Model approvals and pricing can change; always verify against the current register before design or deployment decisions.		 Internal Policy Internal — SEB Cloud Portal
7 SEB AI Resource Directory
Developer Garden, intranet policies, SharePoint communities, GitHub repos, SEBx blog, key contacts (daaa@seb.se, cloudcoreteam@seb.se), AI Community channels.		 Internal Directory Internal — SEB Intranet
8 JPMorganChase — 2025 Annual Letter to Shareholders (Jamie Dimon)
$185.6B revenue, 20% ROTCE. AI strategy, Security & Resiliency Initiative, workforce investment philosophy, geopolitical risk assessment, technology modernisation perspective.		 Public Letter jpmorganchase.com ↗
9 McKinsey — Paving the Road for AI Agents (April 2026)
Interview with Factory CEO Matan Grinberg. Infrastructure readiness ("paving roads"), tacit knowledge as agent enemy, delegation-first engineering, phased adoption measurement. Sovereign AI and Rewired 2.0 research on operating model change.		 Interview / Research mckinsey.com ↗
10 BCG — Enterprise as Code: An Operating Model for the AI Era (December 2025)
Codifying operations as structured logic for AI readiness. Platform imperative, resilience design, readiness-determines-results thesis. "Design Your Company for AI" (2026) extends to organisational redesign.		 Research Article bcg.com ↗
11 Bain — AI's Next Operating Model (April 2026)
Episodic vs. long-running agents. Institutional memory, persistence governance, knowledge portability. Financial services identified as early proving ground. "Governance, Trust and the Data Foundation" and "From Roadmap to Reality" companion pieces.		 Research Brief bain.com ↗
12 Fenergo — CLM Platform, Agentic AI & FinCrime OS (2025-2026)
FenX composable CLM platform, agentic AI agents for KYC/AML, FinCrime Operating System vision. Vendor roadmap directly relevant to SEB's FenX deployment and custom agent boundary decisions.		 Vendor Documentation fenergo.com ↗
13 SEB NPA & Change Risk Management (April 2026)
NPA 3-step process, NAMIS system, Change Risk Management framework reform (autumn 2026 rollout). 1st-line risk ownership, streamlined NPA for significant changes only. Relevance to KAICY and CLM AI initiatives.		 Internal Policy Internal — SEB Intranet
14 Original SEB–Bain estimate of potential KYC outreach effort reduction: about 31%. This is a planning estimate, not an established measured outcome. Baseline, population, assumptions and exact model date are not supplied. Internal Documentation Internal — CLM Development SharePoint
15 MCP & Agentic AI Architecture (April 2026)
Model Context Protocol specification, agent anatomy (reasoning engine, tools, memory, instructions), orchestration patterns (hierarchical, molecules, convoys), multi-agent architectures, CLM MCP server design.		 Technical Reference modelcontextprotocol.io ↗
16 SEB Instruction for Model Risk Management
Model lifecycle (10 phases: origination → decommission), tiering decision tree (Q1–Q5), Tier 1 = HIGH risk (CRO validates annually), Tier 2 = MODERATE (owner validates biennially), Tier 3 = LOW (owner validates triennially). Roles: model owner, model developer, model validator, CRO Function.		 Internal Policy (30 pages) Internal — SEB Corpintra
17 SEB Guideline for Validation of Tier 2 and Tier 3 Models
7-section validation template: Background, Scope & Methodology, Model Governance, Model Design & Data, Implementation, Performance, Overall Assessment (traffic-light rating).		 Internal Guideline (9 pages) Internal — SEB Corpintra
18 SensAIa Model Validation v1
Completed Tier 2 validation for PWM&FO call transcription AI. Demonstrates filled template, assessment methodology, and CRO Function review process. Direct precedent for KAICY.		 Internal Document (9 pages) Internal — PWM&FO Data Office
19 SensAIa NPAC Proposal & Approval (August 2024)
NPA submitted and conditionally approved 27 Aug 2024. 8 conditions across 5 areas. PWM&FO NPAC committee. NAMIS ID 018543. Demonstrates “approved with conditions” pattern.		 Internal Document Internal — NAMIS / PWM&FO
20 SEB ACAA Classification Template v1.0
4-section structure: Pre-assessment, Role of AI in the System, Risk Classification, Sign-off. Mandatory for all AI systems since 12 Dec 2025.		 Internal Template (12 pages) Internal — SEB SharePoint (Data & Analytics)
21 SEB Way-to-Engage with AI (Division Operating Model)
Official guidance: “Start in M365 Copilot → Scale in Copilot Studio → Engineer in Vertex AI.” Defines Hub–Division contract for AI platform services.		 Internal Guidance Internal — SEB SharePoint (Data & Analytics)
22 SEB CEO Letter to Shareholders 2025
Strategic priorities, technology investment philosophy, operational resilience focus. Context for AI investment narrative.		 Public Letter Internal — SEB Investor Relations
23 SEB AI & Automation Sub-Strategy v1.0 (SEB Group Technology — Strategy & Change, 8 May 2026)
Reusable secure foundations + decentralised delivery; machine-readable institutional knowledge as strategic AI infrastructure; data products as a foundational Horizon 1 capability; AI across design, coding, testing, review and architecture; use AI from inception; Refactor→Rearchitect→Reinvent 80/15/5 focus; integrate AI into normal portfolio governance rather than a standalone AI backlog.		 Internal Strategy Internal — SEB Group Technology
24 Freda — Platform, Discover, Orchestrate, Deploy & Agents (public pages)
Public description of a four-layer legal-AI architecture (Regulatory Engine, Company Graph, Operating Plane, Agentic Execution) used here only as logical-architecture inspiration for CLM. Not proof of Freda’s internal implementation at any scale.		 Public Vendor Material freda.com ↗
25 ACCA / Accounting and Business — “Firms keep AI on tight leash” (2026)
Interviews with senior people across 11 professional-services firms describing a 20-60-20 human/AI/human working pattern. Source for the 20/60/20 heuristic — treated as emerging practice, not a standard.		 Industry Article Public — ACCA / Accounting and Business
26 Robert Menetray — “I Found Out AI Steals 60% of My Work” (2026)
Documents a 20% human planning / 60% AI execution / 20% human review development workflow, explicitly calling the percentages rough and context-specific.		 Practitioner Article Public
27 CLM AI Operating Model Knowledge v1.0 (internal AI-assisted synthesis, 9 Oct 2026)
Working knowledge synthesis connecting the sub-strategy, this Hub, and the AMLR governing spec into the four-layer CLM Intelligence Model (Section 11). Explicitly labelled a working synthesis, not an approved SEB architecture — cited here for traceability per its own evidence rule.		 AI-Assisted Synthesis Internal — CLM Development

Additional Context Sources

  • GDPR — Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — EUR-Lex ↗
  • SEB Instruction for Artificial Intelligence Risks — 6-pillar framework (Valid & Reliable, Fair, Explainable, Transparent, Third-Party & Data, Resilient & Secure) — Risk Instructions (Intranet) ↗
  • SEB Model Risk Management Instruction — tiering decision tree, model cards, model versioning — Developer Garden ↗
  • European Banking Authority — Supervisory Priorities 2025-27 — operational risk, geopolitical resilience
  • Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) — open-source agent framework on GCP — ADK Docs ↗
  • EU Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI — EC Digital Strategy ↗
  • Accenture Global Risk Study 2024-25 — risk function maturity benchmarks (cited within Ref 1)
  • Accenture Banking IT Executives Survey 2025 — AI adoption expectations by function (cited within Ref 1)
  • Accenture Pulse of Change Survey 2025 — CTO readiness assessment (cited within Ref 1)
  • UNESCO AI Ethics Recommendation — UNESCO ↗
Source Integrity

All industry data points are from published or verifiable sources. All SEB-specific information is from official internal documentation. Where benchmarks are cited (e.g., Deloitte CLM figures), they represent observed ranges from controlled pilots, not guaranteed outcomes. Internal SEB sources require appropriate access credentials.
